Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verses 1–2:

Surat (al-Shura)

It is also called Surat (Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf, and 'Ayn Sin Qaf). It was revealed, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, in Makkah. Many scholars stated its Meccan character without exception. In al-Bahr it is said: it is Meccan except for four verses, from His saying, ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except affection among kin﴾ to the end of the four verses. Muqatil said: among it is a Medinan verse, His saying, ﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants﴾ up to ﴿the breasts﴾. Some excepted His saying, ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated"﴾ and so on. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: What supports this is what al-Tabarani and al-Hakim narrated regarding its occasion of revelation, that it was revealed concerning the Ansar. And His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿Had Allah expanded the provision﴾ and so on, for it was revealed concerning the People of the Suffah, may Allah be pleased with them. He also excepted ﴿And those who, when wrong is inflicted upon them﴾ up to His saying, ﴿any way [of blame]﴾, related by Ibn al-Furs. What indicates the exception of other than these in some narrations will come, Allah willing. It is also permissible that the general statement is based on what is most prevalent. The number of its verses is fifty-three in the Kufan count and fifty in other counts. The difference lies in Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf and His saying, ﴿like mountains﴾, as detailed by al-Dani and others. The connection of its beginning to the end of the surah before it is that each includes mention of the Qur'an, the repelling of the disbelievers' slander against it, and consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ).

"In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ha Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn Sin Qaf﴾. Perhaps these two are names of the surah, and two verses are supported after them. The separation between them in writing, and the fact that its naming is (Ayn Sin Qaf) without mention of (Ha Mim), [support this]. It is also said: they are one name and one verse, and its proper form is to be written joined, as in (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad), but it was separated so that the opening of the surah would be in the pattern of the openings of its siblings, where each was written separately. According to the first view, they are two predicates of an omitted subject. It is said: (Ha Mim) is the subject and (Ayn Sin Qaf) its predicate; according to the second view, the whole is one predicate. It is also said: (Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf) is an indication of the destruction of two cities built on a river from the rivers of the East, a river running between them, in which every stubborn tyrant gathers. Allah sends upon one of them fire at night, so it becomes black and dark, burned as if it had never been in its place, and He sinks the other in the next night. This was narrated from Hudhayfah. It is also said: Ha Mim is one of the names of Allah, 'Ayn indicates the punishment of the day of Badr, Sin indicates His saying, ﴿And those who wronged will know what return they will be returned to﴾, and Qaf indicates a calamity from the sky that strikes people. This was narrated with a weak chain from Abu Dharr. What most prevails in opinion is that none of the two narrations is established.

In al-Bahr, the commentators mentioned regarding (Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf) disordered sayings, none of which is fit, and we have turned away from mentioning them. What we mentioned first has been chosen by more than one scholar. Among them are those who chose that they are disjoined letters brought for awakening. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read (Ha Mim Sin Qaf) without the 'Ayn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 3:

The words of the Exalted, ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, are a new independent statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to confirm that the content of this surah agrees with what is found in the multiplicity of revealed books sent to all the earlier messengers in calling to monotheism (tawhid) and guiding to the truth. Or [it is brought to confirm] that its revelation, after highlighting its name and drawing attention to the greatness of its status, [is as described]. The kaf (ك) is the object (maf'ul) of (yuhi) according to the first view, meaning: He reveals [something] like what is in this surah of meanings. Or, according to the second view, it is an adjective (na't) of an emphatic verbal noun (masdar muakkad), meaning: He reveals a revelation like its revelation to you and to the messengers, that is, through the angel. In both views it is a noun, as is the position of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, a grammarian). If you wish, consider it a particle (harf), and treat the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) as an object, or as attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective.

As for the view of the Allamah (al-Allamah) in his second opinion in al-Talwih, that the particle of Allah (jar Allah) does not permit beginning with a verb, and that a subject (mubtada', the nominal subject) must be assumed in every case where the verb occurs at the beginning, this is not an accepted statement. They have disputed it at length, to the point that it is said that no justification for it has become apparent.

Abu al-Baqa (Abu al-Baqa', the grammarian) permitted ﴿kadhalika﴾ to be a subject (mubtada'), with (yuhi) as its predicate (khabar), and the returning pronoun (al-a'id) omitted, meaning: "Something like that, He reveals it to you," and so on. The omission of "mithl" (like) is common in eloquent usage. Yes, this view goes against the apparent sense. The demonstrative reference, as we have indicated, is either to what is in the surah or to its revelation. The indication of distance (al-dalalah 'ala al-bu'd) is because of the distance of the status of the thing referred to in excellence. The present tense form (sighat al-mudari') is used to narrate a past state, to indicate its continuance across past times, and that the revelation of the like of it is the habit of the Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that it is in the sense of prevalence (al-taghallub), for the revelation to those who passed away has passed, and to him, upon whom be prayer and peace, some of it is past and some is future. It has also been permitted that it be in its literal sense, with an implied verb to which "ila alladhina" (to those who) is attached, meaning: "and it was revealed to those who..." This, as you see, is [weak]. In making the content of the surah, or its revelation, the thing compared (mushabbah bihi) there is an exaltation of it that is not hidden.

Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, Ayyash, and Mahbub, both of them from Abu Amr, read (yuha) in the passive voice, on the basis that ﴿kadhalika﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and (yuha) is its predicate (khabar), whose subject is its pronoun; or it is a verbal noun (masdar), and (yuha) is attributed to (ilayka). ﴿Allah﴾ is raised according to al-Sakkaki as the agent (fa'il) of (yuha), which occurs in answer to the question "Who reveals?" similar to what they have established in the words of the Exalted, ﴿In it, men glorify Him in the mornings and evenings﴾ with the reading (yusabbahu) in the passive voice, and in the words of the poet:

"Let Yazid weep, one who is a supplicant in a dispute, and one bewildered by what the calamities cast down."

Al-Zamakhshari said: its raising is by what (yuha) indicates, as if a speaker had said, "Who is the one who reveals?" and it was said, "Allah." The reason it was assessed this way, according to what the author of al-Kashshaf said, is to show that revelation is an accepted and known matter, and the purpose of the statement is only to establish that it is among His attributes, that revelation belongs to Him, not to establish that He is a revealer. He did not accept the view that there is no difference between this and the words of the Exalted, ﴿In it, men glorify Him in the mornings and evenings﴾, but rather he required a difference, because the present verb there is not in its literal sense, and it was not used to indicate continuity, and they have something to say about it.

﴿Al-'Aziz al-Hakim﴾ (the Almighty, the All-Wise) are two adjectives (sifatan) of Him, the Exalted, according to the two shaykhs (al-shaykhan). Abu Hayyan permitted that the glorious name (al-ism al-jalil) be a subject (mubtada'), and what follows it be its predicate (khabar). It has been said: ﴿Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ through to the end of the surah stands in place of the agent (fa'il) of (yuhi), meaning: "these words."

Abu Haywa and al-A'sha, from Abu Bakr, and Aban read (nuhi) with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah). Thus ﴿Allah﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar), or ﴿al-'Aziz al-Hakim﴾ are two adjectives.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ is a *khabar* (predicate) for Him (the subject). According to the aforementioned possibilities, it is an *istinaf* (resumptive, new sentence) that establishes His might and wisdom, exalted is He and glorified.

The heavens almost split apart (﴿تَكادُ السَّماواتُ﴾). It is also read as (yakādu) with the letter ya, ﴿yatafaṭṭarna﴾ meaning they split, crack open, from the greatness of God, exalted is He, and His majesty, may His glory be exalted. This was narrated from Qatadah. A group of scholars, including al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The heavens almost split (yatafaṭṭarna) from the weight." It was also said: it is from the people's calling a partner and a child to Him, glorified is He, as in Surah Maryam. This is supported by His words, exalted is He, after this: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾. So the mention of ﴿the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ after this is because they deserved, by this statement, the descent of punishment upon them, but it was turned away from them due to the precedence of His mercy, mighty and majestic is He. The verse, according to this view, is introduced for declaring Him free of imperfection after affirming His sovereignty and greatness. The first view is preferable in this context, because the discourse is driven toward explaining His greatness and exaltedness, may His majesty be exalted, and this is supported by the absence of a conjunction (ʿāṭif). Next to it is what was narrated from al-Habr (the scholar, i.e., Ibn Abbas). Although the verse includes this meaning, the purpose for which the discourse is driven, its indication of this meaning according to the first view is more evident.

The two Basrans and Abu Bakr read (yanfaṭirna) with the letter nūn. The first is more eloquent, because the verb of intensification (tafʿīl) and the reflexive (tafaʿʿul) form, which are designed for emphasis, are in contrast to the second, since it is an inflected reflexive (infiʿāl) corresponding to the triliteral. Yunus narrated from Abu Amr that he read (tatafaṭṭarna) with two letters tā' and a final nūn, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, and (tanfaṭirna) with one tā' and a nūn, according to what is in al-Bahr from Ibn Khalawayh. This, according to both narrations, is anomalous with respect to analogy and usage, because the Arabs do not combine two feminine markers, so they do not say al-nisāʾu tuqimna (the women establish) nor al-wālidātu turḍiʿna (the mothers nurse). The reason for it is the emphasis of the feminine, like the emphasis of address in ʾa-ra-aytaka (have you seen yourself), and similar to it is what Abu ʿUmar al-Zahid narrated in the Nawādir of Ibn al-Aʿrabi: al-ibilu tatashammamna (the camels sniff).

﴿مِن فَوْقِهِنَّ﴾ (from above them) means that the splitting begins from their upper side. Specifying it, according to the first view, as the cause of the splitting, is because the greatest signs and those most indicative of greatness and majesty, such as the Throne, the Footstool, and the angels, are from that direction, and for this reason it is the direction of supplication. According to the third view, it indicates that splitting from below them is by a stronger argument, because that monstrous word, when it occurred on the earth, affected them from above, so that it affecting them from below is more fitting. Likewise according to the second view, because the custom is that the roof of a house, for example, splits from below when a weight is placed upon it. It was said that the pronoun refers to the earth, meaning its kind, so it includes the seven (earths), and for this reason the pronoun is plural, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān al-Akhfash said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and what is meant is from above the sects and the deviant groups. In this consideration the pronoun is feminine. In this there is an indication that the splitting is because of the sayings of those groups, and in this there is what there is.

﴿والمَلائِكَةُ يُسَبِّحُونَ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (And the angels glorify with the praise of their Lord) means they declare Him free, glorified is He, from what is not befitting to Him, may His majesty be exalted, while being joined with His praise, mighty and majestic is He. It was also said: they pray. The apparent meaning regarding the angels is generality. Muqatil said: what is meant by them is the bearers of the Throne. ﴿ويَسْتَغْفِرُونَ لِمَن في الأرْضِ﴾ (And they seek forgiveness for those on the earth) by striving in what would bring about their forgiveness, such as intercession, inspiration, and arranging the affairs that bring one closer to obedience, such as helping in some matters of livelihood, repelling obstacles, and seeking the delay of punishment, hoping for the faith of the disbeliever and the repentance of the sinner. This includes both the believer and the disbeliever. Indeed, if istighfār (seeking forgiveness) is explained as striving in what repels an expected defect, it would include animals and even inanimate things. This, in what has been mentioned, is a mursal (unrestricted) metonymy (majāz mursal) and a metaphor (istiʿāra).

Al-Suddi and Qatadah said: what is meant by "those on the earth" is the believers, due to His words in another verse: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾. In this case, istighfār is taken in its literal sense. It was also said: it means intercession.

﴿ألا إنَّ اللَّهَ هو الغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ (Indeed, God is the Forgiving, the Merciful). For there is no created being except that it has a great share of His mercy, exalted is He, and indeed He, glorified is He, is the Possessor of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing. In this there is an indication of the acceptance of the angels' seeking forgiveness, peace be upon them, and that He, glorified is He, gives them more than what they asked for in forgiveness, out of mercy. The verse, on the view that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the heavens almost split apart﴾ is for explaining His greatness, may His majesty be exalted, is confirming of what that indicated and emphasizing, because the angels' glorification and declaring Him free is due to the increase of His greatness, blessed and exalted is He, and the magnitude of His majesty, may He be exalted and high. The seeking of forgiveness for others is out of fear for them from the force of His dominion, mighty and majestic is He. The concluding statement, with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God...﴾ and so on,

is clear according to this view. And on the view that the splitting of the heavens is due to the attribution of a child and a partner, it is an explanation of the perfection of His holiness, exalted is He, above what is attributed to Him, mighty and majestic is He. Then their glorification is of what the disbelievers say, and their seeking forgiveness is for the believers who disassociated themselves from what was issued by these. The concluding statement is for indicating the reason for not hastening the punishment despite their deserving it, and it generalized some of those for whom forgiveness is sought and included the angels' seeking forgiveness within the reason for not hastening the punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 6:

﴿And those who take protectors other than Him﴾ — partners and equals — ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾ — Vigilant over their states and their deeds, so He will recompense them for them. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ — i.e., not one entrusted with them, nor one to whom their affair has been committed; rather, your duty is only conveyance (al-balagh) and warning (al-indhar). Here wakil is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, whether from the derived form (al-mazid) or from the triliteral root (al-thulathi). What is in this verse of conciliation (al-muwada'ah), according to what is in al-Bahr, is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 7:

﴿And thus did We reveal to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾. "Thus" (dhalika) is a reference to the verbal noun (masdar) of "We revealed" (awhayna). The position (mahall) of the kaf, according to the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, a grammarian) that it occurs as a noun, is accusative in the sense of a verbal noun (ʿala al-masdariyya). "An Arabic Qur'an" (Qur'anan) is the direct object of "We revealed." That is: and like that wondrous, clear revelation that conveys meaning, We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an with no ambiguity in it, neither for you nor for your people. It has also been said: it refers to what preceded, namely ﴿Allah is Guardian over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾. Then the kaf is the direct object of "We revealed," and "an Arabic Qur'an" is a circumstantial state (hal) of the object: that is, We revealed it to you, and it is an Arabic Qur'an. Its accusative case has also been permitted as an expression of praise (madh) or as an apposition (badal) to "thus."

It has been said that it is better that it refer to the meaning of the preceding verse, that He, exalted is He, is the Guardian over them, and that he, upon whom be prayers and peace, is only a warner, because this has greater benefit and more comprehensive returns. There must necessarily be a metaphorical usage (tajawwuz) in "an Arabic Qur'an," since it is not correct to say "We revealed that meaning, and it is an Arabic Qur'an," because Qur'anic-ness and Arabic-ness are attributes of the wording (lafz), not the meaning. But the matter is easy because of its closeness to the literal sense, owing to the strong connection between wording and meaning, such that each of them may be described by what is described of the other, along with the eloquence of metaphor.

﴿That you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾: that is, the people of the Mother of Cities, by way of metonymy in the relation (tajawwuz fi al-nisba), or by supplying an omitted noun (taqdir al-mudaf). The Mother of Cities is Makkah. It was so named, as al-Raghib said, because it is reported that the world was spread out from beneath it, so it is like the root (asl) for it, and "mother" (umm) is said of anything that is the root of something. It may also be said that it is the mother of the towns around it, because it came into being before them, not the mother of all the cities of the world. It may also be said of a town: it is the mother of towns, considering the need of the people of the towns for it.

﴿And those around it﴾: of the Arabs, according to the view of many. The ones mentioned were singled out for mention because the surah is Meccan and they are closest to him, upon whom be prayers and peace, and he was the first to warn them. Or it is to remove what might be imagined, that the people of Makkah and those around it hoped for his intercession, upon whom be prayers and peace, even if they did not believe, on account of kinship, residence and neighborhood; so he singled them out for warning to remove that vain hope. It has also been said: "those around it" refers to all the people of the earth, and al-Baghawi chose this, and likewise al-Qushayri, who said: because the Ka'bah is the navel of the earth and the world surrounds what is in it, namely Makkah. But this, in my view, hardly holds with their statement that its breadth is complete and its length is ... and that the inhabited part is more in the northern direction than in the southern.

﴿And that you may warn of the Day of Assembly﴾: that is, the Day of Resurrection, because creatures are gathered in it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾. It has also been said: spirits and bodies are gathered in it; and it has been said: deeds and doers.

The verb "to warn" (indhar) takes two objects, and the second may sometimes be introduced by a preposition (bi). Here the second object of the first is omitted, namely ﴿the Day of Assembly﴾, and what is meant by it is His punishment; and the first object of the second, namely ﴿the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾, is omitted. Thus what is affirmed in the second is omitted from the first, and what is affirmed in the first is omitted from the second, and this is from what is called (ihtibak). Jar Allah said: the first is general in warning about the affairs of this world and the Hereafter; then it was specified by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that you may warn of the Day of Assembly﴾, the Day of Resurrection, as an increase in warning and a clarification of the greatness of its terrors, because singling it out by mention indicates this; and likewise placing the warning upon it a second time.

The apparent view regarding this is that the omission of the second object from the first is for the sake of generality, although omitting the first from the second is also for that reason: "and that you may warn everyone on the Day of Assembly." It has been said: "the Day of Assembly" is an adverbial of time, so both objects are omitted. It is also read (liyundhira) with the third-person yā' prefix, with the subject being the pronoun of the Qur'an, since the shift of person (iltifat) is not fitting here.

﴿There is no doubt in it﴾: an interjected statement at the end of the speech, confirming what precedes it. It may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Day of Assembly," or a new sentence (istinaf).

﴿A party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾: that is, after their gathering at the place of standing, for they are gathered there first, then separated after the reckoning. "A party" (fariq) is the subject (mubtada'), "in the Garden" is its description, and the predicate is omitted; likewise "a party in the Blaze," meaning: among them is a party who is in the Garden and among them a party who is in the Fire. The pronoun in "among them" refers to those gathered, indicated by the word "gathering." The subject-predicate sentence is a resumed statement answering an implied question: "then how will their condition be?" Or it is a circumstantial clause, and there is no awkwardness in it; the requirement of a waw in it is not accepted. It has been permitted that "fariq" be the agent of an implied adverbial, though this is weak; and that it be the subject with the implied adverbial in the position of its description, and "in the Garden" its predicate, i.e., a party which is among them, settled in the Garden. It may also be the subject whose predicate is what follows, without any implied adverbial being a description. The beginning with an indefinite noun is permissible because it is within a context of detail and division, as in the verse:

*So one garment I have worn, and another I trail.*

It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "those gathered are a party," etc.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (fariqan wa fariqan) with both in the accusative. It has been said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) of an implied verb, i.e., they separated, that is, those gathered as a party and a party; or a state of their implied gathering pronoun, since the definite article (al) took its place: "and that you may warn on the day of their gathering, scattered." This is from the metaphor of approaching (majaz al-musharafa), i.e., on the verge of separating. Or the state is implied, so it does not require that their separation occur during their gathering. Or it may be said that their gathering at one time does not contradict the separation of their places, as you say: they prayed at one time in scattered mosques. So what is meant is scattered between the abodes of reward and punishment. When "gathering" is taken to mean the joining of spirits to bodies or deeds to doers, no reconciliation is needed at all. It has also been permitted that the accusative be governed by an implied or stated "warn," the meaning being: you warn a party of the people of the Garden and a party of the people of the Blaze, since warning does not take place in the Garden or the Blaze. Its strain is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 42, verse 8:

﴿And if God had willed,﴾ He would have made them one community, ﴿He would have made them﴾, that is, in this world, ﴿one community﴾, either guided or astray. This is an elaboration of what Ibn 'Abbas summarized in his words, "upon one religion." So the meaning of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾, is that He admits into His mercy whomever He wills to admit into it, and He admits whomever He wills into His punishment, to be admitted into it. There is no doubt that His will, exalted is He, regarding each of the two admissions, follows the deserving of each of the two groups for the admission that He admits them to. Necessarily, the difference between mercy and punishment entails a difference in the condition of those who enter each of them, with certainty. So He did not will to make all of them one community, but made them two groups. The phrase ﴿and the wrongdoers have no protector or helper﴾ was used instead of the expected "and whomever He wills He admits into His punishment and retribution." This is to indicate that admission into punishment comes from the side of those who enter it, due to their bad choice, and not from His side, Mighty and Majestic, as is the case with admission into mercy.

Al-Zamakhshari chose that what is meant is "one community of believers." This is what Muqatil said: "upon the religion of Islam," as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have brought them together upon guidance﴾, and His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.﴾ The meaning is: and if God, exalted is He, had willed the will of power, He would have compelled them to faith. But He, glorified is He, willed the will of wisdom, imposed the obligation on them, and based their affair on what they choose, so that He would admit the believers into His mercy. They are the ones meant by His statement, exalted is He, ﴿whom He wills﴾. And He left the wrongdoers without protector or helper. The discourse is connected to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those who take protectors other than Him—God is Guardian over them, and you are not a manager over them.﴾ It serves as a justification for the prohibition against the Prophet's intense eagerness, may God bless him and grant him peace, for their faith. So "the wrongdoers" is an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun referring to "those who took [protectors]," in order to convey that their wrongdoing is the cause of what follows it. Or it is for the category as a whole, and it encompasses them in an initial sense. He turned away from the apparent wording to what is in the sublime *nazm* (compositional arrangement), since the discourse is about warning, and it is more eloquent in frightening them, because it signals that their being in punishment is a settled matter. What is at issue is whether, after its certainty, there is anyone who can rescue them by averting or lifting it. When this is negated, it is known that they are in a punishment from which there is no escape.

It has been objected that the assumption that all would be made believers is contradicted by the opening of the *istidrak* (corrective turn) with the admission of some of them into His mercy, exalted is He, since all of them would then be among those who enter it. So the fitting thing then would be to open with the removal of some of them from among them and their admission into His punishment. It may be said: since the verse is connected to what you have heard, the meaning is: "And if God, exalted is He, had willed, He would have made all of them believers, as you wish and are eager for. But He, glorified is He, did not will that. Rather, He made some of them believers, as you wished, and made the others, namely those who took protectors other than Him, disbelievers for whom there is no escape from punishment, as wisdom requires." The opening with what was stated is fitting, as is not hidden from one who has a taste for the styles of discourse. However, according to this, the apparent wording would be "admits whom He wills" rather than "admits whom He wills," but it was turned from it to "admits whom He wills" as a narration of the past state.

Shaykh al-Islam said: What the noble composition and its context require is that what is meant is unity in disbelief, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community, and God sent the prophets﴾, and the rest of the verse, according to one of the two interpretations. So the meaning is: and if God, exalted is He, had willed, He would have made them one community united in disbelief, by not sending to them a messenger to warn them of what was mentioned of the Day of Assembly and its various terrors, so they would remain in the disbelief they are in. But He admits whom He wills into His mercy, glorified is He, meaning: it is His affair, exalted is His affair, that He sends to all a messenger who warns them of what was mentioned. Some of them are affected by the warning and turn their choice toward the truth, and God grants them success in faith and acts of obedience and admits them into His mercy, exalted and majestic is He. The others are not affected by it and persist in their error. They are the wrongdoers. They remain in the world in the disbelief they are in, and in the Hereafter they will go to the Blaze without a guardian to manage their affair or a helper to rescue them from punishment. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that between His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ and the rest of the verse, and His statement, glorified is He, ﴿And if God had willed, He would have made them one community,﴾ with the meaning he chose here in both, there is a kind of contradiction. So reflect on all of this, and God, exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 9:

﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustan'afa) that confirms what precedes it regarding the negation that the wrongdoers have any protector or helper. The words of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's tafsir) suggest that it is connected to the statement of the Exalted: "And those who have taken..." (etc.), meaning: Set aside your concern for their affairs, cut off your hope in their faith, and [consider] such-and-such. Have not those who took protectors besides Allah, the Exalted, [done so], while He, glorified is He, is the True Protector, capable of everything, and they turned away from Him, Mighty and Majestic, toward what has no relation whatsoever to Him, exalted is He? As for His statement, glorified is He, ﴿And thus We have revealed﴾ (to the end of the verse), it is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) emphasizing the content of the two verses.

The particle ﴿Am﴾ (umm), according to both opinions, is disjunctive (munqati'a), and it is in most cases to be understood as equivalent to bal (rather) together with the hamza (interrogative). A group of scholars here understood it as both. However, bal according to the second opinion is for turning away (idrab), and according to the first opinion it is for transition from explaining what precedes to explaining what follows. As for the hamza, it has been said that it is for denying the occurrence of the event and finding it reprehensible; and it has been said that it is not, but rather for denying the occurrence and negating it in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, since the intended meaning is to explain that what they did is not taking protectors in any respect, because that is a consequence of the idols being protectors, which is the most evident of impossibilities. That is, rather, they took, transgressing beyond Allah, the Exalted, protectors from among the idols and others.

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾ It has been said that this is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: If they seek a protector in truth, then Allah, the Exalted, is the Protector in truth, and there is no protector in truth other than Him, Mighty and Majestic. Its being the answer to the condition is in the sense of a statement and the like.

In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's tafsir) it is said: There is no need to posit an elided condition, and the statement is complete without it. Perhaps he means what has been said: that it is a conjunction with what precedes it, and that it is a justification (ta'lil) for the denial derived from the interrogative, like your saying: "Will you strike Zayd? He is your brother," meaning: It is not fitting for you to strike him, for he is your brother.

It has been objected that the usage in such a case is known to be with the conjunction "wa" (and), and that justification is appropriate only in explicit denial, and it also does not suit the sense of the past tense.

﴿And He gives life to the dead﴾ That is, this is His characteristic, like saying: "So-and-so hosts the guest and protects the sanctuary." ﴿And He is capable of everything﴾ So He, glorified is He, is the one deserving to be taken as protector; so let them single Him out for taking, rather than those who have no power over anything at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 10:

"﴿And whatever you differ about, its judgment rests with God﴾" to the end is a quotation of the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to the believers. That is: whatever the disbelievers have opposed you in regarding the matters of religion, such as taking God Most High alone as a protector, and you have differed with them, then its judgment rests with God, which is the rewarding of the upholders of truth and the punishing of the upholders of falsehood. It is also permissible that it be speech from His side, Most High, containing consolation, and His saying, Most High: ﴿That is God﴾ and so on, would be with an implied "say" (qul). The Imam (al-Razi) regarded it as part of the beginning of the speech. In any case, the reference to Him, Most High, is in respect of His being described by what preceded of the attributes, according to what al-Tibi said: that He, Most High, is the One who gives life to the dead, that He, glorified be He, is over all things capable, and that He, mighty and majestic, is the One to whom the judgment of what they differ about belongs. And in al-Irshad he said: that is, that great-in-authority Judge, ﴿God is my Lord﴾, my Owner, ﴿in Him I have put my trust﴾ in all my affairs especially, not in other than Him, ﴿and to Him I turn penitently﴾, I return in every difficult matter that befalls me, not to anyone besides Him. And since trust is one matter that is continuous, and turning penitently is multiple and renewed according to the renewal of its causes, the past tense form was preferred in the first and the present tense form in the second. It has also been said: "And whatever you differ about and dispute, of any matter among the disputes, then judge it by the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and do not prefer the judgment of anyone else over his judgment," like His saying, Most High: ﴿If you dispute about anything, refer it to God and the Messenger﴾.

It has also been said: "And whatever you differ about, of any matter of the interpretation of a verse which has become confused for you, then return in its explanation to the clear (muhkam) of the Book of God Most High and the apparent (zahir) of the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." It has also been said: "And whatever disagreement has arisen between you about it, of the sciences which do not relate to your obligations and for which you have no way to knowledge, then say: God Most High knows best," like the knowledge of the Spirit. It has been objected to all of these that it is contrary to the context, since the speech is directed to the polytheists, and it is therefore specific to the believers. The apparent sense of the words of the Imam is to choose the specificity, for he said regarding the purpose of the noble arrangement: that He, Most High, just as He forbade His Messenger (ﷺ) from compelling the disbelievers to faith, likewise forbade the believers from initiating with him disputes and contentions. He mentioned that the deniers of analogy (qiyas) argued by it, saying: either its meaning is that ﴿whatever you differ about, its judgment is derived from the text of God Most High﴾, or from analogy to what He, glorified be He, stated explicitly. The second is void, because it would require that all rulings be based on analogy, so the first is determined. A proponent may say: why should it not be permissible that the meaning is "its judgment is known from the explanation of God Most High, whether that explanation is by text or by analogy"? It was answered that the purpose of referring the matter to God Most High is to end disagreement, by His saying: ﴿And whatever you differ about﴾, and returning to analogy strengthens disagreement, so it is obligatory to return to the texts. End of quotation. And you know that the texts are not sufficient for all rulings, and that the verse, as you have heard it first, is such that it hardly can be valid as evidence for this point from the outset. In al-Kashshaf: it is not permissible to take the difference in it as the difference of the jurists (mujtahidun) concerning the rulings of the Sharia, because ijtihad is not permissible in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ). It is not hidden from you that this question is disputed. Most scholars held that the aforementioned ijtihad is permissible by reason, and among them some deemed it impossible. Then among those who permit it, some denied that it had been commanded in practice, and this is the view of Abu Ali and his son Abu Hashim, and to it went the author of al-Kashshaf. Mentioning what contradicts it is a report of the position of others, even if it is not followed by a rebuttal, as is his habit in most cases. Among them are those who claimed its occurrence by conjecture, and among them those who affirmed its occurrence definitively. It has been said that this is the most correct view among the usulis. Among them are those who suspended judgment. The detailed discussion of these matters is in the books of usul al-fiqh. What we say here is: the argument from the verse for prohibiting it hardly holds, and at the least it can be said that it is an argument based on something that admits of possibility.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 11 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ is another predicate of ﴿that﴾, or a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Originator; or an adjective of ﴿my Lord﴾; or a substitute for it; or a subject whose predicate is ﴿He has made for you﴾. Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) read it in the genitive case, on the basis that it is a substitute for the pronoun in (ilayhi) or (alayhi), or an attribute of the Great Name in His saying, Exalted is He: (ila Allah). The clause that lies between the attribute and the thing described is a parenthetical clause. The meaning of ﴿Originator﴾ has already been explained. ﴿He made﴾ means He created. ﴿For you, out of yourselves﴾ means from your own kind, ﴿spouses﴾ meaning wives.

The placing of the prepositional phrase before the explicit object is for the reason already mentioned more than once. ﴿And of the livestock, spouses﴾ means: He created for the livestock, from their own kind, spouses, just as He created for you spouses from yourselves. Thus there is an implied clause, indicated by the context; or it means: He created for you from the livestock kinds or males and females. ﴿He multiplies you﴾ means He increases you. It is said: Allah dhara'a the creation, that is, He scattered them and multiplied them, and dhar'' and dharr are two near-synonyms. ﴿In it﴾ means: in what He has mentioned of the arrangement, namely that He, glory to Him, made for people and livestock spouses, so that propagation occurs among them. He made the multiplication occur within this making, as it takes place in its midst and course, so it is like its source. It is also permissible for "in" (fi) to indicate causation. In ﴿He multiplies you﴾ the addressees, who are rational, predominate over the absent non-rational ones, so there is one act of predominance that involves two aspects of predominance. This is because the livestock are absent and non-rational; when they are included in the address to rational beings, there is predominance of both reason and address together. This predominance, I mean predominance on account of address and reason, is among the rulings with two causes, which here are address and reason. This is what Jar Allah meant, and there is nothing wrong with it, since the cause is not a real one. Ibn al-Munir claimed that the correct view is that they are two distinct rulings, not overlapping: the first is its coming in the form describing a rational pronoun, whether addressed or absent; the second is its coming after that in the form of address. The first is for the predominance of reason and the second for the predominance of address. This is nothing, and it is not needed. The words of the author of al-Miftah allow the reading of two predominances: first, the addressees predominating over the absent; second, the rational predominating over the non-rational. Al-Tibi said: the context rejects this, because it would lead to the original being "He multiplies you and it, He multiplies you (feminine) and it," but the original is only "He multiplies you and it," because the "kum" in ﴿He multiplies you﴾ is the very same "kum" in ﴿made for you from yourselves spouses﴾, except that it predominates here over the absent, so there is in "yadhra'ukum" only one predominance. End of quote. Then it should not be said that the multiplication is a ruling given two causes in the verse: one being making people spouses, and the second making the livestock spouses. It may be that this is what Jar Allah meant, since the ruling is absolute dispersal and its cause is the combination; and if each part of it is taken as a cause, then every dispersal is also a ruling, so where is the single ruling with multiple causes? Understand this. From Ibn 'Abbas: the meaning of ﴿He multiplies you﴾ in it is: He makes for you in it a livelihood by which you live. Close to this is the saying of Ibn Zayd: He provides for you in it. The apparent sense of this is that the pronoun refers to the making of spouses from the livestock.

Mujahid said: that is, He creates you as offspring after offspring and generation after generation. It is evident from this that the pronoun refers to the making mentioned in ﴿He has made for you from yourselves spouses﴾; it is also permissible that it be as in the first view. It is understood from this that dhar' is more specific than khalq (creation), and Ibn 'Atiyyah explicitly stated this, saying: the word dhara'a adds to the word khalaqa another meaning not found in khalaqa, namely the succession of layers over the passage of time. Al-'Utbi said: the pronoun in ﴿in it﴾ refers to the womb, because it is in the sense of what has been mentioned, and the meaning is: He creates you in the wombs of females. In a report from Ibn Zayd, that He, when He created from the heavens and the earth... This is as you see, and similar to what precedes it. And Allah knows best.

﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ is a negation of likeness in every respect. Included in this is the negation that there is anything like Him, glory to Him, that would pair with Him, mighty and majestic; and this is the point of the connection of this verse with what precedes it. Or the meaning is: there is nothing like Him, exalted is He, in the matters of which the wondrous arrangement just mentioned is one; thus it connects with what precedes it too. By "like Him" is meant His very essence, exalted is He. So there is no difference in meaning between "there is nothing like His essence" and "there is nothing like Him", except that the second is an allusive expression containing exaggeration: likeness is negated of one who would be like Him and share His attributes, so how much more of Himself. This does not require the existence of a like, since the supposition suffices for exaggeration. Similar things are common in Arabic speech, such as the verse of Aws ibn Hajar:

There is no creature like the youth Zuhayr who could match him in virtues.

And the saying of another:

And slain men like palm trunks, covered by a pouring, abundant rain.

And the saying of another:

Sa'd ibn Zayd, when you see their excellence, there is no one among people who is like them.

Ibn Qutaybah and others mentioned that the Arabs use "like" (mithl) in place of the self, saying "Your like does not stinge," meaning "you do not stinge", by way of allusive expression; and you have heard its benefit. In al-Kashshaf it is said that it indicates the emphasis of affirming that ruling sought and its firm establishment, for two reasons: first, it is a comprehensive supposition which requires that ruling; so when you say "Your like does not stinge," it shows that the cause of not stinging is present, unlike when you say "You do not stinge." Second, when it is made to refer to a group who do not stinge, it is more indicative of not stinging, because he is counted among them. From this is the saying: "His peers have grown up" meaning his age-mates and his like in age; and the saying of Ruqayqah daughter of Abi Sayfi ibn Hashim, concerning the watering of 'Abd al-Muttalib: "Indeed, among them is the good and pure one, his peer," meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); and other examples.

It has been said that mithl has the meaning of attribute, and shay' is also an expression for it; this is related by al-Raghib, who then said: the meaning is "like His attribute", an attribute, as an alert that He, exalted is He, though described by many things by which human beings are described, those attributes are not His in the manner they are used of humans.

Al-Tabari and others held that mithl is an additional emphatic element, like the kaf in the saying:

Yesterday they were in hoped-for ease, but now they have become like stubble eaten.

And the saying of another:

I recognized the abode at al-Gharriyyin, and the high places, like the kuma stones of the hearth-stones.

Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying it is not good, because mithl is a noun and nouns are not added, unlike the kaf, which is a particle and so suitable for addition. It is attributed to al-Zajjaj, Ibn Jinni and most scholars that the kaf is an additional emphatic element. Ibn al-Munir rejected this, saying that the kaf indicates emphasis of the comparison, not emphasis of the negation, and the negation of an unqualified likeness is more forceful than the negation of an emphasized likeness; so the verse is not like the two halves of the two verses. The same is said, as transmitted from al-Tabari and those with him. It was answered that it indicates emphasis of the comparison: if negation, then negation; and if affirmation, then affirmation; so the objection is dispelled. Yes, the first is the correct view.

As for mithl: al-Raghib said it is the most general of the words laid down for resemblance. A "nidd" is said of what shares only the substance; "shibh" of what shares only the quality; "musawi" of what shares only the quantity; "shakl" of what shares only the measure and dimension; and "mithl" is general to all of these. For this reason, when Allah, exalted is He, willed to negate resemblance in every respect, He singled it out by mention. Al-Imam al-Razi mentioned that the two likes, according to the theologians, are those each of which stands in place of the other in its reality and quiddity; and he took the "mithl" in the verse in this sense: that nothing equals Allah, exalted is He, in the reality of the essence. He said it is not valid that the meaning be "there is nothing like Him in attributes", because servants are described as knowing and capable, just as Allah, exalted is He, is described thus; and likewise they are described as known and mentioned, while Allah, exalted is He, is described thus too. He extended the discussion on this point, though something in his heart remained about it.

In the commentary on Jawharat al-Tawhid: know that the early Mu'tazilah, such as al-Jubba'i and his son Abu Hashim, held that likeness is sharing in the most specific attributes of the self; so the likeness of Zayd to 'Umar, according to them, is his sharing with him in rationality only. The Muhaqqiqun among the Maturidiyyah held that likeness is sharing in the essential attributes, such as animality and rationality, for Zayd and 'Amr. Among the necessary consequences of sharing in an essential attribute are two things: first, sharing in what is necessary, possible and impossible; second, that each of them can stand in place of the other. Two like things, though they share in the essential attributes, must still differ in some other respect so that plurality and distinction are realized, and so that likeness is valid. It is attributed to al-Ash'ari that he stipulates for likeness complete equality in every respect.

Objection has been raised that, on this reading, there is no plurality, and therefore no likeness. It has also been objected that the people of language unanimously agree on the correctness of our saying, "Zayd is like ʿAmr in jurisprudence (fiqh) when he equals him in it and fills his place, even if they differ in many attributes." And there is the hadith, "Wheat for wheat, like for like (mithlan bi-mithlin)," which is meant as equality in measure (kayl) and not in weight, the number of grains, or their attributes. It may be answered that its intent is equality in the respect by which likeness holds, so that if Zayd and ʿAmr share in jurisprudence and there is equality between them in it such that each can take the place of the other, it is correct to say that they are alike in it. Otherwise, this does not contradict the doctrine of the Maturidiyya (the school of al-Maturidi).

In this (verse) there is also the point that He, mighty and majestic, has no likeness (mumathil) in His essence or His attributes. Thus no essence fills the place of His essence, exalted be He, and no attribute fills the place of His attribute, may His attributes be exalted. By "attribute" is meant the real, existential attribute (al-sifa al-haqiqiyya al-wujudiyya).

From here you will know the problem with the statement of the Imam: "It is not correct that the meaning be: 'There is nothing like Him, exalted be He, in the attributes,' because servants are described as being knowing and capable, just as Allah, glorified be He, is described with that. The meaning of that is that He, exalted be He, has no attribute like His attribute, glorified be He." It is clearly known that the knowledge and power of the servants are not like the knowledge and power of Allah, mighty and majestic, that is, they do not fill their place (sadda-ayni masaddahuma).

As for His being mentioned (madhkur) and the like, that is not among the attributes that are considered as subsisting in His essence, exalted be He, as is not hidden.

Jahm ibn Safwan claimed that the purpose of this verse is to show that He, exalted be He, is not named by the name "thing" (shay'), because every thing is a likeness (mithl) to the like of itself. So His saying, exalted be He, ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ means: "There is nothing like the like of Him," and this entails that He, glorified be He, is not named by the name "thing." Thus he did not take the "like" (mithl) as a metonymy (kinaya) for the essence, as you have heard, nor did he judge it to be superfluous, nor the kaf (ka-) to be superfluous. Yet even with this, and closing one's eyes to what is in his statement, his aim is not achieved. For we may take the statement "there is nothing like the like of Him" as also a negation of likeness by way of metonymy, but in a different manner: that it is a negation of a thing by negating its necessary concomitant (lazim), since the negation of the concomitant entails the negation of what it necessitates (malzum). As one says: "My brother Zayd has no brother," where "brother of Zayd" is the malzum and "brother" is its lazim. It is necessary that Zayd's brother have a brother who is Zayd. So you negated this lazim, and the intended meaning is the negation of its malzum, that is, "Zayd has no brother," since if he had a brother, that brother would have a brother who is Zayd. Similarly, you negated that the like of Allah, exalted be He, has a like. The intended meaning is the negation of His like, glorified and exalted be He, since if He had a like, He would be a like, given the premise that He exists.

The difference between this and what preceded it is that its basis is establishing the necessary connection between the existence of a like and the existence of the like of the like, so that the negation of the lazim is a metonymy for the negation of the malzum without attention being paid to the fact that the rule for likes is one, and that it applies in negation but not in affirmation. For the negation of the lazim entails the negation of the malzum, but not conversely. This is unlike what preceded, whose basis is that the rule for two likes is one, otherwise they would not be two likes, and it does not need to establish a necessary connection between the existence of a like and the like of a like. It applies in both negation and affirmation, as you have heard in the examples. This is not at all part of the theological method (al-madhhab al-kalami).

As for the first point, it is because it is the presentation of an argument (hujja), and there is not even a hint of one in the verse, let alone a presentation. As for the second point, it is because then the argument would be a conditional syllogism (qiyas istithna'i) in which the negation of the consequent is stated, thus: "If He, glorified be He, had a like, He, exalted be His majesty, would be a like of the like of Him. But He is not a like of His like. So it is necessary to demonstrate the falsity of the consequent so that the argument is complete."

Page 20

Since it is not self-evident. Rather, the existence of a like and the existence of the like of a like at the same level in knowledge and ignorance do not allow one to be taken as proof of the other. But it has been said that what is understood from "there is nothing like the like of Him" on that supposition is the negation that there be a like of His like other than Him, exalted be He, by the indication of the idafa (annexation) construction, just as what is understood from the speaker's saying, "If anyone enters my house, then such-and-such," is that someone other than the speaker (is meant). Also, we do not concede that if a like of Him, glorified be He, existed, He, exalted and majestic, would be a like of the like of Him, because the existence of a like of Him, glorified be He, is impossible, and an impossibility may entail an impossibility.

It is answered to the first point that the noun of "is not" (laysa), "thing" (shay'), is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so the verse covers the negation of any thing that would be a like of the like of Him. There is no doubt that, on the supposition of the existence of a like, it is true of it that it is a thing that is a like of the like of Him. The idafa does not require its exclusion from the generality of "thing." This is unlike the example mentioned, for the rational indication (qarina aqliyya) shows the restriction of "anyone" to other than the speaker, since his intention is to prevent anyone else from entering.

As for the second point, the existence of a like of a thing in an absolute sense entails the like of that thing, apart from consideration of the particularity of that thing, and this is clear. So the denial, by allowing that Allah's essence has a like while He Himself is not a like of the like of Him, is sheer obstinacy.

Furthermore, this way, because of how much debate and counter-debate it involves compared with the other ways mentioned earlier, we did not mention it when we mentioned them. Yet despite its flaws, it is better than the view of the superfluity (of the kaf or of mithl), as will not be hidden from one whom Allah, mighty and majestic, has granted success.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾: the One who perceives with complete perception, not by way of imagination or supposition, all audible things, and not through the affecting of a sense organ or the arrival of air. ﴿The All-Seeing﴾: the One who perceives with complete perception all visible things or all existing things, not by way of imagination or supposition, and not through the affecting of a sense organ or the arrival of a ray of light. Hearing and sight are therefore attributes distinct from knowledge, according to what is apparent. Some scholars reduced them to the attribute of knowledge, and the full discussion of this is in the section on speech (al-kalam).

He, glorified be He, mentioned the negation of likeness before the affirmation of hearing and sight because it is more important in itself and in view of the context.

﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾. Its explanation has already been given in Surat az-Zumar, and likewise His saying: ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾.

It is also read as (يُقَدِّرُ), with the doubled letter (tashdid), and ﴿Indeed He is Knowing of all things﴾ is an intensive form, meaning that He is thorough in encompassing everything. So He does whatever He does, exalted is His majesty, in the way that it ought to be done. The sentence gives the reason for what precedes it and prepares for what follows from

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 42, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus﴾. This indicates that what God, glorified is He, has prescribed for them proceeds from perfect knowledge and wisdom. Stating that it is ascribed to those mentioned, peace be upon them, is also a reminder that it is an ancient religion on which the messengers agreed. The address is to His Community (ﷺ), meaning: He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah and those after him from the possessors of revealed laws (*arbab al-shara'i*) and the famous prophets of the *Ulu al-'Azm* (the resolute messengers), peace be upon them, and commanded it to them as an emphatic command. Mentioning those specifically is due to the elevated status and great fame that have been pointed out, and to win over the hearts of the disbelievers toward following, since all of them agreed on the prophethood of some of them, and because the Jews were particular to Moses and the Christians to Jesus, peace be upon them. Otherwise, there is no prophet who was not commanded with what they were commanded: establishing the religion of Islam, which is *tawhid* (the affirmation of God's oneness), and the fundamentals of the laws and rulings that do not differ with the differing of nations and the changing of eras. This is indicated by the word "enjoined," for it expresses emphasis on the command and concern for the matter commanded.

As for the meaning of His revealing to him (ﷺ), it is either what was mentioned at the beginning of the noble surah and in His saying: ﴿And thus We revealed to you﴾ (the verse), or what encompasses those and others among the revelations that occurred in various contexts, among which is His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham, a *hanif* (a pure monotheist)﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed that your God is one God﴾, and other than that. The choice of "revealing" over what comes before and after it, namely "enjoining," is to observe what occurred in the mentioned verses, and because revelation contains a clear statement of his messengerhood (ﷺ), which crushes the denial of the disbelievers. The shift to the plural of majesty (*nun al-'azamah*) is to show complete care for His revealing it. In this there is an indication that his law (ﷺ) is the law that receives the utmost care, and for this reason it is expressed with *alladhi* and *allati*, which are the origin of the relative pronouns. That is the secret behind placing "that which was revealed to him" (peace and blessings be upon him) before what follows it, despite the latter preceding it in time. And the placing of Noah's enjoinment first is for the sake of hastening to show that what is prescribed for them is an ancient religion. It has been said that he, peace be upon him, was the first of the messengers. The address is directed to him, peace be upon him, by way of *iltifat* (shift in address), to honor him and to draw attention to the fact that God prescribed it for them through his tongue (ﷺ).

﴿That you establish the religion﴾, meaning the religion of Islam, which is the oneness of God, obedience to Him, belief in His books, His messengers, the Day of Recompense, and all that by which the servant becomes a believer. Establishing it means making its pillars upright, protecting it from any deviation, and persevering in it. The *an* is verbal (*masdariyyah*), and the discussion of its connection to the imperative and prohibition has preceded. Or it is the lightened form of the heavy *anna* (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*), because of the sense of knowing in *shara'a* (he prescribed). The verbal noun (*al-masdar*) is either in the accusative, as a substitute (*badal*) for the object of *shara'a* and the two items conjoined to it, or in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is omitted. The clause is an answer to a question arising from the vagueness of what was prescribed, as if it were said: "And what is that?" Then it is answered: "It is: *an aqimu al-din* (that you establish the religion)." It has also been said that it is in the genitive, as a substitute for the pronoun in *bihi* (with which), and it does not necessitate that the relative pronoun remain without a returning pronoun, because the substituted-for item is not, in reality, intended to be dropped. Yes, Shaykh al-Islam said: "It is not so, because, along with its leading to the removal of it from the scope of revelation to the Prophet (ﷺ), it entails that the address in the later prohibition against division is to the mentioned prophets, peace be upon them, and directing the prohibition to their communities is an obvious forced interpretation. Moreover, the more evident view is that it is directed to his Community (ﷺ), and that they are the ones who divide." Then he stated what he considered more evident, and we will point to it, God willing, Exalted is He.

It is also permitted that it be a substitute for *al-din* (the religion). It is also permitted that *an* be explanatory (*mufassirah*), since what precedes it contains the meaning of saying without its letters. The address in *aqimu* (establish) and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not divide over it﴾, according to what many of the great scholars chose, encompasses the Prophet (ﷺ) and his followers, and the prophets and nations before them. The pronoun in *fihi* (in it) refers to the religion, meaning: do not divide in the religion, which is an expression for what has preceded of the fundamentals, such that some bring it and others do not, or that some bring some of it and not others. This is the meaning intended by Muqatil, i.e., do not differ concerning it. This prohibition does not include disagreement concerning the subsidiary matters (*furu'*), for they are not among the fundamentals intended here, and the prophets did not unite on them, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way (*shir'ah wa minhaj*)﴾. Some have included some subsidiary matters among the fundamentals of religion intended here.

Mujahid said: "No prophet was sent except that he was commanded to establish prayer, give zakat, acknowledge God, and obey Him, glorified is He, and that is establishing the religion." Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "There was not with Adam, peace be upon him, except his sons, and obligatory duties were not prescribed for him, nor were prohibitions legislated for him. He was only alerting to some matters, limited to some necessities of livelihood. The matter continued until Noah, peace be upon him, when God sent him with the prohibition of mothers and daughters, imposed on him obligations, and clarified for him the etiquette in religions. This continued to be reinforced through the messengers and supported by the prophets, one after another, law after law, until God, glorified is He, sealed it with the best of creeds through the tongue of the most noble of messengers. So the meaning of the verse is: We have legislated for you, from what We legislated for the prophets, one religion in its fundamentals, which are: *tawhid*, prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage, drawing near through righteous deeds, truthfulness, fulfilling covenants, returning trusts, maintaining family ties, prohibiting arrogance, adultery, harming creatures, aggression against animals, plunging into base matters, and what leads to the ruin of manliness. All of this is prescribed as one religion and one united creed, which did not differ on the tongues of the prophets, even if their numbers differed. The meaning of ﴿Establish the religion and do not divide over it﴾ is: make it standing, meaning constant and continuous, without disagreement or disorder concerning it." End of quotation.

Perhaps by "prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage" he meant their general forms, not what we know of them in our law, for the five daily prayers, the specific zakat, and the fasting of Ramadan are, according to the correct view, particular to this Community. The apparent view is that the pilgrimage to the House was not legislated for the community of Moses and the community of Jesus, peace be upon them both, nor for most of the nations before them. Moreover, the verse is Meccan, and the familiar zakat and fasting of Ramadan were not legislated except in Medina. In sum, there is no doubt that religions differ in subsidiary matters. Yes, it is not far-fetched that they agree in what belongs to noble character and avoiding vices.

﴿It is grievous﴾, meaning it is great and burdensome, ﴿upon the polytheists, what you call them to﴾, by way of continuous renewal, of *tawhid* and rejecting the worship of idols. The mention of "polytheists" indicates that this is intended, and it is the root of all fundamentals and the greatest of what burdened them, as the verses indicate. Or it is what you call them to of establishing the religion and not dividing over it. ﴿God chooses for Himself whom He wills﴾: a consolation to him (ﷺ) that among them are those who respond. *Yajtabi* (chooses) is from *ijtiba'* (selection), meaning *istifa'* (choosing). The pronoun in *ilayhi* (to Him) refers to God, Exalted is He, as Muhyi al-Sunnah and others mentioned. Likewise the pronoun in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And guides to Himself whoever turns back﴾. That is: He selects to Himself, glorified is He, whomever He wills to select, and singles him out, glorified is He, with a divine overflow from which various kinds of blessings are obtained, and He, Mighty and Majestic, guides by direction and success whoever turns toward Him, exalted is His majesty. The verb *ijtiba'* is construed with *ila* (to) because of the sense of gathering, as is understood from the words of al-Raghib. Some of them took it from *jibaya* (collecting), in the sense of gathering, as one says: "I collected water in the basin," meaning I gathered it in it. Some of them chose that the pronoun *ilayhi* in both places refers to *li-ma* (for what), because of the coherence of the pronouns, meaning: He draws in and gathers whomever He wills to draw in and gather to what you call them to. Others chose that it refers to the religion, for a verbal reason: the unity of what is divided over and what is gathered upon. Al-Zamakhshari chose that it is from *jibaya* in the sense of gathering, with the pronoun returning to the religion, and what Muhyi al-Sunnah and others mentioned. In *al-Kashf* it is said: "The latter is more apparent and richer in benefit. As for the second, it indicates that the people of *ijtiba'* are not the people of guidance, and both groups are the people of religion and *tawhid* who did not divide over it, and according to the choice of one group, it is a single group." As for the first, it is because *ijtiba'* in the sense of *istifa'* is more commonly used, and because it indicates that the people of religion are God's elite whom He selected for Himself and chose for His own self, glorified is He. As for what al-Zamakhshari preferred, it is an apparent statement built on the premise that the discourse concerns not dividing in religion, so it fits gathering and arriving at it. It has also been said: "*What you call them to*" means "what you call them to believe in it," and what is meant by it is the messengerhood, i.e., your messengerhood burdened them, and our singling you out for messengerhood and revelation instead of them was great in their sight. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God chooses for Himself whom He wills﴾ is a rebuttal of them, in the manner of ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾. What we have previously mentioned is more apparent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 14:

﴿And they did not become divided﴾, i.e., the nations of the prophets after the death of their prophets, as in al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), since the time of Noah, peace be upon him, concerning the religion to which they were called and about which they differed at some point in time. ﴿Except after knowledge had come to them﴾ from their prophets, that division is misguidance, corruption, and a matter for which a threat has been made. This supports what was indicated earlier, that the earlier and later nations were commanded to unite in the word and to establish the religion. The word "knowledge" here means its cause, by majaz mursal (a metonymic figure, where the word used is related to the intended meaning by a connection other than resemblance). It is also permissible that the figurative usage lies in the attribution (isnad), and that the statement contains an omitted modifier, i.e., "the cause of knowledge came to them." It may also be said that "came" is a metaphor for "occurred." The exception, according to what we have indicated, is an istithna mufarragh (an exception whose excluded element is not stated, so the exception takes on the sense required by the context) from the most general of times. It is also permissible that it is from the most general of states, i.e., they did not become divided in any state except the state of the coming of knowledge. ﴿Out of mutual rebellion among themselves﴾, i.e., enmity. The "baghy" (rebellion, transgression) is the cause of it, as injustice, overstepping, and enmity are its cause, and it is what calls to division; or [baghy means] seeking worldly gain and leadership. It is also permissible that baghy is a verbal noun of baghā, meaning "sought." ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, which is His promise, may He be exalted, to delay punishing them, ﴿until a specified term﴾, known to Him, may He be glorified, which is the Day of Resurrection, or the last of their appointed lifespans, ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ by the annihilation of the wrongdoers at the moment they divided, because of the enormity of what they committed. ﴿And indeed those who were given the Scripture after them﴾ are the People of the Book who were in the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Zayd ibn Ali read (وُرِّثُوا) [wuriththū] in the passive voice with the wāw doubled. ﴿Are in grave doubt concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning their Scripture, so they did not believe in it with true belief. ﴿Disquieting﴾, i.e., causing unease, or causing suspicion. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) that emphasizes that this division of theirs remains among their descendants, joined to it is doubt about their Scripture despite their attribution to it. Thus they divided after the knowledge that came to them from the Prophet sent to them, who confirms their Scripture, and they divided before him out of doubt about their Scripture, so they did not believe in it and did not affirm its truth.

[p. 23]

﴿Therefore﴾, that is: if the matter is as has been mentioned, then for the sake of that division, and because of the diversification of disbelief into branches among the earlier nations that resulted from it, ﴿call﴾ (people) to harmony and agreement upon the primordial upright religion (al-millah al-hanifiyyah, the original monotheistic creed). ﴿And be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾, that is: persist in the call as it was revealed to you. It has also been said that the reference is to His saying, ﴿He has prescribed for you﴾, and what is connected to it. It is narrated from al-Wahidi: that is, for the sake of the charge that you share with Noah and those after him, and for the sake of that command to establish (the religion) and the prohibition of division, ﴿call﴾. What was mentioned first is preferable, because His saying, ﴿that you establish﴾, includes the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his followers, as you have heard. This is supported by ﴿Hard upon the polytheists is what you call them to﴾. Thus His saying, ﴿Therefore call﴾ etc., is not a consequence of it, because of the apparent repetition, which would be the derivation of a command from a command. As for its being a consequence of their division, it is clear in the sense of: "Because of what they introduced of division and innovated, so you remain upon the call with which you were commanded, and be steadfast." This is evident to the one who reflects.

Some people took the referent to be the previous law, and did not include in it the command to establish (the religion), lest there be repetition. That is: because He prescribed for them the upright, ancient religion, worthy of being competed for by those who compete, therefore ﴿call﴾. It has been said that it refers to the Book. It has been said that it refers to the knowledge mentioned in His saying, ﴿knowledge came to them﴾. It has also been said that it refers to doubt, and this was preferred on account of proximity, but it is not so. The lam (in ﴿Therefore﴾) in all the above opinions is for causation. It has been said that in some of them it means "to" (ilā), with the following being the object of the call. You know that there is no need, in the case of that interpretation, to take it to mean "to," since the verb "call" also takes it, as in the poet's saying:

"I called for what befell me, Miswar"

This is narrated from al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. In any case, the first fa' is the response to an implied condition, as we have indicated, and the second fa' emphasizes the first. It has been said: after the Flood, people were one nation, monotheists, but their descendants differed after their death, when God Most High sent the prophets as bringers of good news and warners. The pronoun in ﴿they divided﴾ refers to the descendants of those monotheists, and ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ remains as previously stated. The first view is more apparent.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿they divided﴾ refers to the People of the Book, who divided after knowledge had come to them about the sending of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. This is like His saying: ﴿Those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear proof came to them﴾. They divided out of envy toward him, peace and blessings be upon him, not due to doubt. By ﴿those who were given the Book after them﴾ is meant the polytheists of Mecca and their factions, since they were given the Qur'an, so "the Book" is the Qur'an, and the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to Him. It has been said it refers to the Messenger, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. He (the author) chose that those who divided are the People of the Book, the Jews and Christians, and the ones given the Book who were in doubt are the polytheists of Mecca and their factions, as Shaykh al-Islam (held). He took as the more probable the address in ﴿Establish the religion and do not divide concerning it﴾ to be addressed to his community, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. He criticized the view that the one who divided is each nation after its prophet, and the view that it refers to the descendants of the monotheists who were after the Flood, saying: What refutes that is His saying: ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord for a specified term, it would have been decided between them﴾. For the well-known nations mentioned were struck by the punishment of annihilation without respite or delay. Moreover, the context of the noble discourse is to explain the conditions of this nation. The reason that those prophets, upon them be peace, were mentioned is to establish that what was prescribed for these people is an ancient religion on which those eminent figures, upon them be blessings and peace, agreed, to emphasize the obligation of establishing it and to strengthen the warning against division and disagreement concerning it. So explaining the division of their nations from it may perhaps give the impression of undermining that aim. End of quotation.

It is answered regarding the first (objection): the pronoun in ﴿between them﴾ refers to those who divided, and you know that by them is meant those who divided after the death of their prophets. They were not struck by the punishment of annihilation; it struck only those who did not believe during the lifetime of their prophets. The application of "those who divided" is not so evident. It has been said: the meaning is ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾ immediately upon their division, without being given time for years. It has been said: the meaning is ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾ by destroying the falsifiers and rewarding the righteous with their reward in the Hereafter. But this, as you see, is weak.
