As for the second (objection): we do not concede that explaining the division of the nations gives the impression of undermining the aim, after explaining that it occurred only after knowledge had come to them that it was misguidance and corruption, a matter deserving threat, and that it was rebellion among themselves, not due to doubt about the validity of the religion. It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿they divided﴾ refers to the polytheists in His saying: ﴿Hard upon the polytheists is what you call them to﴾.

It is related in al-Bahr from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "And they did not divide" means Quraysh, and "the knowledge" is Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. They used to wish that a prophet would be sent to them, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that if a warner came to them…﴾. It may be objected to this: the meaning of "those who were given the Book" is the People of the Book who were contemporaries of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. And the meaning of "after them," according to Abu Hayyan, is "after their predecessors."

Al-Tabarsi narrated from al-Suddi what indicates that the meaning is "after their rabbis." The relative clause is explained as the common People of the Book. It has been said: the pronoun in "after them" refers to the polytheists also, and the "after" is in terms of rank, as was said regarding His saying: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾. It is not hidden from you that there is no harm in the pronoun of ﴿they divided﴾ returning to the polytheists, if there could be found for "those who were given the Book" an interpretation acceptable to reason. And God Most High is the Granter of success.

The object of ﴿be steadfast﴾ was taken to be the call, whose relevance is not hidden. It was also permitted to make it general, so that ﴿be steadfast﴾ is a command to steadfastness in all his affairs, upon him be blessings and peace. Steadfastness is to be upon a straight path. Al-Raghib explained it as adhering to the straight way, so there is no need for the interpretation of it as persistence, i.e., "persist in steadfastness." ﴿And do not follow their desires﴾, that is, do not follow any of their false desires, and the idafah (genitive construction) here is generic. ﴿And say: I believe in whatever Book God has sent down﴾, that is, in all the books that were revealed, because "mā" is a word of generality, and the indefinite "Book" in the phrase, being specified, supports this. In this statement there is affirmation of the truth, clarification of the agreement of the books on fundamentals, an attempt to win over the hearts of the People of the Two Books, and an implicit rebuke of them for not believing in all of them. ﴿And I am commanded to act justly between you﴾, that is, God commanded me by what He commanded me, so that I may act justly between you in conveying the laws and rulings; so I do not favor any one person over another with any of them. It has been said: that I may judge justly between you when you dispute. It has been said: by conveying the laws and resolving disputes, and many have preferred this. It has been said: so that I may level myself and you, and not command you to do what I do not do, nor oppose you in what I forbid you, nor distinguish between your lesser and your greater in the implementation of God's, Mighty and Majestic is He, judgment. So the lam is for causation, and the commanded matter is omitted. It has been said: the lam is extra, meaning: I was commanded that I act justly; this requires the implied preposition bi (i.e., "that I act justly"), and it is not free from distance. ﴿God is our Lord and your Lord﴾, that is, the Creator of all and the Manager of its affairs, so the meaning is not limited to the speaker and the addressees. ﴿For us are our deeds﴾: their reward does not pass us, whether reward or punishment. ﴿And for you are your deeds﾿: their effects do not go beyond you, so that we benefit from your good deeds and are harmed by your evil deeds. ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾, that is, no disputation and no contention, because the truth has become manifest, so there remains no need for argument, nor any basis for opposition except obstinacy and stubbornness. The word ḥujjah here comes in its original sense, for it is originally a verbal noun meaning "arguing," as al-Raghib mentioned, and it has become common in the sense of "proof," which is not what is meant here. ﴿God will gather us together﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and to Him is the final return﴾, so He, glorified is He, will judge between us and you. There is nothing in the verse that indicates the complete abandonment of the disbelievers, so as to make it abrogated (mansukha, i.e., superseded) by the verse of the sword. Abu Hayyan claimed that what appears from it is a temporary truce, abrogated by that verse.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 42, verse 16:

﴿Those who dispute concerning Allah﴾: that is, they argue against His religion, said Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a group of the Children of Israel who intended to turn people away from Islam and lead them astray. They said: "Our Book is before your Book, and our Prophet is before your Prophet, so our religion is superior to your religion." In another narration, instead of "so our religion is superior to your religion," it says: "so we are more deserving of Allah, the Exalted, than you are."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah that he said: When ﴿When the help of Allah and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the polytheists in Makkah said to the believers who were among them: "People have entered the religion of Allah in multitudes. So either leave our midst or abandon Islam." The argument in this matter is not evident, and perhaps they mention what is in it for this reason.

﴿After it has been responded to﴾: that is, after people have responded to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or to His religion, and entered it and submitted to it because the proof became manifest and the path became clear. The expression "responded to" refers to this on account of their being called to it.

﴿Their argument is void in the sight of their Lord﴾: it is refuted, false, and not accepted by Him, the Mighty and Majestic. Rather, they have no argument at all. He called their falsehoods an "argument" (ḥujjah), which means "proof," here only in accommodation to them and to their claim of falsehood.

It is also permissible for the pronoun in ﴿to Him﴾ to refer to the Messenger (ﷺ), since he is in the position of the one mentioned, and the one who responds is the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab). Their response to him (ﷺ) is their acknowledgment of his attributes and their seeking victory through him before his mission (ﷺ). If they are the ones disputing, then the meaning is as if it said: "Those who dispute concerning the religion of Allah after they responded to His Messenger and acknowledged his attributes, their argument against him is false, because it contains a denial of what they had acknowledged before, and clear evidence confirms him."

It was also said: the one who responds is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the pronoun in ﴿to Him﴾ refers to His Messenger (ﷺ). Allah's response to him (ﷺ) is by manifesting the miracles that indicate his truthfulness. al-Jubbaʾi took this view, saying: that is, after Allah answered his supplication concerning the disbelievers of Badr, so that He killed them by the hands of the believers; and his supplication against the people of Makkah, so that they suffered drought; and his supplication for the oppressed, so that Allah delivered them from the hands of Quraysh; and other matters too lengthy to enumerate. The nullity of their argument is because what their claim implies has been shown to be contrary to that. This clearly indicates that this verse is Madinan, because the battle of Badr occurred after the Hijrah, and interpreting ﴿responded to﴾ as a promise is very contrary to the apparent meaning. The same applies to what was narrated from ʿIkrimah. It was also said: interpreting "response" as the response of the People of the Book also implies that, since there was no one among them in Makkah. It was also said: it does not imply that, because the news of their response and their acknowledgment of his attributes (ﷺ) reached the people of Makkah while he (ﷺ) was in Makkah, and the disputants are understood to be them, so there is no obstacle to its being Makkan.

﴿Upon them is wrath﴾: a great one, for their obstinate rejection of the truth after it became manifest. ﴿And for them is a severe punishment﴾: whose extent cannot be measured.

[p. 26]

﴿Allah is the One who sent down the Book﴾ (the genus of the Book, or the specific Book known [to the audience], or all the Books) ﴿with the truth﴾ (accompanied by the truth, far removed from falsehood in its rulings and its reports; or accompanied by what is right and necessary of beliefs and rulings) ﴿and the balance﴾ (i.e., justice, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada and others said; or the Law by which rights are weighed and people are made equal). On both interpretations there is a metaphor (istiʿara), and attributing the sending down to it is figurative (majaz), because sending down is a property of bodies, while the one who sends down in the literal sense (haqiqa) is the one who conveys it. Some scholars took the subject to be the command (al-amr), i.e., He sent down the command with the balance, and this was criticised on the grounds that it too needs interpretation. It may be said that attributing sending down, and likewise descent, to the command is very common, so it has become like the literal usage. It is also permissible to use sending down figuratively and to say something similar regarding ﴿He sent down the Book﴾. It is reported from Mujahid that the balance is the well-known instrument, and on this view the sending down is literal. It is also permitted that it is by way of a command to use it. The first view is preferred, because al-Zamakhshari reported regarding iron that it was sent down to Noah and he was commanded to weigh with it. That the intended meaning is the balance of deeds is far-fetched here.

﴿And what will make you know﴾ (i.e., what thing makes you a knower, ʿalim) ﴿that perhaps the Hour﴾ (i.e., the coming of the Hour, which the Book that speaks the truth has reported). The speech therefore has an implied masculine noun (mudaf mudhakkar) in it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿is near﴾ is in reality a predicate of that (implied noun), since the omitted word, by the indication of the context, is like the stated word, and this is one reason for the masculine form. It is also permitted that it is because the Hour is interpreted as the Resurrection (al-baʿth). And ﴿near﴾ may be of the pattern of tamir and laban (i.e., possessing nearness), meaning having nearness, and there are other aspects that were mentioned earlier in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near﴾. Whatever the case, the meaning is that the Hour is on the wing of coming. So follow the Book, persevere in justice, and act by the Law before the Day overtakes you, the Day on which deeds are weighed and their recompense is paid in full.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 18:

﴿They seek to hasten it, those who do not believe in it﴾ — a hastening of denial and mockery. They used to say: "When is it? Would that it would come, so that it becomes clear to us whether it is that upon which we are, or like that upon which Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions are."

﴿And those who believe are fearful of it﴾ — that is, they are afraid of it while being solicitous about it. Indeed, al-ishfaq (solicitude, apprehension) is a care mixed with fear. When it is construed with "min" (from/of), as here, the sense of fear is more evident; when it is construed with "ʿala" (upon), the sense of care is more evident. Their care for it is due to their expectation of reward. Al-Jalabi claimed that the verse is of the type of al-ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis), and the original is: "Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, so they are not fearful of it; and those who believe are fearful of it, so they do not seek to hasten it."

﴿And they know that it is the truth﴾ — the matter that is certain, that will undoubtedly occur.

﴿Certainly, those who dispute concerning the Hour﴾ — that is, who argue about it. Its root is from "miritu al-naqata," when I milked her udder for milking. The application of al-muma'ara (disputation) to argument is because each of the two disputants draws out what is in the possession of his companion. It is also possible that it derives from al-mirya, meaning hesitation regarding a matter, which is more specific than doubt; the sense of reciprocity (al-mufa'ala) is not intended here. So the meaning is: those who waver concerning the matter of the Hour and doubt it,

﴿are in far error﴾ — far from the truth. For the Resurrection is the nearest of the unseen matters to the perceptible ones, since it is known from the possibility of it, from the revival of the earth after its death and other such things. Thus whoever is not guided to it is further and further away from being guided to what lies beyond it.

Allah is Subtle with His servants ﴿اللَّهُ لَطِيفٌ بِعِبادِهِ﴾: Most Kind (barr), of far-reaching kindness toward them. His grace overflows to all of them in its various forms, beyond what minds can grasp. The root of the word *lutf* (subtlety, gentleness) and its intensive form *lattif* indicate this, and the indefinite form of the word signals intensity in both quantity and quality. The Proof of Islam (*Hujjat al-Islam*, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali), may God have mercy on him, said: "Only one who knows the finest and most hidden benefits, and what is subtlest among them, deserves this name, and then pursues the path of gentleness rather than harshness in bringing them to the one who benefits. When gentleness in action and subtlety in perception combine, the meaning of *al-Latif* is complete, and this perfection is conceivable only in God, exalted is His majesty." Thus the forms of kindness reflect intensity in quantity, and that they are beyond the reach of minds reflects the intensity in quality, since when something is extremely fine it becomes more and more hidden. The word "servants," being a plural noun made possessive by the pronoun of God, indicates totality and comprehensiveness. Muqatil also took it in this general sense, but said: "Subtle toward the pious and the wicked, in that He did not let them starve to death."

Abu Hayyan said: "Subtle with His servants," meaning kind to His believing servants and to those whose eternal abode in Paradise has been decreed. The blessings seen by the disbeliever are not subtlety; they are respite, except when they lead to mercy and death upon Islam. Al-Tibi reported this specification from al-Wahidi and inclined to prefer it. He claimed that the possessive in "His servants" is one of honour, since the Majestic Revelation mostly uses it in such a sense, so "servants" is restricted to His friends, the believers. He understood subtlety as the granting of guidance, the enabling of obedience, the perfections of the Hereafter and the noble honours. He applied the same understanding to provision in His saying: ﴿يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ (He provides for whom He wills), and said that its use in these senses is like its use in His saying: ﴿لِيَجْزِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ أحْسَنَ ما عَمِلُوا ويَزِيدَهم مِن فَضْلِهِ واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مِن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾ (That Allah may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty; and Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning).

He made His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿وهُوَ القَوِيُّ العَزِيزُ﴾ (And He is the Strong, the Mighty), indicate a reason, as if it were said: He shows subtlety toward His believing servants alone, and not toward those with whom He is angry by the sheer will of Glorified is He, because He, Exalted is He, is Strong and capable of restricting His mercy and honour to whomever He wills of His servants, and He is Mighty, Dominant, whom none can prevent from what He wills, Glorified is He. He claimed that the verse would then be parallel in structure to His saying, Exalted is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 20:**

﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We shall increase for him in his tilth.﴾ [The verse] is parallel to His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness. He has certainly succeeded who purifies it, and he has certainly failed who corrupts it.﴾ The discourse is arranged in the most complete order, and its parts fit together most firmly. At that point it cannot be said that His saying, ﴿He provides for whom He wills﴾, is a ruling that follows from what precedes, so its generality should have covered [all], and generality is more evident. As for the claim of specification regarding ﴿He provides for whom He wills﴾, the author of al-Taqrib has answered it, saying: "He only specified provision for whom He wills, although He is benevolent to all of them, because He, Exalted is He, may single out one person with one blessing and another with a different one. So the generality is for the genus of benevolence, and the specification is for its type." Jar Allah [al-Zamakhshari] pointed out that there is no specification in reality, for God, Exalted is He, is abundantly benevolent to all His servants. ﴿He provides for whom He wills﴾, [meaning] He gives whatever He wills of it, Glorified is He, to whomever He wills; so ﴿He provides for whom He wills﴾ is an explanation of its distribution among all of them, and provision is nothing but the particular share of each one. Since [the verse] encompasses both abodes, the saying of God, Exalted is He, ﴿Whoever desires﴾ etc., fits perfectly. This does not depend on what al-Tibi said. Perhaps the matter of concluding with the two glorious names is more evident according to the view of generality, and the reasoning [implied] is more fitting. So it is as if it were said: "Gentle to His servants, generally beneficent to them, because He, Exalted is He, is the Mighty, the Overpowering in might, who has overcome, and whose might has overcome, all powers, Glorified is He. He provides for whom He wills, because He is the Almighty, who is not overcome in what He wills." So each of the two glorious names looks to a ruling. Understand this.

*How many subtle kindnesses of God are there, whose hidden depth escapes the understanding of the intelligent.*

The word ḥarth (tilth) originally means casting seed into the ground, and it is applied to the crop that results from it. It is also used for the fruits and outcomes of deeds, by way of a metaphor (isti'arah) based on likening them to the grains produced from seeds; this implies the likening of deeds to seeds. That is: whoever, by his deeds, desires the reward of the Hereafter, We shall multiply his reward for him, from tenfold up to seven hundredfold and beyond. ﴿And whoever desires﴾ by his deeds ﴿the tilth of this world﴾, which is its goods and its pleasures, ﴿We shall give him of it﴾, that is, some of it, according to what We have decreed for him in accordance with his seeking and his desire; ﴿and he has no share in the Hereafter﴾, since his aspiration is confined to this world.

Ibn Muqsim, al-Za'farani, and Mahbub and al-Minqari, both on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read *yazid* and *yu'tihi* with ya' in both places. Sallam read *nu'tihu* with a ḍammah on the hā' (ha'), which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. In the verse, the conditional verb (fi'l al-shart) is in the past tense and the response (jawab) is in the present tense in the jussive (majzum). Abu Hayyan said: "We know of no disagreement about the permissibility of jazm (the jussive) in such a construction, and that it is eloquent and preferred without restriction, except what was mentioned by the author of Kitab al-I'rab (the book on grammatical analysis), Abu al-Hakam ibn 'Udhrah, on the authority of some grammarians, that it does not occur in eloquent speech except when the conditional verb is *kana* (was). And it occurs with it only because it is the origin of verbs." The text of Sibawayh and the majority is that it is not restricted to *kana*; rather, all other verbs are like it in this. Sibawayh cited for al-Farazdaq:

*They sent a messenger that, if the people should gain power over you, they would quench their chests [of anger], those who harbor resentment.*

And he also said:

*Live, for if you promise me that you will not betray me, we shall be like one who, O wolf, keeps company [with another].*

[page 28]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 21:**

﴿Or do they have partners (in disbelief), namely the devils, ﴿who have legislated for them﴾, that is, for these disbelievers contemporary with you, through enticement and embellishment, ﴿in religion that for which Allah has not given permission﴾, such as polytheism, denying the Resurrection, and working for the world.

"Am" (or) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), carrying the meaning of "bal" (rather), the interrogative hamzah that serves to affirm, rebuke, and shift away from what preceded, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion﴾, and so on. The conjunction with it, and what came in between the two verses, is a completion of the first. The delay of the shift (idrab) indicates that they are in a law that opposes what Allah, exalted is He, has prescribed in every respect. Thus polytheism is set against establishing the religion and remaining steadfast upon it, and denying the Resurrection is set against His words: ﴿Those who believe are fearful of it and know that it is the truth﴾, and working for the world is set against His words, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾. This is clearer than making the shift refer to what preceded in His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is hard upon the polytheists﴾, as is not hidden.

It has been said: their partners are their idols, and their attribution to them is because they are the ones who made them partners with Allah, glorified is He. Attributing legislation to them is because they are the cause of their misguidance and temptation, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they have led many astray﴾. It is also permissible that the interrogative implied here be for denial, meaning: they have no legislation nor any legislator, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they have gods that protect them from Us?﴾. In any case, the pronoun in (shara'u, they legislated) refers to the partners, and the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾ refers to the disbelievers.

It is also permissible, on the interpretation of the partners as idols, that the first pronoun refer to the disbelievers and the second to the partners, meaning: the disbelievers legislated for their idols and laid down, from beliefs and rulings, what Allah, exalted is He, has not permitted, such as believing that they are gods and that worshipping them brings them closer to Allah, glorified is He, and like the designation of the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah, and other things. This is, as you see, far-fetched.

﴿And had it not been for the decisive word﴾, that is, the judgment and the prior decree from Him, exalted is He, to delay the punishment until the Day of Resurrection or until the end of their lives, ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾, that is, between the disbelievers and the believers in this world, or at the time they separate by punishment and reward. It is also permissible that the meaning be: had it not been for what Allah, exalted is He, promised them of the decision in the Hereafter, the matter would have been decided between them. Thus "fasl" here means "bayan" (clarification), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾. It has been said: the pronoun in "baynahum" refers to the disbelievers and their partners, in whichever sense it is taken.

﴿And indeed the wrongdoers﴾, and they are those spoken of, or the more general category including them, and they enter [the Fire] first; ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter. And in al-Bahr: that is, in this world, by killing, captivity, and plunder, and in the Hereafter, by the Fire.

Al-A'raj and Muslim ibn Jundub read "wa-anna" with a fath on the hamzah, conjoining it to ﴿the decisive word﴾, meaning: had it not been for the prior decree to delay the punishment and the determination that the wrongdoers have a painful punishment in the Hereafter; or had it not been for the promise that the decision will take place on the Day of Resurrection, and the determination that the wrongdoers have..., the matter would have been decided between them. The conjunction under both interpretations is a completion of clarification, not a purely explanatory one.

[p. 29]

﴿You see the wrongdoers﴾ is a resumed sentence (*jumla mustani'a*) explaining what came before. The address is to anyone who is capable of seeing, aimed at emphasising the wretchedness of their condition: "You, whoever is capable of sight, see the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection ﴿fearful﴾, dreading intensely ﴿of what they have earned﴾ in the world of evil deeds." It has been said that the statement involves an omitted noun (*muḍāf*) in its construction.

The "min" (from) is connected to *al-ishfāq* (fear): "fearful of the consequence of what they earned." ﴿And it﴾, that is, the consequence, ﴿befalls them﴾, that is, it is realised for them and overtakes them. Some scholars chose that there is no omission and that "min" is causal (*ta'līliyya*), because it falls within the threat (*wa'īd*). The clause is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*) indicating that their fear will not benefit them. The choice of *wāqi'* (falls, present participle) over *yaqa'u* (will fall) implies that the meaning is about the future, because fear arises from anticipation, unlike grief; the participle shows its certainty and that it is inevitable. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *mushfiqīn*. What you have heard clearly indicates that it is a future-oriented circumstantial clause (*ḥāl muqaddara*).

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds, in the meadows of the gardens﴾, that is, they will abide in the most pleasant and pure parts of them.

Al-Rāghib said: they are their finest qualities and delights. The root of *rawḍa* is a pool of water and greenery. The common dialectal pronunciation of its plural with a vowel-less "w" is as in *al-manzil*. The dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrika is to vocalise it with a fatha, saying *rawaḍāt*, treating the weak letter as if it were sound, like *jafanāt*. To our knowledge, no one has recited it in their dialect.

﴿For them is whatever they wish for with their Lord﴾, that is, whatever they desire of the various kinds of delights is theirs with their Lord. Thus the adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*) is connected to the element connected to the prepositional phrase that serves as the predicate of *mā*, or to it. Jār Allāh (al-Zamakhsharī) chose this and denied that it is connected to *yashā'ūn* (they wish), even though that is the apparent grammatical reading. The author of al-Kashf (*ṣāḥib al-Kashf*) explained this by saying that it is a statement in the context of emphasising the lasting bliss that the people of Paradise will enjoy. Thus it is conveyed that they are in the most pleasant place of Paradise and its finest seat, by His saying "in the meadows of the gardens," because a meadow of Paradise is its most pleasant place, especially since the construct here indicates its distinction in nobility and goodness. The following statement "for them is whatever they wish" also further conveys that they have whatever they desire from their Lord. There is no doubt that if you say, "I have with so-and-so whatever I wish," it is more emphatic in securing all your requests from him than if you say, "I have whatever I wish with so-and-so," in terms of the seeker and the one sought from.

As for the first, it indicates that everything you wish for exists and is granted to you by him. The second indicates that whatever you wish is granted with him, not that everything you wish is granted. As for the second, you describe him as granting all desires; and in the second you describe him as having whatever you wish granted to you, either from him or from another. Then, in the first there is emphasis on establishing and confirming this, as you say, "I have with you and in your keeping such-and-such." God, exalted is His majesty, informs that this is a right for them, established and decreed in the obligation of His bounty, glorified is He; this is not so in the second.

Then he said: Perhaps the better view is that ﴿with their Lord﴾ be taken as another predicate, meaning: those who believed and did righteous deeds are with their Lord, in the meadows of the gardens, for them therein is whatever they wish. It was placed later in order to follow the path of emphasis in ascending from the lower to the higher, and in observance of the order of existence as well. The guest and the visitor alight in the most pleasant place, then whatever they desire is brought before them. The essence of all this is that the Lord of the house singles them out with nearness and honour. If he makes it a circumstantial clause from the subject of *yashā'ūn* or from the prepositional pronoun in ﴿for them﴾, this meaning is also conveyed, but it falls short of what we have chosen, because it comes as a supplementary element (*faḍla*), whereas it is intended in itself as a principal element (*'umda*). By my life, what he chose is good in meaning, except that it is further removed in wording than what Jār Allāh chose. What is more suitable for the revelation is not hidden from you.

In a report from Abū Ẓabya, he said: Indeed, flocks of the people of Paradise will be shaded by a cloud, which will say, "What shall I rain upon you?" So no one among the people calls out but that it rains upon him, to the extent that the speaker among them says, "Rain upon us maidens, of equal age (*kawā'ib atrāban*)."

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned of the state of the believers. The sense of distance in it indicates the remoteness of the status of what is referred to. ﴿It is the great bounty﴾ which its measure cannot be estimated, its extent cannot be reached, and beside which whatever others have in the world becomes insignificant.

[Page 30]

﴿That﴾ refers to the great bounty, or the reward understood from the context, which is ﴿that which Allah gives good news of to His servants who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾. That is, He gives good news of it. The particle (bi, "of") was omitted, and then the pronoun referring back to the relative (al-mawṣūl) was omitted, in keeping with their habit of omitting gradually. As al-Shihab said, there is no obstacle to omitting both at once. It is also permissible that ﴿that﴾ be a reference to the good news understood from ﴿gives good news﴾ later on. A demonstrative may refer to something understood only afterward, as they have established regarding the verse ﴿Thus We have made you a justly balanced community﴾ and similar verses. The pronoun referring back to the relative is in the accusative, governed by ﴿gives good news﴾, as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, a verbal noun used for emphasis or specification), because it is a pronoun for the verbal noun. That is: that good news, He gives it to His servants.

Abu Hayyan claimed that it does not make sense to take the demonstrative as referring to the good news, since the word "good news" (bushrā) has not been mentioned earlier, nor anything indicating it. This arises from heedlessness toward what you have just heard. So there is no need to answer him: the fact that what preceded constituted good news for the believers is sufficient for this to be valid. He then said: Some grammarians made the relative ﴿alladhī﴾ a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle. Ibn Malik related this from Yunus, and interpreted this verse accordingly, meaning: that is the good news of Allah, the Exalted, to His servants. But this is not valid, because it asserts a shared meaning between two things of different definitions without evidence, and the nominal status of ﴿alladhī﴾ is established, so one should not deviate from it for something that no evidence or even doubt supports.

ʿAbdullah ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jahdari, al-Aʿmash, Talha (in one narration), al-Kisa'i, and Hamza read ﴿yubashshiru﴾ as a triliteral verb (yabshuru). Mujahid and Humayd ibn Qays read it with a damma on the yāʾ and a light shīn, from abshara. This form is transitive by the hamza, from bashira (intransitive, with the shīn vowelled with kasra). If it is bashara (with fatha on the shīn), it is transitive. Bashsharra with the doubled shīn is for intensification, not for transitivity, because the form that is already transitive to one object, in its light form, is not made transitive by doubling. So the doubling in it is for intensification, not for transitivity.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾, that is, for what I undertake for you of conveying and giving good news and other things, ﴿a reward﴾, that is, any benefit at all. In common usage the word is specific to wealth. ﴿Except affection﴾, that is, except your affection for me, ﴿concerning the near kin﴾, that is, because of my kinship with you. Here "in" (fī) indicates causation, like its use in the hadith: "a woman entered the Fire because of a cat." So it has the meaning of "for" (lām), since cause and reason are close in meaning. This meaning was taken by Mujahid, Qatada, and a group of others. The address is either to the Quraysh, as some have said: they gathered wealth for him and wanted to bribe him so that he would stop cursing their gods, but he did not do so, and the verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) had kinship with all of them. Ahmad, al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Tirmidhi, and others related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was asked about the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿except affection concerning the near kin﴾. Said ibn Jubayr said: "The near kin of the family of Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "You have been hasty. The Prophet (ﷺ) had no clan of the Quraysh without having kinship with them." Or it refers to the Ansar, based on what has been said: they came to him with wealth so that he might use it to help with what befell him, and the verse was revealed, and he returned it. The Prophet (ﷺ) also had kinship with them, because they were his maternal relatives. The mother of ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Salma bint Zayd al-Najjariyya, was from them, and likewise the maternal relatives of Amina, his mother (ﷺ), were, according to some histories, also from the Ansar. Or it refers to all the Arabs, because of his (ﷺ) kinship with them all in general. How could it not be so, since they are either ʿAdnanites, and the Quraysh are among them, or Qahtanites, and the Ansar are among them? His kinship with each of these groups is well known, and that entails his kinship with all the Arabs. Quda'a are from Qahtan and are not a separate division, according to what most genealogists hold. The meaning is: if you do not recognize my right because of my prophethood and because I am a universal mercy and complete blessing, then at least show affection for me for the sake of the right of kinship and the ties of kinship which you take care to preserve and protect.

The summary is: I do not ask you for anything except affection for me and the protection of my rights because of my kinship with you, and that is an obligation upon you. Something similar is related in the two Sahihs from Ibn ʿAbbas. Indeed, this was narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, in many reports, and their apparent meaning is that the address is to the Quraysh. Among them is what Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Saʿd, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related

[Page 31]

from al-Shaʿbi, who said: "People argued a great deal about us concerning this verse: ﴿Say: I do not ask you...﴾ etc. So we wrote to Ibn ʿAbbas asking him, and he wrote, may Allah be pleased with him: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was of the middle of the lineage among the Quraysh; there was no clan among their clans except that he had descendants from it." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾, for what I call you to, ﴿except affection concerning the near kin﴾, that you love me because of my kinship with you and protect me through it. Among them is what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani related from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had kinship with all of the Quraysh. When they denied him and refused to follow him, he said: O people, if you refuse to follow me, then protect my kinship among you. Let no one other than you among the Arabs be more worthy of protecting and supporting me than you." The apparent meaning of these reports is that the verse was revealed in Mecca. The claim that it was about the Ansar would imply that it was Medinan. The exception is connected (istithnāʾ muttaṣil, an exception of the same kind as what precedes), based on what I have stated regarding the generalization of the reward.

It has been said: there is no need for generalization. That affection mentioned is one of the forms of the reward is a sufficient claim for the exception to be connected. It has also been said that the exception is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, an exception of a different kind from what precedes), either based on the view that affection for the Prophet (ﷺ) is not a reward at all in relation to him (ﷺ), or because it is obligatory upon them so that they may be praised for maintaining the ties of kinship, so its benefit returns to them. The disconnected view is more decisive, because of the apparent conflict between this verse and the verses that negate asking for any reward at all. A group went to the view that the meaning is: I do not ask you for any reward except your love for my family and my kin. In al-Bahr it is stated that this is the view of Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. The "in" (fī) in ﴿concerning﴾ is for figurative location, and ﴿the near kin﴾ means "the relatives." The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause, that is: except affection established and firmly rooted among my relatives. Because of the eminence of this meaning, the verse did not say "except affection for the near kin." It is mentioned that according to the first view it is like this too. The matter of the exception being connected or disconnected is as previously mentioned. The meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) kinship in this view is said to be: the children of ʿAbd al-Muttalib. It has also been said: ʿAli, Fatima, and their children, may Allah be pleased with them all. This has been related as a raised (marfuʿ) report. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh related by way of Ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Say: I do not ask you...﴾ etc., they said: O Messenger of Allah, who are your kin whose affection is obligatory? He said: ʿAli, Fatima, and their children, peace be upon the Prophet and upon them."

The chain of this report, according to what al-Suyuti said in al-Durr al-Manthur, is weak, and Ibn Hajar stated its weakness in his takhrij of the hadiths of al-Kashshaf. Furthermore, even if it were sound, Ibn ʿAbbas would not have said what is related from him in the Sahihs and elsewhere, which has already been mentioned. However, it has been related from a group of the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt) what supports this. Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Daylam, who said: "When ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, was brought as a captive and set up on the steps of Damascus, a man from the people of Syria stood up and said: Praise be to Allah who killed you and uprooted you! ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: Have you read the Qur'an? He said: Yes. He said: Have you read the Ha Mim (surahs)? He said: Yes. He said: Have you not read: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it except affection concerning the near kin﴾? He said: Then are you truly they? He said: Yes." Dhadhan related from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "Regarding us, in the Ha Mim (surahs) there is a verse which none but a believer preserves the affection for us," and then he recited this verse. To this the poet al-Kumayt alluded in his words:

We found for you in the Ha Mim a verse, its interpretation by one of us who is pious and eloquent.

To Allah, the Exalted, belongs the excellence of the noble ʿUmar al-Haythi, one of the contemporary relatives (of the Prophet), when he says:

By what sign will Yazid come on the day when the scrolls of deeds are recited?
And the Messenger of the Lord of the Throne will stand reciting, while all creation is struck dumb: "Say, I ask..."

According to this view, the address is to the whole community, not to the Ansar alone, even if what appears to indicate otherwise has been transmitted, since they are all obligated to show affection for the People of the House. Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i related from Zayd ibn Arqam that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I remind you of Allah concerning my House (Ahl al-Bayt)." al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as good, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Love Allah for the blessings He provides you with, love me for the love of Allah, and love the People of my House for my love." Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim related from Abu Saʿid, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no one hates us, the People of the House, except that Allah will cause him to enter the Fire." And there are other reports too numerous to count. Some of these reports indicate that the term "the near kin" is general and includes the descendants of ʿAbd al-Muttalib.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as sound), and al-Nasa'i related from al-Muttalib ibn Rabiʿa, who said: "al-ʿAbbas entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: We go out and see the Quraysh talking, and when they see us they fall silent. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry, and sweat appeared between his eyes, and then he said: By Allah, faith does not enter the heart of a Muslim man until he loves you for the sake of Allah and for my kinship." This is clear if "the near kin" is restricted to the believers among them. Otherwise, it has been said that the ruling is abrogated (mansukh, that is, replaced by a later ruling). But this is open to question. The truth is the obligation to love the kin of the Prophet (ﷺ) because they are his kin, whatever their condition. How excellent is what has been said:

I have been courteous to your family for your sake, even though they are enemies; for the sake of one eye, a thousand eyes are honored.

The closer the bond of kinship, the stronger the call for affection. So the affection of the ʿAlids, the Fatimids, is more binding than love for the ʿAbbasids, according to the view that "the near kin" is general. And according to the view that it is specific, this affection too varies according to the variation in aspects and considerations. The effects of that affection are reverence, respect, and fulfilling its rights in the most complete manner. Yet many people have neglected this, to the point that they counted following these paths as rafḍ (rejectionism, a term used for certain Shiʿi groups). As for me, I say the words of al-Shafiʿi, the one who cures the blind:

O rider, stop at al-Muhassab in Mina, and call out to the one who dwells in Khayf and the one who rises,
At dawn when the pilgrims pour out toward Mina, in a flood like the surging Euphrates in spate:
If loving the family of Muhammad is rafḍ, then let both humans and jinn bear witness that I am a rafiḍi.

[Page 33]

Despite this, I do not regard leaving the creed that the great scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunnis) hold concerning the Companions (sahabah) as religiously acceptable. I consider love for them an obligation upon me, one made clear, since the Lawgiver (al-Shari') has also made it obligatory, and manifest proofs have been established for it.

Among the curiosities is what al-Imam related from some preachers (al-mudhakkirin), who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of my household (Ahl al-Bayt) is like the Ark of Noah: whoever boards it is saved, and whoever stays behind from it perishes." He (ﷺ) also said: "My Companions are like the stars: whichever of them you follow, you will be guided." Now we are in the sea of moral responsibility (bahr al-taklif), and the waves of doubts (shubuhat) and desires (shahawat) strike us. The one who rides the sea needs two things: first, a ship free of defects, and second, bright stars that rise. When he boards that ship and fixes his gaze upon those stars, hope of safety becomes strong. Therefore our companions, the Ahl al-Sunnah, boarded the ship of love for the family of Muhammad (ﷺ) and fixed their gaze upon the stars of the Companions, hoping to win safety and felicity in this world and the Hereafter. End of quotation. Many people, regarding both the family and the Companions, go to one of two extremes: negligence (tafrit) or excess (ifrat). What lies between them is the straight path (al-sirat al-mustaqim). May God keep us firm upon that path.

ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Qasim said: The meaning is: "I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that you love one another and maintain your kinship ties." The particle (fi) and the exception are clear.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from al-Hasan that the meaning is: "I do not ask you for any reward for it, except seeking nearness to God through righteous deeds." Thus "al-qurba" means "kinship," but the intended sense is not blood kinship (qarabat al-nasab). It is said that the exception may be either connected (muttasil) or disconnected (munqati') grammatically. Al-Khafaji inclined to the view that it is disconnected (munqati'), and that it is in the manner of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords..." (the verse)

I think the preceding statement is also like this.

Zayd ibn ʿAli (may God be pleased with them both) recited: (illa mawaddatan fi al-qurba).

Among the Shi'ah (Shi'a) is one who cited this verse as evidence for the Imamate of ʿAli (may God ennoble his face). He said: ʿAli is one whose love is obligatory; everyone whose love is obligatory is one whose obedience is obligatory; and everyone whose obedience is obligatory holds the Imamate. The conclusion: ʿAli holds the Imamate. They made the verse the minor premise (sughra). However, there is much to discuss in their argument, as is not hidden. First, the use of the verse for the minor premise is not complete except on the view that its meaning is: "I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that you love my kinsfolk and love my household." But the majority went to the first meaning. It has been said regarding this meaning that it is not suitable to the station of prophethood, because it invites suspicion, for most seekers of worldly gain do something and ask for a reward for it which benefits their children and relatives. Also, it contradicts the words of God: ﴿And you ask them for no reward for it.﴾ Second, we do not accept that every object of obligatory love is an object of obligatory obedience. Ibn Babawayh (Ibn Babuya) mentioned in the book al-Iʿtiqadat that the Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'ah) agreed on the obligation of loving the ʿAlawiyyah (descendants of ʿAli), though obedience to each of them is not obligatory. Third, we do not accept that every object of obligatory obedience holds the Imamate, meaning the supreme leadership (al-zaʿamah al-kubra); otherwise every prophet in his time would hold it. The verse ﴿Indeed God has sent Talut to you as king﴾ rejects this. Fourth, the verse requires that the minor premise be that the People of the House are those whose obedience is obligatory, and when this is the minor premise, their syllogism does not produce the conclusion they mentioned, even if you grant all its premises. Rather, it produces that the People of the House hold the Imamate, and they do not affirm its generality. There are other discussions besides these. So reflect and do not be heedless.

﴿And whoever earns a good deed﴾: that is, whoever acquires any good deed whatsoever. The statement is a concluding addition (tadhyil). It has been said that the intended "good deed" is love for the kinsfolk of the Messenger (ﷺ), and this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi. It is also said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him), because of his intense love for the People of the House, and the story of Fadak. The "ʿawali" (the upper parts of Medina) do not reject this for one who has a sound heart. The discussion of this is a completion (tatmim). Probably the first view is preferable. Love for the family of the Messenger (may blessings and peace be upon him) is among the greatest good deeds, and it enters into "good deed" here by primary entry (dukhul awwali).

﴿We will increase for him therein﴾: that is, in the good deed, ﴿good﴾, by multiplying the reward for it, for by it the goodness of the good deed is increased. Thus "fi" is for locality (zarfiyyah), and "husnan" is either a direct object (maf'ul bihi) or a specification (tamyiz). Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿAbd al-Warith from Abu ʿAmr, and Ahmad ibn Jubayr from al-Kisa'i read (yazid) with the letter ya', meaning "God will increase." ʿAbd al-Warith from Abu ʿAmr read (husna) without tanwin. It is a verbal noun (masdar) like bushra, or an adjective for an implied noun, meaning: an adjective or quality that is good (husna).

﴿Indeed God is Forgiving﴾: concealing the sins of His servants. ﴿Appreciative﴾: rewarding whoever among them obeys, by giving the reward in full and adding more out of His bounty. Al-Suddi said: Forgiving of the sins of the family of Muhammad (ﷺ), Appreciative of their good deeds.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 24:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented against Allah a lie"?﴾ Rather, do they say it? ﴿Invented﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) ﴿against Allah a lie﴾ by claiming prophethood or (claiming) the Qur'an. The hamza is for reproachful denial (al-inkar al-tawbikhi), and "bal" (rather) is for transition (al-idrab) without negation. It is a transition more severe than the first, and more severe still. For affirming what they hold of the law (al-shar'), even if it is evil and polytheism, is closer than making the clear truth, supported by the luminous proof, from the most moderate of them in merit, gentleness and intellect, a fabrication, then another fabrication, against Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is as if it were said: Can they restrain themselves from uttering the attribution of the like of this to him, (ﷺ),
[p. 34]
from fabrication, then from fabrication against Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is the greatest and most shameful of fabrications? Yet their tongues do not burn.

In this there is the clearest indication of his (ﷺ) distance from fabrication. How could it be otherwise, when it is followed by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿If Allah willed, He would seal up your heart﴾? For this style implies the improbability of fabrication from one like him (ﷺ), and that it is, in remoteness, like associating partners with Allah, Glorified is He, and entering into the category of those whose hearts are sealed. It is as if it were said: If Allah, Glorified is He, willed, He would make you one of those sealed upon their hearts, so that you would fabricate a lie against Him. For none dares to fabricate a lie against Allah, Exalted is He, except one who is in a state like theirs. This is in the sense of "If He willed, He would make you one of them," because they are the fabricators, who legislated in the religion what Allah, Exalted is He, did not permit. How excellent is this allusion (al-ta'ridh) that they are the fabricators, and that in this very statement of theirs about his fabrication, they are fabricators.

Similar to the verse, as mentioned, is the saying of a trustee who was accused of betrayal: "Perhaps Allah, Exalted is He, has abandoned me; perhaps Allah, Exalted is He, has blinded my heart." He does not intend to affirm abandonment or blindness of heart, but only to deny that the like of him should be called a traitor, and to point out that from accusing him of treachery a great matter has been composed. So the statement is a justification (ta'lil) for denying their saying. He used "in" (if) although the non-willing of Him, Exalted is He, is certain. It is said this is a loosening of the reins (irkha'an lil-'inan), and it is said it is an indication of His greatness, Exalted is He, and that He, Glorified is He, is free of need of the worlds.

Then he appended with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah erases falsehood and establishes the truth by His words﴾, as an emphasis on what is understood from what precedes, that he is not in any way a fabricator. That is: how could it be fabrication, when it is among His custom, Exalted is He, to erase falsehood and eradicate it, and to establish truth by His revelation or by His decree? What he (ﷺ) brought grows every day in strength and in dispersal. So if he were a fabricator, as they claim, Allah, Exalted is He, would have exposed his fabrication, eradicated it, and cast the truth upon its falsehood, so that it crushes it.

The imperfect verb (al-fi'l al-mudari') here denotes continuity. The sentence is a new (ibtida'i) one, so "yamhu" (erases) is in the nominative, not the jussive, not conjoined to "yakhtim" (seal). The waw was dropped in the orthography in most copies of the Qur'an, following its dropping in pronunciation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, as in ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell﴾.

﴿And man supplicates for evil﴾. The analogical expectation was to write it, but the orthography of the Mushaf need not follow analogy. The resumption (isti'naf) rather than conjunction with "yakhtim" is supported by the repetition of the Glorious Name and the nominative of "yuhiqq." This is what Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned for the two clauses and the explanation of their connection with what precedes them. He examined this closely and brought what the scholars found admirable, until al-'Allama al-Tibi said: "If he had in his book nothing but this, it would suffice him as distinction and excellence." He also permitted, regarding His words ﴿And He erases﴾ etc., that it be a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of victory, that is: Allah, Exalted is He, will erase their falsehood and what they slandered you with, and will establish the truth you are upon, through the Qur'an and His decree which cannot be turned back. In that case it is an interjected clause (i'tiradh) that confirms what the discourse had already established: that they are the falsifiers in this attribution to one who is the most truthful of people in speech, with the truest report, from the truest speaker.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, regarding the first clause, he said: it is an evidence (istishhad) for the invalidity of what they said, by showing that he (ﷺ), if he had fabricated a lie against Allah, Exalted is He, would certainly have been prevented from it. Its verification is that their claim that the Qur'an is a fabrication against Him, Exalted is He, is a statement that He, Glorified is He, does not will its descent upon the Prophet (ﷺ), but wills its non-descent from him. Among the necessities of this is preventing him from it with certainty. It is as if it were said:
[p. 35]
If it were a fabrication against Him, Exalted is He, the non-occurrence of it from you would be willed. And if He willed that, He would seal your heart, so that no meaning of it would occur to your mind and you would not utter a letter of it. Since the matter is not so, but the revelation has repeatedly come down time after time, it is clear that it is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned in the second clause what Jar Allah mentioned of the two aspects. The objections to his words are not hidden from you, along with the prohibition, and that in it is the making of the object of the will something other than what the answer indicates, namely that referred-to non-occurrence. The obvious reading is that the object is the sealing, according to what is well known in similar constructions. That is: if Allah, Exalted is He, wills the sealing upon your heart, He will seal it. And the impression that the Qur'an originates from him (ﷺ) and is not sent down upon him (ﷺ).

Al-Samarqandi said: the meaning is: If He wills, He will seal your heart as He did with them. This is a consolation to him (ﷺ), and a reminder of His kindness to him and His honoring him, so that he may thank his Lord, Glorified is He, and have mercy upon one whose heart was sealed, who thereby deserved the anger of his Lord. Had it not been so, they would not have dared to attribute it to him for the reasons mentioned. So the consequence (al-tafri') is considered in relation to the implied meaning. Its essence is that they dared this because they are stamped upon misguidance. End of quotation. In it there is a trace of what al-Zamakhshari mentioned.

From Qatada and a group: "If Allah wills, He will seal your heart" means: He will make you forget the Qur'an. The intended meaning, as Ibn 'Atiyya said, is the refutation of the disbelievers' saying and the demonstration of its falsehood, as if it were said: How could you be a fabricator, when you are under the sight and hearing of Allah, Exalted is He, who is capable, and if He willed He would seal your heart, so that you would not understand nor speak, and your fabrication would not continue? In this there is that the wording is too narrow to express this meaning.

Al-Qushayri mentioned that the meaning is: "If Allah, Exalted is He, wills, He will seal the hearts of the disbelievers and their tongues, and hasten punishment upon them." He shifted from the third person to the second, and from the plural to the singular. Its essence is: "He will seal your heart, O speaker who says that he (ﷺ) fabricated a lie against Allah, Exalted is He." In this there is as much remoteness as there is, along with the fact that the disbelievers are sealed upon their hearts.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: the meaning is: "If He wills, He will bind your heart with patience regarding their harm, so that their saying that you are a fabricator does not grieve you." There is no obstacle to conjoining "yamhu" to the answer of the condition; indeed this is the apparent reading, so the dropping of the waw would be due to the jussive particle. In that case "yuhiqq" is a resumed clause, meaning: "If He wills, He will erase their falsehood swiftly. But He, Glorified is He, did not do so, for a wisdom, or absolutely; and He did so in the Hereafter and made manifest His religion." It was also said: there is no obstacle to conjoining to some of the earlier opinions as well, that is: "If He wills, He will erase your fabrication, if you had fabricated." This is, as you see, weak. Likewise it was permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (hali), though this requires supposing a subject (mubtada'), and that involves an unnecessary strain.

It may be said that the clause "If Allah wills, He will seal" is part of their statement, as a consequence (mufarra'an) of "he fabricated." It is as if it were said: "He fabricated a lie against Allah. If Allah wills, He will seal his heart because of his fabrication, so that he understands nothing." Or it is as if it were said: "You fabricated against Allah; if He wills, He will seal your heart as the recompense for that." However, the point of choosing the third person in one of the two clauses and the second person in the other is not apparent. That it indicates that whoever fabricates deserves to be confronted with the recompense is not, in my view, something that gladdens the hearer. Perhaps the better reading is that "If He wills" etc. is a consequence of their words, coming out in the form of mockery toward them. There is then no harm in conjoining "yamhu" to the answer of the condition, and by "falsehood" is meant what is falsehood in their opinion. It is as if it were said: "Do they say, 'He fabricated against Allah'? Then, if Allah wills, He will seal your heart, and erase what they claim to be falsehood." This is like saying to one who informs you that Zayd fabricated against you, while you know he did not fabricate, but merely conveyed for you what you had commanded him: "Then we will discipline him, take revenge on him, and erase his fabrication," intending by that to mock the speaker. So reflect.

This verse, as al-Khafaji said, is among the most difficult of what has passed in the speech of the Mighty Exalted. May Allah grant us and you success in understanding its meanings and standing upon its secret and what is hidden in it.

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. He, Glorified is He, knows what is in your breast and in theirs, and so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, orders the matter according to that.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 25:**

﴿He it is who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ by overlooking what they have repented of. The verb *yaqbalu* (accepts) takes *ʿan* because it implies *al-ibanah* (removing, turning away from), and takes *min* because it implies *al-akhdh* (taking), as in His saying, ﴿And nothing prevented their contributions from being accepted from them﴾, meaning *tu'khadh* (taken). It has also been said that *al-qabul* here implies *al-tajawuz* (overlooking), and that the sentence has an elided noun, meaning: He accepts repentance, overlooking the sins of His servants. But this is a forced reading.

*Tawbah* (repentance) is that a person turns back from the ugly act and from neglecting an obligation at the present time, regrets what has passed, and resolves not to return to it in the future.

[p. 36]

And they added: the discharge of it by whatever means is possible, if the sin involves a right of a servant. This is done by returning the right to him or to his agent, or by seeking his pardon if he is alive, or by returning it to his heirs if he is dead. And they added: [seek out] the judge, if he is trustworthy, and he is like the elixir, and who has seen the elixir? If one is unable to do any of that, he gives charity on his behalf, and otherwise he prays for him and seeks forgiveness.

In *al-Kashf* it is said: the discharge is included in the return, since returning from it is not valid while one is still involved in it. It has been preferred that the reality of repentance is the return, and that regret and resolve are only so that the return becomes a withdrawal, and so that it is verified as the repentance that we have been urged to. This agrees with what is in *al-Ihya* (*Ihya' ʿUlum al-Din* of al-Ghazali), that repentance is in reality the name of that state, and the rest are conditions of its realisation. It is also required that the motive for returning, together with regret and resolve, be religious. If one returns because of some other obstacle, such as physical weakness or a fine for that, it is not part of repentance at all. Al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) pointed to this by stating that the return is because what one returns from is ugly and a neglect of an obligation. Excluded from this is the case where one returns seeking praise, or out of showing off, or for reputation, because the ugliness of the ugly act means that it entails punishment in the next life and blame in this life. So if one returns from what came before, it is not a return from that.

Jabir narrated that a Bedouin entered the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Allah, I ask You for forgiveness and I turn to You in repentance," and he said *Allahu Akbar*. When he finished his prayer, Ali, may Allah honour his face, said to him: "Quickness of the tongue in seeking forgiveness is the repentance of liars, and your repentance needs repentance." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is repentance?" He said: "It is a term that applies to six meanings: regret for the sins of the past; restoring the obligations that were neglected; returning the wrongs taken; melting the self in obedience just as you had nurtured it in disobedience; making the self taste the bitterness of obedience just as you made it taste the sweetness of disobedience; and weeping in place of every laugh you laughed." This may mean that repentance is the combination of all these matters, so that what is meant is its most complete form. It may also mean that it is the name of each one of them individually. The first is more apparent.

It has been disputed whether repentance from some sins while persisting in others is valid. What the scholars of the Sunnah hold is that it is valid, because of the apparent meanings of the verses and hadiths, and because the definition truly applies to it. Most of the Mu'tazilah hold that it is not valid. Abu Hashim among them said: if one repents from an ugly act because it is ugly, it is obligatory that he repent from all ugly acts; and if he repents from it not merely because of its ugliness but for another purpose, his repentance is not valid. This has been objected to: it is possible that the motive is the severity of the ugliness, or another religious matter. Also, the same applies to doing a good act: if one does good because it is good, it is obligatory that he do every good; and if he does it for another purpose, it is not accepted. There is discussion on this.

The Mu'tazilah used the verse to argue that it is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to accept repentance. The people of the Sunnah used it to argue against obligation, on the basis of the praise it contains, since there is no praise for what is obligatory. There is also discussion on this. The more beneficial approach in this context is the evidences for the negation of obligation upon Him, exalted and majestic is He, absolutely.

﴿And pardons evil deeds﴾, both minor and major, for whomever He wills, without requiring anything such as repentance for major sins or avoidance of major sins for minor ones.

Al-Tibi said: the meaning is that it is among His majesty's nature, exalted is His majesty, to accept the repentance of His servants when they repent, and to pardon their evil deeds purely by His mercy or by the intercession of an intercessor. The Mu'tazilah said: that is, He pardons major sins when repented of, and minor sins when major sins are avoided. Thus pardoning evil deeds on this view is more general than accepting repentance, because it includes minor sins when major ones are avoided, and this is generalisation after specification. The apparent meaning is with the people of the Sunnah, since the glorious wording has no indication of restricting the evil deeds. Yes, what is meant by them excludes *shirk* (associating partners with Allah), by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus).

﴿And He knows what you do﴾, with the second person (*ta'*) according to Hafs, al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisai), and Alqamah and ʿAbd Allah, and with the third person (*ya'*) according to the majority. On the first reading there is *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person). *Ma* is a relative pronoun and the returning pronoun is elided, meaning: He knows what you do, whatever it is of good or evil, so He rewards with reward and punishment; or He overlooks by pardon as His will, which is founded on wisdom and benefits, dictates, glory be to Him and exalted is He.

[p. 37]

It has been said: He knows that, so He rewards the one who repents and overlooks others when He wills, glory be to Him. The first is more apparent. In *al-Kashshaf*: He, glory be to Him, knows that, so He rewards good deeds and punishes evil deeds. In *al-Kashf*, after quoting it, he said: it is, that is, His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And He knows﴾ etc. is a *tadhyil* (a concluding generalisation) of the preceding speech, affirming what was mentioned of acceptance and pardon, because when He, exalted is He, knows both the deeds and the doers, He recompenses each for what he did, so it is more fitting that He recompense these doers of good for their deeds. Then in it there is gentleness and encouragement to be wary of Him, exalted is He, and to be sincere toward Him, glory be to Him, in making repentance pure. We also do not deny that it is a *tadhyil* with emphasis, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 26:

﴿And He responds to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is coordinated with "He it is who accepts repentance" (yaqbalu al-tawbah), so its subject is the pronoun referring to Him, the Exalted, and "those who believe" is the object without any supplied word. This is based on the view that yastajību (responds) is transitive by itself, just as it is transitive with the preposition lām, as in "I thanked him" (shakartuhu) and "I thanked him" (shakartu lahu). Alternatively, the lām is supplied, so that it belongs to the category of ḥadhf wa-l-īṣāl (omitting a particle and making the verb transitive directly). The original form is yastajību lil-ladhīna āmanū, based on the view that it takes lām for the one who calls and directly for the supplication. A similar usage is his saying:

"And a caller who called, 'O you who answers to generosity,' but at that moment no responder responded to him."

Ajāba and istajāba have the same meaning, i.e., "And Allah responds to those who believe when they call upon Him," and the sense is that He answers their supplication. Some have allowed that the speech contains this omitted noun (muḍāf), and it has been said: "This is better than the view of making the verb transitive by omitting the particle, because omitting the noun when it causes no ambiguity is common (qiyās) and that is attested (masmūʿ)." It is also permissible that the meaning is that He rewards them for their obedience, for obedience, insofar as it seeks what follows from it of reward, resembles supplication, and the rewarding for it resembles answering. For this reason praise is called supplication, because what follows from it is what follows from supplication. Sufyan was asked about his saying, upon him be blessings and peace, in the ḥadīth: "The most frequent of my supplication and the supplication of the prophets before me is: There is no god but Allah alone, without partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable." He said: "This is like His saying, the Exalted, in the ḥadīth qudsī: 'Whoever is occupied with remembering Me instead of asking Me, I shall give him the best of what I give those who ask.'" Do you not see the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt to Ibn Jud'an when he came to him seeking his gift:

"Shall I mention my need, or has your praise sufficed me? Indeed your nature is modesty.
When a man praises you one day, the praise suffices him from exposing you (to requests)."

They also counted among this his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "The best supplication is 'Praise be to Allah'," in the sense that praise indicates supplication and request by way of kināya (metonymy) and taʿrīḍ (allusion). It has been said that it is the application of the term supplication to praise because of its resemblance to it in seeking what follows from it. It is also permissible that the word "responding" be taken in its literal meaning (ḥaqīqah) together with "rewarding," based on the view that it is valid to combine the literal and the figurative (majāz) meanings, i.e., He responds to their supplication and rewards them for their obedience. ﴿And He increases them﴾ beyond what they asked and deserved ﴿from His bounty﴾, the vast, may His majesty be exalted. It has been said that the subject of ﴿And those who believe respond﴾ is (the believers), which Abu Hayyan preferred, and the sentence is coordinated with the whole statement of His saying: ﴿He it is who accepts repentance﴾ and so on, i.e., they submit to Allah, the Exalted, and respond to Him, glorified be He, when He calls them. This is what has been narrated from Ibn Jubayr. And it is reported of Ibrahim ibn Adham that he was asked: "Why is it that we call upon Him but are not answered?" He said: "Because He, glorified be He, called you and you did not respond to Him." Then he recited: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾.

﴿And those who believe respond﴾: this confirms this aspect, because he (may his secret be sanctified) mentioned that Allah, the Exalted, has called you by His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾, and he mentioned that the believer is the one who answers the call of his Lord, the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿And those who believe respond﴾. So whoever does not answer His call, the Exalted, He does not answer his call either. That the subject is His pronoun has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Muʿadh ibn Jabal, which requires it. ﴿And He increases them﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it. On the other view it is coordinated with an implied element, i.e., He will fully pay them their rewards and add to them over these, in the manner of ﴿And they both said, "Praise be to Allah who has preferred us"﴾ and His saying, glorified be He: ﴿from His bounty﴾, which is connected to "He increases them" without restriction. It is permissible that it be connected to both verbs by tanāzuʿ (syntactic contention), since responding and reward are both a bounty from Him, the Exalted, like the increase.

Whichever is the case, the apparent meaning is the generality of "those who believe." It is narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that "when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to Medina and Islam became firmly established, the Anṣār said among themselves: 'Let us go to the Messenger of Allah, upon him be blessings and peace, and say to him: If affairs trouble you, these are our wealth, dispose of them as you wish.' Then this was revealed: Say, ﴿I do not ask you for it any reward except affection for relatives﴾. He recited it to them and said: 'You love my relatives after me.' So they went out satisfied. But the hypocrites said: 'This is something he has fabricated in his gathering, intending by it the honour of his relatives after him.' Then this was revealed: ﴿Or do they say, 'He has invented about Allah a lie'?﴾ He sent for them and recited it to them, and they wept and regretted. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿And He it is who accepts repentance from His servants﴾. So the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent to them and gave them good news and said: ﴿And those who believe respond﴾, and they are those who submitted to his saying." This was mentioned by al-Tabarsi, and something close to it was mentioned in al-Durr al-Manthur, but he said: "Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat, and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn Jubayr with a weak chain." What predominates in the mind is that it is fabricated. ﴿But the disbelievers, for them is a severe punishment﴾, in place of what the believers have of response and bounty.

[Page 38]

[Page 39]

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 42, verse 27:

﴿If Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth﴾. That is, they would become arrogant in it out of insolence and would exceed the limit that befits servants. Or, some of them would wrong others, for wealth is a cause of insolence and of rising above others. The condition of Qarun is sufficient as a lesson. In a hadith (a report of the Prophet's words or actions) it is said: «What I fear most for my community is the splendour of this world and its abundance.» One of the Arabs said:

*The rain of Wasmi has made grow between us and the Banu Ruman / a nabi' tree and a shawhat tree.*

Baghy (rebellion, transgression) originally means seeking more than what is due, whether by exceeding in quantity and amount or in attribute and manner.

﴿But He sends down﴾: *yunazzilu* is read with the doubled letter (tashdid). Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it without doubling, from *inzal*. ﴿in measure﴾: by determining, ﴿what He wills﴾: which is what His wisdom requires, exalted is His majesty. ﴿Indeed He is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾: encompassing the hidden and manifest matters of their affairs. So He determines for each one of them, at every time, what befits His dignity. He makes some poor and some rich, withholds and gives, restricts and expands, according to what Divine wisdom requires. If He made them all rich, they would rebel; if He made them all poor, they would perish.

The verse has been questioned on the ground that wealth may cause rebellion, but poverty may also do so, so the conditional would not hold. Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) answered that there is no doubt that rebellion is less with poverty and more, and more prevalent, with expansion. Both are apparent causes for advancing into rebellion or refraining from it. So if expansion were universal, rebellion would prevail until the situation is reversed from what it is now. And Allah, Exalted, knows best, intends that the order of the world remains as it is, even though some rebellion may occasionally come from the rich and likewise from the poor. But in one of them there is something that restrains the other. As for making all of them poor, weakness and destruction would necessarily follow. And if He expanded provision for all of them, even though need is natural, there would be rebellion beyond measure, because the order of the world depends on poverty more than on wealth. This is an obvious and manifest matter. Moreover, total poverty cannot be imagined with rebellion, because of general weakness, and because the poor person does not find what he needs with others so as to wrong them. As for total wealth, rebellion is complete with it. What is the custom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the one that combines both matters: it includes fear in the rich of the poor, which restrains him from wrongdoing, and fear in the poor of the rich, greater than it, which calls him to cooperation so that he may attain his aim, and restrains him from rebellion. Then rebellion from one or the other may occasionally happen. Thus has the author of *al-Kashshaf* established it. Then he said: "This is a good answer with no artificiality in it." This is an allusion to the rebuttal of the scholar al-Tibi, for he claimed that it was a contrived answer and that the objection was strong. He himself went to the view that by ﴿His servants﴾ is meant those whom Allah, Exalted, has honoured and made among His friends. Then he said: "The concluding statement supports him, in the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed He is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾."

[Page 39]

The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, meaning: indeed He, Exalted, is All-Aware of the conditions of His honoured servants, All-Seeing of what sets them right and what ruins them. To this one refers what was reported from him, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ): "When Allah loves a servant, He protects him from the world as one of you protects his sick person from water."
