And the statement of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt strengthens this: "We looked at the wealth of the Banu Qurayzah, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa', and we wished for it, and then the verse ﴿If Allah were to expand provision…﴾ was revealed." And the statement of Amr ibn Hurayth: "Some people from the Ahl al-Suffah (companions of the Prophet who lived in the shaded area of the mosque) asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that Allah make them rich and expand wealth and provision for them, and then this was revealed." And the commentary of Muhyi al-Sunnah (al-Baghawi) follows this. End.

It is not hidden that what is more fitting for the condition of the honoured and chosen servants of Allah, Exalted, is that wealth should not make them insolent, because of the purity of their inner selves, the strength of their turning toward the sacred enclosures, their hearts' greater attachment to their Beloved, their standing upon the realities of things, and the completeness of their knowledge of the ends of the worldly life's adornments. And the people of this world, if they reflected on this with true reflection, their matter would become trivial and their passion would diminish, as it has been said:

*If the lover reflected on the ultimate beauty of the One who captivates him, he would not be captivated.*

So the better view is what preceded. Or it may be said that this applies to some of the believing servants. So reflect.

﴿And it is He who sends down the rain﴾, that is, the rain by which He brings relief to them from drought. For this reason, the word *ghayth* is reserved for beneficial rain, so one does not say *ghayth* for every rain. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿yunzilu﴾ with a light (unstressed) *nun*.

﴿after they have despaired﴾, that is, they gave up hope of it. Restricting its sending down to this condition, although it occurs without this condition too, serves to remind of the completeness of the blessing. Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read ﴿qanitu﴾ with a *kasra* on the *nun*.

﴿and spreads His mercy﴾, that is, the benefits of the rain and its effects on everything: on the plain, the mountain, the plants and the animals. Or, His vast mercy, which encompasses what has been mentioned in an initial, general way. It has been said that the mercy here is the appearance of the sun, because when the rain lasts long people become weary, so the sun comes after it with a great effect. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, but it is nothing. Even more remote is what al-Suddi said, that the mercy here is the rain itself, so that the same blessing is counted twice with two expressions. In any case, the pronoun in ﴿His mercy﴾ refers to God, glorified and exalted, though on the first view it may be taken to refer to the rain.

﴿And He is the Protector﴾, who looks after His servants with kindness and the spreading of mercy, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, who alone deserves praise for that, not any other than Him, glorified is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 29:

﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ in the wondrous craftsmanship they possess, for they, by their essence and attributes, point to His great affairs, may He be exalted. Whoever has even a little fairness and awareness will be certain that such things could not have proceeded from nature, which lacks awareness.

﴿And what He has scattered throughout them﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿the heavens﴾, meaning: and among His signs is the creation of that which He has scattered; or it is a conjunction with ﴿creation﴾, meaning: and among His signs is what He has scattered. Ma (ما) may be a relative pronoun or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), and the relative reading is more apparent, and there is no need to posit an elided noun, i.e., "the creation of that which He scattered," contrary to Abu Hayyan. ﴿of living creature﴾, i.e., an animal that has movement and motion. The apparent meaning of the verse is that such creatures exist in the heavens and on the earth, and Mujahid said this, and he explained "dabbah" (living creature) as humans and angels. It is possible that the angels have walking alongside flying. Ibn al-Munir objected to this, saying that applying "dabbah" to humans is far-fetched in the usage of the language, so how much more so to angels; and he claimed that the more correct view is that living creatures are only on the earth. Whatever is in one of the two things is truly said to be in both collectively, so the verse follows the style of ﴿From both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾. This is because His saying in al-Baqarah: ﴿And He scattered therein every kind of living creature﴾ indicates that living creatures are specific to the earth, since the context of elaboration would require mentioning it if it were otherwise, relying on the principle of the "concept of the title" (mafhum al-laqab), which the majority do not hold. The answer is that the one in al-Baqarah, since it is an address to the dull, the intelligent, the seeker of guidance, and the obstinate, is phrased with what is known to all, namely the scattering of living creatures on the earth. Here, however, it is phrased in a condensed and abbreviated form, because of what has been repeated in the Qur'an, especially in this surah, regarding His complete power over every possibility. So it is said: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has scattered throughout them﴾, placing the word "creation" first, to indicate multiplicity, which points to perfection of power. It is clarified by His saying: ﴿of living creature﴾, as a generalization and a predominance for non-rational beings in both the heavenly and earthly realms, to affirm that they are created. For it is established in the sound hadiths what indicates the existence of living creatures in the heaven, such as the mounts of the people of Paradise and others, and likewise what indicates the existence of angels like the wild goats. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that in every heaven there are animals and creatures in various forms and differing states which we do not know, and nothing of them is mentioned in the reports, since He, exalted, said: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾. Today the astronomers imagine that creatures appear to them through their telescopes in the body of the moon, but they have not verified the matter, due to deficiency in the instruments, as they claim. It may be that there are such creatures in other than the moon, and denying this is not among what is known of the religion by necessity, so that affirming it would be harmful. It has also been said: the intended meaning of the heavens is the directions of height opposite the regions, for example, and in the air of every climate, indeed every city, indeed every piece of the earth, there are living creatures whose multitude none can count except God, some of which are perceived without any instrument and some with its aid. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the clouds, and in them are animals of what is in them. All of this, on the view that it contains, is not necessary. Likewise, there is no need for what many have held, that the intended meaning of "dabbah" is "the living," figuratively, either by using the restricted for the general, or by applying a thing to its necessary concomitant or its effect to its cause, since life is a cause of movement, even if the living creature is not a cause of life; this would be a figurative metonymy (majaz mursal tab'i), because resorting to that is a departure from the apparent meaning, and one does not depart from the apparent meaning except when a proof indicates otherwise. And where is that proof? Rather, the proof stands on the existence of living creatures in the heaven just as they exist on the earth.

﴿And He is, over their gathering﴾, i.e., their assembling after resurrection for reckoning, ﴿when He wills﴾ that, ﴿All-Powerful﴾, of complete and perfect power. And ("when", idha) is connected to what precedes it, not to "All-Powerful", because what is conditioned by the will is His gathering them, not His power, glorified is He. It enters upon the past tense just as it enters upon the present, and from this is his saying:

"And when I will, I raise from them, at the end of the night, one who is agile and terrified."

As for the statement of the author of al-Kashf: one may distinguish between "idha" and "idha ma", the apparent meaning being that it is not in its proper place. Al-Khafaji stated that there is no difference, and he considered the claim of a difference to be a delusion. Likewise, he stated that it enters upon both verbs, whether as a temporal or a conditional particle. Al-Tibi restricted that to when it carries the sense of time, as it does here. As for the pronoun in "their gathering", it has been said that it refers to the heavens and the earth and what is in them, by predominance, and this, as you see, is weak. It has also been said that it refers to the living creatures understood from what preceded, and the pronoun for the rational beings is by predominance, suited to the gathering being for reckoning. And it has been said that it refers to people, understood from that, and perhaps this is the preferable view.

[Page 41]

﴿Whatever affliction befalls you﴾, i.e., any affliction from the afflictions of this world, such as sickness and the other calamities. ﴿it is because of what your hands have earned﴾, i.e., it is because of your sins which you have committed. *Ma* is a relative pronoun serving as the subject (*mubtada'*), and when the subject is a relative pronoun whose relative clause is a verbal sentence, the *fa'* (fa) often enters the predicate because it carries the meaning of a conditional, since it indicates that the predicate is dependent upon it. Therefore the *fa'* is used here.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far in one narration, and Shayba read *bima* without the *fa'*, because it is not obligatory, and the placing of the subject as a relative pronoun is sufficient to indicate the aforementioned meaning. It is reported from Ibn Malik that he said: "The difference between the two readings shows that *ma* is a relative pronoun, so in some places the *fa'* is used in its predicate and in others it is not, reducing the likened (*al-mushabbah*) from the likened-to (*al-mushabbah bihi*)." It is permitted that *ma* be a conditional, and Abu Hayyan favored this in the reading with the *fa'*, and took it as a relative pronoun in the other reading, based on the view that omitting the *fa'* from the response of the conditional is restricted to poetry according to Sibawayh, as in the verse:

*"Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them."*

Al-Akhfash and some of the grammarians of Baghdad permitted this absolutely. From it is the Almighty's saying: ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' said: Omitting the *fa'* from the response is good when the condition is in the past tense, and from this is known the added excellence of omitting it here on the view that *ma* is a relative pronoun. ﴿And He pardons much﴾, i.e., of the sins, so He does not punish for them with an affliction, immediately or later, it is said.

It is permitted that the intended meaning of "much" is "many of the people." The apparent meaning is the first, and it is what the reports attest to. At-Tirmidhi related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant is struck by a misfortune, great or small, except because of a sin, and what Allah pardons is greater." Then he recited: ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from al-Hasan that he said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you﴾ and so on, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, there is no scratch of a twig, nor twitch of a vein, nor stumbling of a stone, nor slip of a foot, except because of a sin, and what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, pardons is greater." Ibn Sa'd related from Abu Mulayka that Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to have headaches, and she would place her hand on her head and say: "It is because of my sin, and what Allah forgives is greater." A sore was seen on the palm of Shurayh, and it was said: "What is this?" He said: "It is because of what my hand has earned." Imran ibn Husayn was asked about his illness, and he said: "The dearest of it to me is the dearest of it to Allah, the Exalted, and this is because of what my hand has earned."

The verse is restricted to those who have sins among the Muslims and others, for whoever has no sin, such as the prophets, peace be upon them, may still be struck by afflictions. In the hadith: "The people most severely tested are the prophets, then the best of them, then the next best." This is either to raise their ranks or for other wisdoms hidden from us. As for children and the insane, it is said that they are not included in the address, because it is addressed to the responsible (*mukallafin*). And even assuming they are included, the restriction to those with sins excludes them, so whatever afflictions befall them are for hidden wisdoms. It is said that in the afflictions of a child there is the raising of his rank, and the rank of his parents or whoever is compassionate toward him, through good patience. Then, afflictions may be a punishment for a sin and a recompense for it, such that one is not punished for it on the Day of Resurrection. What supports this is what Ahmad related in his Musnad, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, and a group related from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, who said: "Shall I not inform you of the best verse in the Book of Allah, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us: ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you, it is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾. I will explain it to you, O 'Ali: whatever sickness, punishment, or trial befalls you in this world is because of what your hands have earned, and Allah is too Generous to repeat the punishment for you in the Hereafter, and what Allah pardoned in this world, Allah, glory be to Him, is too Generous to return after His pardon."

Some have claimed that these afflictions cannot be a recompense, because this world is the abode of obligation, so if recompense occurred in it, it would be an abode of both recompense and obligation at once, which is impossible; rather they are only trials. The report from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, refutes this, as does what is authentically established that the prescribed punishments (*hudud*), other than the punishment for highway robbery, are expiations. And there is no impossibility in this world being the abode of obligation while some individuals experience what is a recompense for their sin, i.e., an expiation for it.

It is related from al-Hasan that he interpreted "affliction" as the prescribed punishment (*hadd*). He said: The meaning is: whatever prescribed punishment of Allah the Exalted befalls you, it is only because of what your hands have earned and your committing what necessitates it. And ﴿He pardons much﴾ means Allah conceals it from the servant so that he is not punished for it. This is something the reports reject, and despite that, it is worthless, and perhaps it was not authentically transmitted from al-Hasan.

In al-Intisaf it is said that this verse baffles the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), and they cannot contrive a trick to turn it away from the sense of its text. For they interpreted the Almighty's saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ as referring to the penitent, but that is not possible for them here, for it establishes partiality in the pardon. And for them it is impossible that the pardon here be restricted to repentance, for that also entails partiality, and they hold that pardon cannot be partial, as al-Imam (al-Razi) related from Abu Hashim, the leader of the Mu'tazila and the one who took up their major doctrine. So there is no place for them except the truth about which there is no doubt, which is to refer the pardon to the will of Allah the Exalted, not conditioned upon repentance.

It has been answered that they may say: the meaning is "He pardons much," so that He does not punish for it in this world, but delays its punishment to the Hereafter for whoever does not repent. And you know what the report of 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, indicates.

﴿And you cannot escape [Allah] on earth﴾, meaning: you will not make Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, incapable of afflicting you with calamities for what your hands have earned, even if you flee to every corner of the earth in every direction of flight. It has also been said: the meaning is that you cannot overpower any of His soldiers on earth, so how much less those in the heavens. ﴿And you have no protector apart from Allah﴾, meaning: no one who shows mercy by granting you compassion when calamities strike you. It has also been said: no one who protects you from them. ﴿Nor any helper﴾, meaning: no one who will repel them from you. The sentence serves as a confirmation of His words, ﴿and He pardons much﴾, meaning: Allah, exalted is He, pardons many of the calamities, since you have no power to overpower Him, glory be to Him, so that you could escape what He has decreed upon you of them. Nor do you have any protector who shows mercy other than Him, mighty and majestic, to show you mercy when they strike you, nor any helper besides Him to help you against them. For this reason it is reported from ʿAli (may Allah honor his face) that this is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an for the believers. The matter of hope is strengthened by what has been said: the meaning of "you are not [able]" through to "you are not able to overpower Allah in repelling your calamities" is that He, glory be to Him, is capable of that.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 32:**

﴿And among His signs are the ships (al-jawari)﴾, that is, the sailing ships (al-sufun al-jawari), i.e., the running ones (al-jariyah). It is then an adjective (sifah) of a deleted noun (mawsuf mahdhuf), by the indication (qarinah) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿in the sea﴾. With that the deletion becomes good; otherwise it is a non-specific adjective (sifah ghayr mukhtassah), and the analogical rule (al-qiyas) for it is that the noun it qualifies should not be deleted and that it should take its place. Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan) allowed that it be said that it is a predominant adjective (sifah ghalibah), like al-Abtah (the name of a valley), and that it may follow the governing words (al-'awamil) without mention of the noun it qualifies. And ﴿in the sea﴾ is connected to al-jawari. And His words, exalted is He: ﴿like mountains (al-a'lam)﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal).

It is also permitted that the first (al-awwal) be likewise. Al-a'lam is the plural of 'alam, which is the mountain; its original meaning is the sign by which a thing is known, like the marker of a road ('alam al-tariq) and the standard of an army ('alam al-jaysh). The mountain was named 'alam for that reason. It is not specific to the mountain on which there is fire for guidance; rather, when that is intended it is qualified, as in the verse of al-Khansa':

"Indeed Sakhr, the guides take him as their lead,
As if he were a sign on whose summit is a fire."

In it there is a subtle hyperbole. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he heard it, said: "May God fight her! She was not content with comparing him to a mountain until she made a fire upon its summit."

Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read (al-jawari) with a ya' when connected (in pause-less recitation), but not when pausing.

Ibn Kathir read it with the ya' in both states, and the rest read it without the ya' in both states; the retention is the original form and the deletion is for lightness. In either case the i'rab is presumed (taqdiri), and it has been heard from some Arabs that the i'rab is shown on the ra' (as a vowel).

﴿If He wills, He stills the wind⁠﻿﻿﻿ ⁠ —﻿ that by which the ships run, and He cancels the cause of its agitation, which is the condensation of the air in the place toward which it moves, and the piling of some of that air upon other parts of it. The cause of this condensation is either that the temperature of the air drops, so its expansion decreases and it condenses, leaving most of the place it had occupied empty; or it is a sudden gathering that occurs in the vapours spread through the air, which empties their place. This, as it is said, is the strongest of the causes. When the air finds an empty space in front of it because of this, it moves forcefully to fill it, so the wind arises and continues until it fills the place. What has been mentioned concerning the cause of the agitation is what the philosophers of the age have stated. As for the earlier scholars, they mentioned other things. Perhaps there are causes other than all of these that none knows but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Affirming causes for both the moving and the stilling of the wind does not contradict attributing events to the Free-Choosing Agent (al-fa'il al-mukhtar, God), exalted is His majesty and far-reaching His bounty.

[Page 43]

Nafi' read (al-Riyah) in the plural, ﴿so they become still upon its back⁠﻿﻿﻿ ⁠ —﻿ so they remain fixed on the surface of the sea, that is, not flowing and not moving at all. Some of the commentators interpreted (yazlalna) as (yabqayna, they remain), in which case (rawakid) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal). The first reading is preferable.

Qatada read (fayazlilna) with a kasra on the lam. The analogical form is the fatha, because the past tense has a kasra on its middle radical, so the kasra in the present tense is anomalous (shadhdh). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is from (zalla, yazallu, and yazillu) with fatha and kasra, like (dalla, yadullu, and yadillu) with the letter dad. Abu Hayyan criticised him, saying that this is not as he stated, because (yadhillu) with fatha is from (dhalaltu) with kasra, and (yadillu) with kasra is from (dhalaltu) with fatha, and both are regular forms.

﴿Indeed, in that⁠﻿﻿﻿ ⁠ —﻿ that which was mentioned of the ships made subservient in the sea, under His command and according to His will, exalted is He ⁠﻿﻿﻿ ⁠ —﻿ are ﴿signs⁠﻿﻿﻿ ⁠ —﻿ great and many, indicating the greatness of His affairs, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿for every steadfast, grateful one⁠﻿﻿﻿ ⁠ —﻿ for everyone who restrains himself from turning toward what is not fitting, and devotes his resolve to contemplating the signs of God and reflecting upon His blessings, exalted is He. Here patience (sabr) is a particular kind of restraint, and reflecting upon His favours is gratitude (shukr).

It is also possible that by these two attributes he has referred to the complete believer, because faith is half patience and half gratitude.

The Imam mentioned that the believer is never free of either ease (sarra') or hardship (darra'). If he is in hardship, he is among the patient; and if he is in ease, he is among the grateful.

﴿Or He may destroy them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿He stills﴾, meaning: or He may destroy them by sending the violent wind that drowns. As many have said, what is meant is the destruction of its people, either by supplying an omitted noun (taqdīr muḍāf), or by metonymy (tajawwuz) through using the place to mean its inhabitants, or by allusion (kināya), since the destruction of the ships necessarily entails the destruction of those in them. The indication that this is intended is His words, ﴿for what they have earned﴾. The original sense is "or He sends them, that is, the winds, and so destroys them," because it is the counterpart (qasīm) of ﴿He stills﴾. So it has been restricted to what is intended by sending them as violent winds, and that is either their destruction or their deliverance. This is what is meant by His words, ﴿and pardons much﴾, for the meaning is: or He sends them and thereby destroys some people for their sins, and delivers others by way of pardoning them. With this, the reason for the jussive form of "pardons" becomes clear, since it carries the sense of "delivers" and is coordinated with "destroys." The reason it is coordinated with the conjunction "and" (wa) is that it falls under the counterpart, which is sending them as violent winds. On this interpretation, the verse includes both stilling them and sending them as violent winds, with destruction and deliverance, and sending them moderately, which is known from His words, Glorified is He, ﴿the ships running﴾, for that is the primary purpose of them.

Some of the eminent scholars said: The verified view is that "pardons" (yaʿfu) is coordinated with His words, ﴿He stills the wind﴾, up to His words, Glorified is He, ﴿for what they have earned﴾. That is why it is coordinated with "and" and not with "or." The meaning is: if He wills, He punishes them by stilling the wind or by making it violent; and if He wills, He pardons much.

Some have permitted taking ﴿He destroys them﴾ in its apparent sense, because the ships are among their possessions, and their loss and damage are also due to their sins, and they liken the verse to His words, ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you﴾, etc.

Al-Aʿmash recited "pardons" (yaʿfū) with a final silent waw, coordinating it with the whole conditional clause (the protasis and the apodosis together), not with the apodosis alone, as in the jussive reading. From the people of Madinah it is reported that they recited "pardons" (yaʿfuwa) with a fatḥa on the waw, as being put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" after the waw. The coordination in this reading is with a verbal noun (maṣdar) drawn out from the preceding speech, as if it were said: "it occurs," and this is coordination on the sense (ʿaṭf ʿalā al-maʿnā). This is the position of the Basrans in such cases. This waw is called the waw of diversion (wāw al-ṣarf), because it diverts the coordination from the preceding jussive verb to the coordination of one verbal noun with another. The position of the Kufans is that the waw itself, with the meaning of the verbal "an," governs the imperfect verb directly.

Al-Radi chose that the waw is either the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), with the verbal noun after it as a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the clause is then circumstantial; or the waw of accompaniment (wāw al-maʿiyya), after which the verb is put in the subjunctive, to indicate the accompaniment of the actions, just as the waw in the object of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu) indicates the accompaniment of nouns. It was thus turned away from the apparent sense so as to be explicit in the meaning of togetherness. The view most prevalent today among grammarians is the Basran position, and on it Abu Hayyan explained the accusative in this reading. Likewise, more than one scholar explained it, among them al-Zajjaj, the accusative in His words, Exalted is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 35:**

﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no escape﴾, i.e., no place of refuge or deliverance from the punishment for that.

They treated the apodosis (*al-jaza'*, the answer clause of a conditional sentence) as equivalent to an independent statement (*al-insha'*), like an interrogative, so that it is as if one of the six matters preceding it had come first. Al-Zamakhshari did not accept this and said: "It is open to question, because of what Sibawayh reported in *al-Kitab*. He said: 'Know that the accusative after the *fa'* and the *wa'* in *in ta'tini ata'ka wa-u'tika* ("if you come to me, I will come to you and give you") is weak, and it is of the type of the saying:

*wa-alhaqu bi-l-Hijazi fa-astarihа*
("and I will go to the Hijaz and rest")

This is permissible, but it is neither within the limit of speech nor its proper manner, except that in the apodosis it is somewhat stronger, because it is not obligatory that he will act, unless the first clause contains an act. When it resembles what does not necessarily require it, such as the interrogative and similar forms, they permitted this, though weakly.' It is not permissible to interpret the widely transmitted recitation as a weak form that is neither within the limit of speech nor its proper manner. Had it been of this category, Sibawayh would not have left it out of his book, and he has mentioned its parallels among the difficult verses." End of quotation.

He (al-Zamakhshari) took the accusative on *ya'lama* (*ya'lama*, "will know") as coordinated with a supposed cause (*'illa muqaddara*), saying: "That is, in order that He may take vengeance upon them, and that those who ... will know." There are many parallels to this in the Mighty Qur'an, except that in those cases the particle of causation (*harf al-ta'lil*) is present, as in the Exalted saying: ﴿and that We may make him a sign for the people﴾, and His glorious saying: ﴿And Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth, and that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned﴾.

Abu Hayyan said: "This supposition is remote, because the destruction of one people and the salvation of another are consequences of the condition. So it is not fitting to say 'in order that He may take vengeance upon them.'"

It is answered that the verse is specific to the criminals, so the intended meaning is destruction. It is also permissible to suppose "in order that He may manifest His great power," and "that those who dispute may know," so the objection stated above does not apply. This supposition is also fitting in explaining the accusative on *ya'fu* ("pardon"), as transmitted from the people of Madinah. When the earlier explanation is challenged by what was reported from Sibawayh, it is said: it is coordinated with a supposed cause, that is, "in order that He may take vengeance upon them and pardon many."

The accusative reading of *ya'lama* is the one recited by most of the Seven.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shaybah, and Zayd ibn 'Ali recited it in the nominative (*bi-l-raf'*). In *al-Kashf* its justification is set out as: it is coordinated with *ya'lamu* on the whole conditional sentence, with the meaning: "And among His signs, which indicate His perfect power, are the ships on the sea." Then he mentioned the mode of indication: that they are subjected to His command, glorious is He, sometimes by including the benefit of those aboard, and sometimes the reverse. Then he said, may He be exalted and majestic: "And those who oppose and do not acknowledge the manifest signs of Allah, the Exalted" in place of His glorious saying "therein," using a pronoun referring to the verse under discussion, as testimony that it is among the signs of Allah, and as an added warning and censure of disputing concerning it. It is also in the style of metonymy (*al-kinaya*), as in the Arabic saying "the Arabs do not break covenants." So when it was said, "If He wills, He stills the wind," and the cause of the indication was mentioned, it came to mean: "Those who reflect upon Our signs and are guided will know and acknowledge it, and those who dispute concerning them and deny will know that they have no escape."

It is also permissible to make it coordinated with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among His signs are the ships﴾, and to treat this alone as signs, since it includes aspects of indication. It is placed in the position of the pronoun, and the meaning is: "And among His signs are the ships, and those who dispute concerning them will know."

Between the coordinated and that to which it is coordinated, an explanation of the aspect of indication was inserted, so as to indicate the requirement of the threat to the disputant, and that it is a sign, indeed signs. It is reported from Ibn al-Hajib that the nominative may be by coordination with the position of the preceding apodosis, in view of its being a sentence, not by coordination of the bare verb, so that the jussive would be required. Thus the two sentences would share the causal relation. There is a discussion of this which will be known from what follows, if Allah the Exalted wills.

It was also recited in the jussive (*bi-l-jazm*): *wa-ya'lam*.

It is explained as coordinated with *ya'fu* ("pardon"), and its causal link to the condition is by considering that the report about the knowledge of the disputants includes, in the future, what will befall them of threat and warning, as it was said:

*sawfa tara idha-njala al-ghubar*
*a-fara-sun tahtaka am himar*

("You will see, when the dust clears, whether it is a horse beneath you or a donkey.")

The meaning on this basis is that if He wills, He sends the wind in a storm, so that He drowns some and saves others by pardon, and warns another group.

It is objected that restricting this warning to the disputants is not evident. Also, their knowledge that there is no escape from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, upon the sending of a storm against the people of the ships, is by way of lesson, and it is not specific to them nor to this particular event alone.

It is answered regarding the first point that the restriction to the disputants is because they are more deserving of warning; and regarding the last, that what is meant is that neither land nor sea saves from His might, mighty and majestic is He, so it is a generalization.

Al-Zamakhshari in *al-Kashf* chose that the explanation is that the verse concerns the unbelievers, in the sense: "If He wills, He sends the wind in a storm, so that He drowns some of them and saves others of them by pardon, and that they may know that they have no escape. So let them not be deceived by the salvation and pardon in this instance." Thus the disputants are the many who are saved, or some of them, and this is on the pattern of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time?﴾

From the whole of what you have heard, the weakness of this recitation becomes apparent to you, and for this reason it was not recited with it among the Seven. Upon all three recitations, the apparent reading is that the subject of *ya'lama* ("will know"), namely *alladhina* ("those who"), and the clause *ma lahum min mahis* ("they have no escape") take the place of the two objects. In *ad-Durr al-Masun* it is stated that in the nominative reading the clause may be verbal and may be nominal, i.e., "and He knows those who..." It is not hidden that the apparent reading on the second possibility is that *alladhina* is the first object, the clause is the second object, and the subject is the implied pronoun of the Exalted. Some have made this obligatory on the jussive reading, with *ya'lama* coordinated with *ya'fu*, lest the speech fall out of its coherence and the purpose of warning become evident, since it is widely known that the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is a metonymy for recompense. And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿Whatever you have been given of anything﴾, i.e., whatever it is of the means of this worldly life. The apparent meaning is that the address is to people in general, though it has been said that it is addressed to the polytheists. "Mā" (مَا) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) serving as the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the nominal sentence), its returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) is omitted, and the sense is "you were given it." The predicate (khabar) is what follows. The particle "fa" (فَ) entered because the clause includes the sense of a conditional (sharṭ, the conditional structure). Abū Ḥayyān said: "It is a conditional clause, the second object of ﴿ʾūtītum﴾ (you were given), and ﴿min shayʾ﴾ (of anything) is an explanatory apposition to it." The words of the Most High, ﴿then the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾, mean: then it is its enjoyment, which you enjoy during the period of your life in it, and this is the response (jawāb) of the conditional. The first reading is more suitable in light of the words of the Most High, ﴿and what is with Allah﴾, of the reward of the Hereafter, ﴿is better﴾ in essence, because its benefit is pure, ﴿and more lasting﴾ in duration, since it does not cease and does not perish. The apparent reading is that "mā" in it is a relative pronoun. The reason the particle "fa" was not used before its predicate, even though the relative subject, when joined to an adverbial phrase (ẓarf), implies the sense of a conditional as well, is that the causal connection of a thing being with Allah the Exalted, for its goodness, is a known and established matter, needing no indication by a particle set for that purpose, unlike what is with other than Him, glorified is He. The expression of it as being "with Allah the Exalted" rather than "what is stored up for that" is also noted. The words of the Most High, ﴿for those who believe﴾, may be either connected to ﴿and more lasting﴾, or the "lām" (لِ) is to specify who possesses this blessing, in which case it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "that is for those who believe."

﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾, not upon anyone else at all. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, that wealth gathered to Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and he gave all of it in charity in the way of Allah the Exalted, so the Muslims blamed him and the disbelievers declared him mistaken, so it was revealed;

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, the relative construction) in His words ﴿And those who avoid the major sins and the grave immoralities, and when they are angered, they forgive﴾ together with what follows it is either a coordinate (ʿatf) on the first relative construction, or it is an expression of praise (madh) in the nominative, being the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, or in the accusative by an implied verb such as *aʿnī* ("I mean") or *amdahu* ("I praise"). The *wāw* is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya), as al-Radi mentioned. Abu al-Baqa overlooked the *wāw*, so he did not mention coordination and mentioned apposition (badal) instead.

The "major sins of wrongdoing" (kabāʾir al-ithm) are either those for which a threat of punishment is prescribed, or those that require a prescribed penalty (ḥadd), or everything that Allah the Exalted has forbidden. The "grave immoralities" (al-fawāḥish) are those whose ugliness is excessive and great. It has been said that the intended meaning of "major sins" is what relates to innovations (bidaʿ) and the drawing out of doubts (shubah), and of "immoralities" what relates to the appetitive faculty (al-quwwa al-shahwāniyya), and of His words ﴿and when they are angered, they forgive﴾ what relates to the irascible faculty (al-quwwa al-ghaḍabiyya). But this, as you see, is far-fetched. The word "wrongdoing" (al-ithm) is intended as a genus, for otherwise it would have said *al-āthām* (the plural).

﴿And when﴾ (idhā) is an adverb of time (ẓarf) governing *yaghfirūna* ("they forgive"). *Hum* ("they") is a subject (mubtada') and not a corroborative emphasis (taʾkīd) of the pronoun in *ghaḍibū* ("they were angered"), though Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr al-Muhit permitted this. The sentence *yaghfirūna* is its predicate (khabar). Placing it first (*hum*) serves to convey restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), because it is a semantic agent (fāʿil maʿnawī). Their being singled out is in view of the fact that they are deserving of this, unlike others, since forgiveness at the time of anger is a rare thing. The verse also hints that they forgive before they ask for forgiveness.

It has been said that *hum* is in the nominative by a verb implied and explained by *yaghfirūna*, and since the verb was omitted, the pronoun became detached; but this is not right. Abu al-Baqa made *idhā* conditional (sharṭiyya) and the sentence *hum yaghfirūna* its response (jawāb). Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it would then necessitate the particle *fa* (then), and its omission is not permitted except in poetry. What is useful for you to recall has been mentioned earlier, so remember it.

Ḥamza and al-Kisaʾi read *kabīra al-ithm* (in the singular), with the intended sense being the genus, or the complete individual instance of it, which is polytheism (shirk). This interpretation was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. There is no problem of repetition, because the intended meaning is continuity and perpetuity.

[Page 46]

It is said: it was revealed concerning the Helpers (al-Ansar). Allah, the Exalted, called them through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ) to believe in him and obey Him, the Glorified, and they responded to Him. So He praised them, may He be exalted, with what He praised them for. On this reading, it is the mention of the particular after the general, to show their nobility for their belief without hesitation or wavering. If the verse is Madinan, the matter is clear. If it is Meccan, then by "the Helpers" is meant those who believed in Madinah before the Hijrah, or it is meant the people of al-'Aqabah.

﴿And their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾: that is, it is subject to consultation and mutual deliberation over opinions among them. This is based on the view that shura (consultation) is a verbal noun like bushra (good news). Otherwise the statement would not be correct, because the matter is "consulted upon," not "consultation." The exception is if it is intended as an intensification. It was objected that one may say "shani al-karam" (my nobility) without a figurative reading, and that "amr" here means "shan" (affair). Yes, if it is taken to mean the matters that are consulted upon, it requires a figurative reading or the intention of intensification. It was also said that the verbal noun is here in the genitive of generality, so the statement is not correct except with a figurative reading. This was refuted: the intended meaning is their affair concerning what is consulted upon, not all their affairs. There is room to examine this.

Al-Raghib said: al-mashwarah is extracting opinion by one party referring to another, from the expression "shurtu al-'asal" and "ashartuhu," meaning "I extracted it." And ash-shura is the matter that is consulted upon. End of quotation. The well-known view is that it is a verbal noun. The sentence is nominal, although the sentence it is coordinated with is verbal, to indicate that consultation was their constant state before Islam and after it.

In the verse there is praise for consultation, especially on the view that it contains the statement with a verbal noun. Al-Bayhaqi, in Shu'ab al-Iman, reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever intends a matter and consults concerning it, and then decides, is guided to the most rightful of affairs." 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bukhari in al-Adab, and Ibn al-Mundhir, reported from al-Hasan, who said: "No people ever consulted among themselves except that they were guided and their affair was set right," then he recited: ﴿And their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾.

Consultation was between the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions concerning matters related to the interests of wars. Likewise among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, after him, (upon him be prayer and peace), and it was also among them concerning rulings, such as fighting the apostates, the inheritance of the grandfather, the number of lashes for wine-drinking, and other things. What is meant is what has no explicit legal text (nass shar'i) concerning it. Otherwise consultation would have no meaning. How could it be fitting for a Muslim to turn away from the ruling of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the opinions of men? And Allah, the Glorified, is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.

What we have said is supported by what al-Khatib reported from 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, a matter befalls us after you on which no Qur'an has been revealed and nothing has been heard from you concerning it." He said: "Gather for it the worshippers of my community and make it a matter of consultation among you, and do not decide it by one opinion." It is also fitting that the one consulted be intelligent, just as it is fitting that he be a worshipper.

Al-Khatib also reported from Abu Hurayrah, as a marfu' hadith: "Seek guidance from the intelligent and you will be rightly guided, and do not disobey him and so regret."

Consultation in the manner we have mentioned is among the causes of the goodness of the earth. In the hadith: "When your rulers are your best and your affair is consultation among you, the surface of the earth is better for you than its belly. And when your rulers are your worst and your wealthy are your misers and your affair is in the hands of your women, the belly of the earth is better for you than its surface." And when it is not in that manner, its corruption of religion and worldly life is greater than its reform.

﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾: that is, in the way of goodness, because it is brought in for praise by the mere act of spending. Perhaps its separation from its companion by the mention of consultation is because responding to Allah and establishing prayer were among its effects. It was also said: it is because it occurs when they gather for the prayers.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 39:

﴿And those who, when tyranny afflicts them, they defend themselves.﴾ That is, they take revenge on those who oppress them, within the limit that Allah has permitted them, and they do not transgress. The sense of restriction (al-ikhtisas) is that they are the specialists in retaliation, whereas others overstep and exceed the limit. It is not meant that they retaliate and do not forgive, so that it would contradict the preceding verse. Rather, it is as if He, glory be to Him, described them as those specialized in forgiveness, whose anger does not overwhelm their forbearance as it does in others, and that they are specialized in retaliation within what has been allowed to them if they are matched in strength, and they do not transgress as others do. Thus they are praiseworthy in both states, between good and better, singled out from among people for this. Some scholars said: each of the two attributes is praiseworthy in its own place. Pardoning a helpless person who admits his wrongdoing is praiseworthy, and the word "forgiveness" implies this. Retaliating against an obstinate adversary is praiseworthy, and the word "retaliation" implies this. If they were applied in reverse, both would be blameworthy. On this basis came the saying of the poet:

When you honour the noble, you make him your possession,
but if you honour the base, he becomes insolent.

Placing generosity where the sword belongs, in the matter of high rank,
is as harmful as placing the sword where generosity belongs.

Each may also be praised and blamed according to other considerations, so there is no contradiction, whether the two described persons are the same in both clauses or not. Some verifying scholars said: the most correct view is that the statement is not to be understood as restriction, but as encouragement to righteousness, meaning they sometimes practise forgiveness and sometimes retaliation, not always, to avoid contradiction. This is not the right view. It is reported from al-Nakha'i that when he recited this verse he said: "They used to dislike that they should humiliate themselves, so that the wicked would dare against them." In this there is an indication that retaliation is against the obstinate adversary, and otherwise there is no humiliation of the self in pardoning the helpless one who admits his fault. Then, the clause (they defend themselves) is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, forming the relative clause of the relative pronoun (alladhina). (Idha) is an adverb of time governing (yantasiruna). It was also permitted that it be a conditional clause, with the sentence being the answer of the condition, and the answer clause together with the condition form the relative clause. Abu Hayyan criticised this with what has been mentioned just above. It was also permitted that (hum) be the subject of an omitted verb, and it is, as you have heard, in (wa-idha ma ghadiba) etc. Al-Hawfi said: it is permissible to make (hum) a emphatic pronoun for the pronoun in (asabahum), and in this there is the separation between the emphasized and the emphasizer by the subject; perhaps this is not prohibited. Nevertheless, the preferred view in parsing is what we indicated earlier.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Rūḥ al-Ma'ānī) on Sūrah 42, verse 40:

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ is an explanation of what was granted to the one who seeks vindication (al-muntaṣir). The naming of the second act, which is the recompense, as "an evil" (sayyi'ah) is said to be by way of *mushākalah* (a rhetorical correspondence in which one term is used for another because of their association). Jār Allāh said: calling both acts "an evil" is because each one harms the one upon whom it falls. In this there is attention to the literal sense of the wording, and an indication that vindication, although praiseworthy, is only praised on condition of observing equivalence, which is difficult. Therefore, within this context, there is an exhortation to pardon as a matter of caution (*iḥtiyāṭ*). His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿But whoever pardons﴾, meaning pardons the one who wronged him, ﴿and makes reconciliation﴾ between himself and the one who is hostile to him, through pardon and overlooking what proceeded from him, ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾, so He, may He be majestic and exalted, will recompense him with the greatest recompense. This is an explicit statement of what that exhortation had hinted at, and a reminder that this, although it is a course of caution, also includes the reconciliation of relations (iṣlāḥ dhāt al-bayn), which is praiseworthy in its present state and its outcome, so that it becomes an additional incitement to it. The leaving of the reward indefinite, and making it a due right upon the Mighty, the Generous, may His majesty be exalted, which indicates its greatness, is an additional encouragement. The particle *fa* (then) is used to elevate it above what precedes, meaning: if the course of vindication is not free from stumbling, then whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, he is traveling the path that is free from stumbling and praised in both abodes.

Page 48

And His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those who exceed the limit in retaliation, is a completion of that meaning and an explicit statement of what was implied concerning the difficulty of observing the path of equivalence, and that it is rarely free of transgression and excess, especially in a state of anger and the flaring up of zeal. Thus he enters the company of those whom Allah, may He be exalted, does not love. According to this meaning, there is no need to treat ﴿But whoever pardons﴾ and what follows as a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ). Moreover, even if it were so, namely that this clause is connected to ﴿the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ as a justification (ta'līl) for what is understood from it, the *fa* would not prevent that, as has been supposed. Many have included those who initiate the evil among the wrongdoers.

﴿And whoever retaliates after he has been wronged﴾: after he has been wronged, with the verb in the passive voice (*al-bina' lil-majhul*). It is also read this way. Then the verbal noun (*al-masdar*, ظُلْمِهِ, "his being wronged") is annexed to its object, or it is the verbal noun of the passive verb. The *lam* is the lam of oath (*lam al-qasam*). It is also permitted that it be the emphatic *lam* (*lam al-ibtida'*), brought for emphasis, and *man* (مَن) is conditional or relative. The verb انْتَصَرَ was construed according to its wording (عَلى لَفْظِها), and ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ مَا عَلَيْهِم مِّن سَبِيلٍ﴾ was construed according to its meaning (عَلى مَعْناها): ﴿then those have no way against them﴾, i.e., there is no way (of blame) against the one who retaliates, nor against the one who censures (*al-'atib*) or the one who finds fault (*al-'a'ib*). The sentence is coordinated with (*fa-man 'afa*, "whoever pardons"). It is brought to make explicit that what was urged there was urged as guidance toward what is best in most cases, not that the one who retaliates is under any blame in any way, presently or ultimately. And to prevent the impression that the urging contradicts what the general notion of "way" (*al-sabil*) implies in its unrestricted sense, it is prefaced with the *lam*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 42:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the blame is only against those who wrong people﴾ is a specification of those against whom there is blame (sabil), after the negation of that for those who take retribution. By "those who wrong people" is meant those who initiate the wrong, or who exceed in retaliation and go beyond what was prescribed for them. Some of them explained it as those who do to them what they do not deserve, and this is more general.

﴿And they transgress in the earth without right﴾, i.e., they act arrogantly in it with tyranny and corruption. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those described with wrongdoing and transgression without right, ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾, because of their wrongdoing and their transgression. By "these wrongdoers and transgressors" is meant the disbelievers. It was said: it includes them and others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 42, verse 43:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ is a warning against wrongdoing and transgression, and against whatever leads in some way to the painful punishment. It also contains an exhortation to what was exhorted earlier, showing concern for it and adding further encouragement to it. Thus, "patience" here is the reconciliation that was deferred in what preceded, now placed first here. It is expressed as "patience" because it is among the qualities of those of firm resolve (*ulu al-'azm*), and as an indication that reconciliation through pardon and overlooking is praiseworthy only when it comes from ability and not from incapacity. "That" (*dhalika*) refers to what was mentioned of patience and forgiveness. "Matters requiring determination" (*'azm al-umur*) means matters that are resolved and decided, or matters that are firm and true.

It is permitted that "man" (*man*) be a relative pronoun or a conditional particle, and that the "lam" be an inceptive lam or an oath lam. When the answer to the oath is used in place of the answer to the condition, [the grammarians] have said so. If the lam is taken as inceptive and "man" as conditional, then the clause "indeed that" is the answer to the condition, and the "fa'" (of consequence) has been omitted from it. Whoever restricts such omission to poetry does not permit this reading. A group of scholars has stated that there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "indeed that, from it, is of the matters requiring determination." They justified this by saying that the clause is a predicate and therefore must have a connecting link (*rabit*), and "that" is not suitable for this role because it refers to patience and forgiveness. [They also argued that] its being sufficient in place of it, because what is meant is his patience, or that "that" is the connecting link with the indication of "whoever" being understood as "of those who possess the matters requiring determination," is far-fetched (*takalluf*).

That said, al-Allama al-Tibi preferred that calling the second act, which is the recompense, "an evil" (*sayyi'a*) is by way of disparagement (*tahjin*) and not by way of *mushakala* (equivalence of wording). He claimed that the one being recompensed is a wrongdoer, and on this basis he linked the clause ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾ to what precedes, saying: "It can be said: when He attributed to the one who retaliates the act of evil in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, and the wrongdoer in this context is one who corrupts what is between people, as evidenced by ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, He gave the reason for the implication of that with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, as if it were said: whoever removes himself [p. 49] from attribution to evil and corruption through pardon and reconciliation is one who acts justly, indeed Allah loves those who act justly. So He placed in its position ﴿then his reward is upon Allah﴾. Whoever occupies himself with retaliation, is attributed to evil, corrupts what is between people, and deprives himself of that great reward, is one who wrongs himself, ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. Thus the verse comes as guidance to the wronged person toward noble character and preference for the way of the messengers."

He also said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever retaliates after being wronged﴾, and so on, is an address to rulers and judges and an instruction on what should be done, as evidenced by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the path is only against those who wrong people﴾, where He repeated the indefinite "path" in its definite form and connected to it ﴿who wrong people﴾, and explained it by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a painful punishment﴾. Likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, and so on, is also an instruction to them on the method of judgment. That is to say: when the rightful party departs from the first [option] and takes retribution from the wrongdoer, then there is no path against him for you, because that has been permitted to him; and when he chooses the better, then there is no path against the wrongdoer for you, because the pardon of the wronged is among the matters requiring determination. So "cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression." End of quotation. But what is in it is not hidden.

In *al-Kashf* [of al-Zamakhshari] it is said that taking what was mentioned as an address to rulers and judges necessitates complication in the speech, so what we have presented before is what is relied upon.

Many reports have come concerning the virtue of those who pardon those who wronged them. Al-Bayhaqi related in *Shu'ab al-Iman* from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Musa son of 'Imran (peace be upon him) said: 'O Lord, who is the most honored of Your servants with You?' He said: 'One who, when he has the power, forgives.'" Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the servants stand for the reckoning, a caller will call: 'Let those whose reward is upon Allah Exalted rise and enter Paradise.' Then he will call a second time: 'Let those whose reward is upon Allah Exalted rise.' They said: 'And who are those whose reward is upon Allah Exalted?' He said: 'Those who pardon people.' So such-and-such thousands rose and entered Paradise without reckoning."

Ahmad and Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayra that a man insulted Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) while the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting. The Prophet (ﷺ) began to marvel and smile. When [the man] increased [his insults], [Abu Bakr] responded to some of his words. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) became angry and stood up. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) caught up with him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, he was insulting me while you were sitting, and when I responded to some of his words, you became angry and stood up." He said: "There was an angel with you defending you; when you responded to some of his words, the devil came down, and I would not sit with the devil." Then he (ﷺ) said: "Three things are of the truth: no servant is wronged by an injustice and then overlooks it for the sake of Allah Exalted, except that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, raises his support by it; and no man opens a door of giving, desiring thereby connection [of kinship], except that Allah Exalted increases him by it in abundance; and no man opens a door of asking, desiring thereby abundance, except that Allah Exalted increases him by it in poverty."

This report raises a difficulty, in that it suggests a rebuke of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and that is a kind of the path negated in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever retaliates after being wronged, those have no path against them﴾. It was answered: we do not concede that; there is in it no more than his (may Allah be pleased with him) being alerted to abandoning what is better, and that is one thing, while rebuke is another thing. Likewise it is not counted as blame, as is not hidden.

Some people restricted the "path" in the verse to sin and punishment, so there is no difficulty for them at all. It was also said: it remains general, except that the verse concerns the common believers, and whoever does not reach the rank of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), for such a person is blamed for insulting even if it is with right in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), before he is given permission for it, verbally or by state. Rather, there appeared from him (ﷺ) what indicates approval of remaining silent about it. The good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near.

The Prophet (ﷺ) did command some individuals to return insult to the insulter. Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) who said: Zaynab (may Allah be pleased with her) entered upon me while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with me. She turned toward me and began to revile me. The Prophet (ﷺ) restrained her, but she did not stop. So he said to me: "Revile her." So I reviled her until her saliva dried in her mouth, while the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brightened with joy.

Perhaps this was from him (ﷺ) as a discretionary rebuke (*ta'zir*) of Zaynab (may Allah be pleased with her) through the tongue of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), because she had a right to responses, meaning that there was benefit in that. Our jurists have mentioned that a judge may discipline one who deserves discipline for insult other than *qadhf* (false accusation of unchastity), and likewise a husband may discipline his wife for insulting him other than [the insult that is] a forbidden [relative], and other matters. So reflect on this.

The apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ requires observing equivalence absolutely. In *Tafsir al-Imam* [al-Razi] it is said that the verse requires the obligation of observing equivalence in all matters except what the evidence specifies, because if equivalence were taken in a specific matter, that is not mentioned in it, and that would entail *ijmal* (generality/ambiguity). And according to what we have said, it would entail bearing *takhsis* (specification). It is known that removing *ijmal* takes precedence over removing *takhsis*.

The jurists introduced specification into it in many cases: sometimes based on another, more specific text, and sometimes based on analogy (*qiyas*). There is no doubt that whoever claims specification has the burden of proof, and the one who is obligated is sufficed by holding to it in all the demands.

From Mujahid and al-Suddi: if one says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," then he should say, "May Allah disgrace you." But if he slanders him with slander that requires the *hadd* (fixed prescribed punishment), then he does not have that right; rather, the *hadd* is what Allah Exalted has commanded.

Abu Hayyan related from the majority that they said: if a believer oppresses a believer, it is not permitted for him to take retribution himself, but rather he refers the matter to the ruler or his deputy. In *Majma' al-Fatawa* it says: retaliation with its like is permitted in what does not necessitate a *hadd*, by permission for it: ﴿And whoever retaliates after being wronged, those have no path against them﴾. But pardon is better: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾.

Ibn al-Humam said: it is better that a person, when he is said something that necessitates discipline, not respond to it. They said: if he says to him, "O wicked one," it is best that he refrain from him and refer him to the judge so that he may discipline him in his presence. But if he responds to this and says, "Rather, you are! No harm."

In *al-Tanwir* and its commentary: if one strikes another without right, and the one struck also strikes him, both are disciplined, as when they insult each other in front of the judge and neither has the upper hand. You know what the apparent meaning of the verse requires, and one does not turn away from it except by a text.

The apparent meaning of the words of al-Allama al-Tibi is that if the wronged party pardons, the wrongdoer is not obligated to be disciplined by beating, imprisonment, or the like. Our jurists have mentioned that *ta'zir* predominantly involves the right of the servant, so acquittal, pardon, oath, testimony upon testimony, and the testimony of one man and two women are permitted in it. It is also a right of Allah Exalted, so there is no pardon in it except when the ruler knows that the doer has been restrained, and so on, to the end of what they said. And what is more likely in my view is that when the ruler, after reflection and detachment from the desires of the self, sees that abandoning *ta'zir* in favor of pardon would be a cause of corruption, of audacity in transgression, and of overstepping the bounds, he should discipline according to what the general public interest requires. He should exert his effort in what contains the reform of the religion and the orderly conduct of the affairs of the Muslims, and beware lest he follow his desire and thereby go astray from the straight path.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 44:

﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him.﴾ That is: for him there is no helper who would take up his cause after Allah has abandoned him to failure (khidhlan). The pronoun in (ba'dihi) refers to Allah, with a noun omitted before it (taqdir mudaf), i.e., "after the abandonment of Allah." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the abandonment (khidhlan) implied by (yudlil), and the clause is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying: ﴿Those, for them is a painful punishment.﴾ He used (man) to refer to the wrongdoer, the transgressor, to mark him as astray and forsaken; or He used it in an indefinite form so that it would encompass him in a primary sense. Then His saying, glory be to Him, (And whoever is patient) etc. is a parenthetical digression (i'tiraDh) relating to what we have pointed to.

﴿And you will see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment﴾: that is, when they see it. The past tense form is used to indicate certainty (tahaqquq). ﴿They will say, "Is there any way of return?"﴾: that is, a return to the world, ﴿"to any way"﴾ so that we may believe and do righteous deeds. It is also permitted that the meaning is: "Is there any way to repel the punishment and prevent it?" The indefiniteness of (maradd) and likewise (sabil) is for emphasis (mubalaghah). The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has also been said that it is a second object (maf'ul thani) of (tara).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 45:

Page 51
﴿And you see them exposed to it﴾, i.e., to the Fire, which is indicated by the mention of punishment; and the clause is like the preceding one. ﴿Humbled﴾, i.e., diminished and made small, ﴿from abasement﴾, i.e., because of abasement, owing to the magnitude of what has befallen them. So "min" (from) is causal (sababiyyah), connected with "humbled." This and what follows it are circumstantial clauses (hal).

It has been permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to the verb ﴿they look﴾ and that a pause be made at ﴿humbled﴾, ﴿with a furtive glance﴾. But the first is more apparent. The word "tarf" (glance) is a verbal noun of "taraf," meaning he moved his eye, and from it comes "tarfat al-'ayn" (the blink of an eye). By "khafiyy" (furtive) is meant weak. "Min" is then inceptive (ibtida'iyyah), i.e., their looking begins with a weak movement of the eyelids, stealthily, as you see the one who is forced to endure looks at the sword. Likewise, the gaze of one who looks at what is hateful: he cannot open his eyelids upon it and fill his eyes with it, as he does when looking at what he loves. It is also permitted that "min" carries the meaning of "ba'" (with).

On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, "khafiyy" means humiliated (dhalil), so "tarf" refers to the eyelid of the eye. It has also been said: they will be raised blind, so they will not look except with their hearts, and that is a look "from a furtive glance." This is a far-fetched interpretation. The two preceding clauses, namely "you see the wrongdoers" and "you see them exposed," are coordinated with "and whomever Allah leads astray." The original sense of the discourse is: "The wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, will say, while they are exposed to it, humbled..." Then it was said "and you see / and you see them" as an address to everyone who is capable of seeing and can take warning from their condition, for added terror, as though he marvels at them in what they are in, so that they may take heed and rejoice. From this it becomes apparent that it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ and his followers.

﴿And those who believed say: Indeed the losers﴾, i.e., they are those who lost themselves and their families by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment, or in accordance with what has passed in Surah al-Zumar. The phrase "those who" is used instead of "they" to record on them the most complete loss, since the intended meaning is that those who are perfect in the attribute of loss, who truly embody its reality, are these.

﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected to "lost," and the discussion concerning this world applies. It has also been permitted that it be connected to "say," and the past tense is used to affirm the certainty of occurrence, i.e., and they will say when they see them in that state. In al-Kashshaf, the apparent view is that it is a statement on the Day of Resurrection, like the loss, by way of the concurrence (tanazu') between the two verbs. But the author of al-Kashshaf preferred, contrary to what his practice seems to indicate, that it be connected to "loss" alone, because the original in "And those who believed say: Indeed the losers..." etc. is "they are the losers," just as the original in "And you see the wrongdoers" is "the wrongdoers, when they saw," then it was said "And those who believed say," in the same manner as "and you see" etc. And just as the seeing is seeing of this world, to summon their punishment which exists in the Hereafter, for the sake of terror, so too the saying: as though they made them present, their punishment being witnessed and what the believers say about them being heard. The address in the seeing was shifted to the third-person in the saying, because the witnessing of the punishment, being more effective in terror, made the punishment near and visible, and they were singled out for address to bring the situation to mind for greater rejoicing. There was not in "loss" that meaning, because it is an intelligible matter, and sensible things are stronger, especially when they are causes of loss. So it was brought in its original form in the third person, and he changed it from the present to the past because it is a statement issuing from the requirement of the situation, which has been fulfilled and has occurred, whether they uttered it or not. It was attributed to the believers to indicate the aforementioned rejoicing and their elation at their deliverance from what they are in. Otherwise, the saying and the seeing belong to everyone capable of saying and seeing. He made it a circumstantial clause, as al-Tibi did, meaning: "and you see them" while indeed the statement of the believers in this world, "Indeed the losers etc.," has come true concerning them, from the style of his saying:

When we trace ancestry, no base woman bore me

In it: this is only resorted to when the literal meaning is impossible, and the reading of concurrence is possible, so there is no impossibility.

Furthermore, in that case it does not appear that it is a statement "in it" except with an external proof. This differs from what Jar Allah mentioned regarding His saying, ﴿And I had already sent to you the warning﴾, of an estimate: "and it is established with you that I had sent," because in the wording there is clear indication of it. He concluded. By my life, he (may his secret be sanctified) has gone far from the meaning in these great verses and has brought what discerning minds find pleasing, so let it be understood.

And His saying, Exalted is He:
Page 52
﴿Indeed the wrongdoers are in a lasting punishment﴾. It is either a continuation of the speech of the believers, in which case what you have heard regarding the original and the nuance of the shift applies to it, or it is a resumed statement of information from Him, Exalted is He, confirming that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verse 46:

﴿And they will have no allies to help them, apart from Allah,﴾ to lift the punishment from them, ﴿as they supposed﴾. ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way﴾ to guidance or to salvation. It has also been said: the meaning is that he has no argument (ḥujjah).

Respond to your Lord ﴿istajibu li-rabbikum﴾, when He calls you to that which brings salvation through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿before there comes a Day which has no averting from Allah﴾. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur) may be connected to the noun *maradd* (averting), and the *ism* of *la* (the noun following *la* of absolute negation), which resembles a noun in an annexed construction (al-shabih bi al-mudaf), is treated like such a noun, so its tanwin (nunation) is dropped. Ibn Malik explicitly stated this in *al-Tashil*. Among its examples is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ), "(There is no preventer of what You have given)," and the Exalted's saying: ﴿There is no reproach against you today﴾, meaning: Allah does not reject it after He has decreed it.

Those who do not accept this view say: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning, "That is from Allah, the Exalted." The sentence is then a resumed sentence (istinaf) answering an implied question, whose assumed form is, "From whom is that?" Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the concealed pronoun in the adverbial phrase which serves as the predicate of *la*. Or it is connected to the negation, or to what the negation implies, as has been said regarding the Exalted's words: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾. It has also been said that it is connected to *ya'ti* (comes), but this was objected to as contrary to what is apparent from the wording and the meaning. It has been said that even with this connection it carries little benefit. It was also permitted that it be an attribute of *yawm* (day), but this was objected to as meaningfully weak. The apparent meaning is that this Day is the Day of Resurrection, not the day of the arrival of death, as has been said. ﴿You will have no refuge that Day﴾, meaning, no refuge to which you can flee so as to be delivered from the punishment, and *malja'* may be a place noun, or it may be a mimi verbal noun (a noun formed with the prefix *mim*). ﴿And you will have no denial﴾: "denial" here is the verbal noun of *ankara* (to deny), used contrary to the usual analogical pattern. The negation of this, together with the Exalted's words quoting them: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (6:23), is because their denial is treated as nonexistent, since it has no benefit, and the proof has been established and the limbs bear witness against them. Or it may be said that the two statements refer to different states and stations. It was also permitted that *nakir* be an intensive active participle (ism fa'il lil-mubalaghah), meaning: you will have no one who denies your states without distinguishing them, so as to show you mercy. But this, as you see, is weak.

[p. 52]

﴿But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾. This is a shift in the discourse, turning it away from addressing people after commanding them to respond, and directing it to the Messenger (ﷺ). That is: if they do not respond and turn away from what you call them to, do not be concerned about them, for We have not sent you as a watcher or one who calls them to account. ﴿Your duty is only to deliver the message﴾, that is, not to guard them, and you have done that.

﴿And when We let man taste mercy from Us﴾, that is, a blessing of health, wealth, security and the like, ﴿he rejoices in it﴾. "Man" is meant generically, covering everyone; in this case it has the sense of "humankind" or "people". For this reason the pronoun is plural in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and if an evil befalls them﴾. The generic sense is not an all-inclusive quantifier, and collectivity does not depend on it. It is as if it were said: "If We afflict people or humankind". ﴿Evil﴾ means affliction from illness, poverty, fear and other things. ﴿Because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, because of the evils that have proceeded from them. ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful﴾, intensely ungrateful: he forgets the blessing altogether, mentions the calamity and magnifies it, and does not reflect on its cause, but claims it has befallen him without his deserving it.

The alif-lam (al-) in it is also generic (li-l-jins). It has been said that in both places it is for specific reference (al-'ahd), meaning the criminals. It has also been said that in the first it is generic and in the second it is for specific reference. Al-Zamakhshari said: he intended by "man" the plural, not the singular, because of the plural pronoun, and he meant only the criminals, since the befalling of an evil "because of what their hands have sent forth" applies only to them. Then he said: "He did not say 'indeed he is ungrateful' in order to record that this kind is marked by ingratitude for blessings, as the Exalted said: (Indeed, man is greatly unjust and ungrateful. Indeed, man is to his Lord ungrateful)." From this al-'Allamah al-Tibi understood that in the first it is for specific reference,
[p. 53]
and that the intended ones are the disbelievers addressed in the saying of the Exalted: "Respond to your Lord" (42:47), (for the order) "then if they turn away" (to Him). He placed the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun to indicate their insistence on disbelief and to make known that they will not refrain from what they are engaged in. And in the second it is generic, so that the meaning is: this is not a novelty from this particular known human being, persistence, because this kind is marked by ingratitude for blessings. Thus condemning the absolute indicates condemnation of the restricted.

In al-Kashf it is said that he meant that "man," i.e., the first, is a generic noun suitable for all and for some; and when evidence establishes the intention of some, it becomes specific.
