Evidence has established, as has passed, that the affliction in the case of non-criminals is for a complete recompense. He did not go so far as to say the alif-lam is for specific reference. He made the saying of the Exalted "indeed, man is ungrateful" generic, so that it serves as a justification for the restricted by way of a fortiori reasoning, and is consistent with what came in many places in the Mighty Book. There is no harm in taking it as a reference back to what precedes, since it is generic too, and the benefit of placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is the one mentioned many times, indeed it is more indicative of the rule established in the principles of jurisprudence. And with both being generic, I say: the attribution of ingratitude, although it is a characteristic of disbelievers, to the generic class is due to their predominance, so it is an attributive metaphor (majaz 'aqli), since it is attributed to the class the state of its majority, because of its association with the majority. It is also permissible to consider the majority of individuals as identical with the class, because they predominate over others, in which case the metaphor is lexical (majaz lughawi). The same applies to the attribution of rejoicing when it means exultation (al-bataru), for that too is a characteristic of disbelievers. Indeed, even if it has its well-known meaning, which is the expansion of the breast with pleasure that is immediate, and this is most common in worldly bodily pleasures, then although it is not exclusive to disbelievers, and occurs among believers too out of necessity or gratitude, it does not encompass all individuals of the class. If you hold that it encompasses them, you would not need this, as when you interpret it as exultation with the intention of specific reference for "man". The befalling of an evil because of sins is also not general to all individuals, so the state of its attribution is known from what we have mentioned. The conditional sentence's opening with "when" (idha), with the attribution of the act of making taste to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) in the past tense, is to alert that the bestowing of blessing is certain in existence and frequent in occurrence, and that it is intended primarily from the absolutely Generous, the Exalted. Likewise, the opening of the second with "indeed" (inna), and the attribution of the befalling in the present tense to the evil, and its causation by their deeds, is to indicate the rarity of its occurrence and that it is far from being included in the sphere of primary intention and direct will. Placing the cause of the recompense in place of the recompense is an intensification in condemning them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 42, verses 49–50:**

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, not to other than Him, glorified is He, either jointly or independently. ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ without any obligation upon Him, glorified is He. ﴿He bestows female [children] upon whom He wills, and He bestows male [children] upon whom He wills﴾. ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren﴾. This is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*), or an explanation of ﴿He creates﴾, or a partial substitution (*badal al-ba'd*) from it, according to what al-Qadi [al-Baydawi] chose. When He, glorified is He, mentioned that man is made to taste mercy and is afflicted with its opposite, He followed this with the fact that to Him, glorified is He, belongs the dominion, and that He, exalted is He, distributes blessing and trial as He wills, by His far-reaching wisdom, not as man wills according to his desire. In this there is an indication that the tasting of mercy is not for exultation and insolence but for gratitude to the One who bestows it, and that the affliction of trial is not for ingratitude and impatience but for returning to the One who tests. It is also an emphasis for denying their ingratitude, from two aspects. The first: the dominion is His, glorified is He, without any rival or partner who disposes of it as He wills; so it is not for one who is the most insignificant part of His dominion, exalted is He, to object and wish to direct the affairs according to his corrupt desire. The second: this vast dominion belongs to that Mighty, Wise One, exalted is His majesty, whose nature is to create what He wills; so how could His disposal be other than in a manner that cannot be conceived as more perfect, nor more fitting to the requirement of wisdom and rightness? At that point nothing remains but submission and occupation with exalting the Bestower who tests, away from ingratitude and self-admiration. It also suited this context that the discourse should indicate from the very beginning that it is an act purely of His will, glorified is He, in which the will of the servant has no place. Therefore the females were placed first and the males were delayed, as if it were said: He creates what He wills; He bestows upon whom He wills of human beings what they do not desire, and He bestows upon whom He wills what they desire. The Arabs used to regard females as a trial, ﴿and when one of them is given the good news of a female, his face becomes darkened, and he is inwardly distressed﴾. Had the delayed been placed first, the arrangement would have been disrupted. The placing [of females first] is not merely for observing the proximity to trial, to be objected to by saying that the preceding verse mentioned mercy first, so that placing males before females would have been appropriate. Regarding the definiteness of ﴿the males﴾, together with what it contains of a corrective response to the matter of delay, there is an alert that they are the familiar ones present in their hearts at the forefront of every thought, and the ones upon whom they have fixed their hopes. When the purpose of this style was fulfilled, it was said: ﴿or He pairs them﴾, that is, the children, ﴿males and females﴾, meaning He creates what He grants them as a pair, because pairing means making a thing a pair. So ﴿males and females﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun. The waw (*wa*) has been said to be for accompaniment (*ma'iyya*), because its proper place is to come after the two divisions in context and in existence, so accompaniment can only be achieved in this way. It has also been said that this is because what is meant is: He bestows upon whom He wills what they do not desire, and He bestows upon whom He wills what they desire, or He bestows both together; not that He, glorified is He, makes of each of the two sexes, males and females, separately a pair. Were it not for this, what was mentioned would have been misunderstood, so reflect upon it. Because it is composed of both, He did not repeat the matter of the will. He placed what is placed first before what is by origin, and He did not make it definite, since there is no reason for that. Then it was said: ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾, that is, he does not have children born to him. He restricted it by the will because this is another division. It seems that *aw* (or) was used in ﴿or He pairs them﴾ rather than the waw, as in the preceding, insofar as it is the counterpart of the exclusive division shared between the first two. It was not used in the last because it is clear that it is the counterpart of the gift shared among the preceding divisions, so reflect. It has also been said: He placed females first as an exhortation to care for them because of their weakness, especially as they were recently associated with the practice of burying daughters alive. In the hadith: "Whoever is tested with some of these daughters and treats them well, they will be a shield for him from the Fire." It has also been said: they were placed first because they are more numerous, so for this reason they are more suitable to the creation whose explanation is intended. It has been said: [they were placed first] to console the hearts of their fathers, since placing them first is an honour, for they are the cause of the increase of His creatures, exalted is He. Al-Tha'alibi said: it is an indication of the blessing contained in their being born first, to the point that the first male child is considered inauspicious, so they say to him: "You were early by two firstborns." From Qatada: it is a blessing for a woman that her first child be a female. It has also been said: the females were placed first and the males delayed and defined in order to preserve the rhyme (*fawasil*). The most suitable to the context is what you have already known. Mujahid said regarding ﴿or He pairs them﴾: pairing is that a woman gives birth to a boy and then gives birth to a girl. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: it is that she gives birth to twins, a boy and a girl. Some claimed that the verse was revealed concerning the prophets, peace be upon them, since Allah, glorified is He, bestowed females upon Shu'ayb and Lut, peace be upon them, and males upon Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and males and females upon His Messenger Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and made Jesus and Yahya, peace be upon them both, barren. End. ﴿Indeed He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful﴾: intensive in knowledge and power, exalted is His glory, so He does what He does with wisdom and choice.

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** (*The Spirit of the Meanings*) by **al-Alusi**, commentary on Surah 42, verse 51 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not for any human﴾, that is, it is not valid for any individual among the children of Adam.

﴿that Allah should speak to him except by revelation (*wahy*), or from behind a veil, or send a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾. Its apparent meaning restricts speech to three categories. The first is *wahy* (revelation), which is what is meant by His saying, ﴿except by revelation﴾. Some scholars explained it as a casting into the heart (*ilqa' fi al-qalb*), whether while awake or while asleep. The casting is more general than *ilham* (inspiration). The revelation to the mother of Musa was *ilham*, while the revelation to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was a casting during sleep and was not *ilham*. The revelation of the Zabur was a casting while awake, as is related from Mujahid, and it was not *ilham*. The difference is that *ilham* does not require the form of an inner speech (*kalam nafsani*), whereas the verbal form is not required for it either. As for the revelation of the Zabur, it requires that form. The term *wahy* has also been used for casting into the heart, in the words of Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

*"Allah inspired me that they had agreed*
*on the camels of Abi Awfa, so I rose on my feet."*

He meant: "He cast into my heart."

The second is hearing speech without the listener seeing the one who speaks to him, as was the case with Musa, and likewise the angels whom Allah addressed in the matter of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, and others. This is what is meant by His words, ﴿or from behind a veil﴾, for it is an illustration of Him, Glorified is He, by the situation of a king who is veiled, speaking to some of his close associates from behind a curtain, so that they hear his voice but do not see his person.

The third is the sending of an angel, which is the usual case for our Prophet ﷺ, and is the case for many of the prophets, peace be upon them. The claim that this is among the special features of the *Ulu al-'Azm* (the resolute messengers) is not correct. This is what is meant by the words of the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿or send a messenger﴾, that is, an angel, ﴿and he reveals﴾, that is, that messenger reveals to the one addressed, who is the human messenger, ﴿by His permission﴾, that is, by His command and facilitation, Glorified is He, ﴿what He wills﴾ to reveal. This indicates that the first category, revelation, is from Allah, Exalted is He, without an intermediary, because the sending of a messenger is described as including the revelation of that messenger.

The Mu'tazili (*Mu'tazilah*, a rationalist theological school) built on this restriction the view that seeing Allah is not possible, because if it were valid, then direct speech (*mushafahah*) would be valid, and so the restriction would not hold. Some said that the meaning of the restriction is that speech is confined to revelation in its well-known sense, to speech from behind a veil, and to the speech of human messengers with their communities. This was judged unlikely, because usage has not consistently applied the term "revelation" to that. Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) said that the words of the Exalted, ﴿except by revelation﴾, mean: except a hidden speech that is grasped swiftly and is not, in itself, composed of separate letters. This includes direct speech, as related in the hadith of the Mi'raj, and what was promised in the hadith of the vision, and the voice heard by Musa, peace be upon him, at the mountain (al-Tur). But the conjunction of His words, ﴿or from behind a veil﴾, to this restricts it to the first category, so the verse is evidence for the permissibility of seeing (Allah), not for its impossibility. Al-Zamakhshari went to the first view, and Sahib al-Kashf (the author of *al-Kashf*), may Allah pardon him, supported it. He said: "As for us, we say, and Allah knows best: the words of the Exalted, ﴿It is not for any human﴾, in general terms, require restriction in a manner that does not confine speech to the prophets, peace be upon them, and includes the address to Maryam, the case of the mother of Musa, and what befalls the *muhaddathun* (those spoken to by inspiration) of this community and others. Therefore, interpreting *wahy* in the manner that al-Zamakhshari adopted is preferable." Then, it follows for al-Qadi that what took place from behind a veil is not revelation, not that he restricts it. That is like your saying, "It was not for you to bestow favour except upon the needy and Zayd," yes, it is possible that Zayd is included among them, in the manner of ﴿His angels and His messengers and Jibril﴾. This harms al-Qadi, because it requires that this category, I mean what took place from behind a veil, be the highest of the ranks, so the second would not be the direct speech.

The estimate "except by revelation without a veil, or from behind a veil" departs from the apparent meaning, and it entails disrupting the structure of the verse, because the words ﴿or send﴾ are conjoined to His words ﴿except by revelation﴾, despite being contrary to the apparent meaning.

On this basis, what was built upon it, the idea of descent (*tanazzul*) from the higher category to what is lower, collapses. Nevertheless, it does not indicate the non-occurrence of the vision, let alone its impossibility. Rather, it indicates that if the vision occurred, speech would not accompany it. This is the correct view, because vision requires annihilation (*fana'*) and subsistence (*baqa'*) through Him, Mighty and Majestic, and this requires lifting the veil of the one addressed, which demands an existential state. Then the perfect one, through his fulfilment of the greatest stations, will be the one who is favoured with witnessing in the aforementioned station of subsistence. Nevertheless, this does not prevent him from his share of hearing the address, because that share belongs to the heart that is veiled from the station of witnessing.

The point is that what is valid by experience (*dhawq*), transmission (*naql*), and reason (*'aql*) is that address from behind a veil is absolutely possible, and this is correct, but it does not benefit the one who denies the vision nor the one who affirms it.

As for the question of ascent (*tarraqi*) among the categories, the answer to it is that the ascent is present between the first and the second, by which the one who spoke with Allah was named *Kalim* (the one who spoke). As for the third, because it is a figurative speech, it was placed after the two categories, and one did not consider that it is more exalted than the first category, for that matter does not relate to speech itself, but rather because it is specific to the prophets, peace be upon them. End of quotation.

It was objected to al-Qadi that the objection does not apply, because revelation in that sense, through the specification mentioned and the restriction derived from the contrast, has become different from what follows it, and it is not of either of the two kinds such that one could proceed to ascent or descent, because it is not conjoined with *aw* (or) but with *wa* (and), as is not hidden. As for the claim that what occurs from behind a veil is not revelation, it is not accepted, because if he means that it is not revelation absolutely, then that is incorrect, since the words of the Exalted after it, ﴿then he reveals by His permission﴾, are an indication that the revelation mentioned earlier is a specific revelation like the one after it. If he means that it is not of the specific revelation mentioned earlier, then this does not harm him, because he has specified what he meant. Yes, the restriction according to what al-Qadi held is not apparent except after noting that it is specific to what occurs through speech, so reflect.

The apparent position is that A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, interpreted the verse in a manner similar to the Mu'tazilah. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and al-Tirmidhi related from her that she said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has lied." Then she recited, ﴿Vision does not comprehend Him, but He comprehends vision, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾.

[p. 56]

﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil﴾. You know that most scholars hold that the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord, Glorified is He, on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey), because of the abundance of reports that explicitly state the vision. Yes, there is no explicit statement that it was with the eye, but the apparent meaning of "vision" is that it was with it. It is related from al-Ash'ari and a group of theologians (*mutakallimun*) that He, Exalted is His majesty, spoke to him, peace be upon him, that night without an intermediary. This is attributed to Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Baqir, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them. This is the apparent meaning of the authentic hadiths concerning the reduction of the prayers and the settlement at fifty reduced to five, and other matters. A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, did not deny the vision except by relying on deduction from the verses. Had she had a report, she would have mentioned it. Her argument by what was mentioned of the verses is not complete. As for the incompleteness of her argument from the verse ﴿Vision does not comprehend Him﴾, it is well known. As for the incompleteness of the argument from the second verse, it is because of what I heard from Sahib al-Kashf, may Allah sanctify his secret.

Al-Khafaji, after establishing the argument that He, Exalted is He, restricted His speech to mankind to three categories, said: "If the one who is addressed by Him, Glorified is He, at the time of speech does not see Him, then one who is other than him will not see Him, Mighty and Majestic, by a fortiori reasoning. And if He, Exalted is He, is not seen by Himself at all, then no one else will see Him, Glorified is He, since there is no one who makes a distinction." It has been answered in the principles (*usul*) that it is possible that the intended meaning is restricting speech in this world to these three categories, or we say that it is permissible for the vision to occur during the time of speech as revelation, since revelation is speech delivered swiftly, and that does not contradict the vision. End of quotation.

It is not hidden from you that the first answer does not benefit us in what we are concerned with, except by committing to the view that what happened to our Prophet, peace be upon him, that night is not considered speech in this world, as al-Sharnabili mentioned in *Ikram Uli al-Albab*, because it took place in the highest kingdom (*malakut*). It is also understood from the words of Sahib al-Kashf that there is a clear objection to the conditional in the way of the inference he established. Some answered that the general statement is specified without any evidence. In *al-Bahr* it is said that it was related: "The Quraysh said: 'Will you not speak to Allah, Exalted is He, and look at Him, if you are a truthful prophet, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke to Musa and looked at him?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: 'Musa, peace be upon him, did not look at Allah, Mighty and Majestic.' Then ﴿It is not for any human﴾ was revealed, the verse." This is evident that the verse did not include oral speech with the vision. Likewise, there was also from the disbelievers an immersion into the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, to Musa, peace be upon him, so the Quraysh and the Jews went in that matter to anthropomorphism (*tajsim*), and so it was revealed. Indeed, its not including that is more effective in repelling the suspicion of anthropomorphism.

In sum, what I find more preferable is what Sahib al-Kashf, may Allah sanctify his secret, said: that the verse neither benefits the one who denies the vision nor the one who affirms it, and what has been mentioned as the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) is not of certain authenticity.

It is understood from the words of some scholars that revelation, just as it occurs by casting into the spirit (*ruwa'*), also occurs by writing (*khatt*). Al-Nakha'i said: "Among the prophets, peace be upon them, there was one for whom a line was drawn on the earth." Its linguistic meaning includes that. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Taymi al-Asbahani said: "The origin of *wahy* is conveying understanding, and whatever through which something is understood, such as inspiration, gesture, or books, is revelation." Al-Raghib said: "The origin of *wahy* is a rapid indication, and because of the speed it includes, it is said: 'a matter of wahy.' That occurs by speech in symbolic and allusive form, and it may occur by a bare sound free of composition, by a gesture with some limbs, and by writing." It has been interpreted in this sense the words of the Exalted, ﴿So he revealed to them that they should glorify [Allah] in the morning﴾. It has been said it is a symbol, it has been said it is an indication, and it has been said it is writing. Subjugation (*taskhir*) has also been considered among revelation, and the words of the Exalted, ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee﴾, have been interpreted in that sense. What the Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, said about this verse will come, if Allah wills.

As for the words "revelation" (*wahyan*), according to al-Zamakhshari, it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) occupying the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), and likewise ﴿that He should send﴾, because it is in the sense of "sending" (*irsalan*). And ﴿from behind a veil﴾ is an adverbial phrase occupying the position of a circumstantial phrase as well, like the words of the Exalted, ﴿and upon their sides﴾. The sense is: "It is not valid that He speak to anyone in any state except by revealing, or by causing to hear from behind a veil, or by sending." Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying: "The occurrence of a verbal noun as a circumstantial phrase is not a general rule, so it is not permissible to say *ja'a Zayd buka'an* meaning *ja'a Zayd baki'an* (Zayd came weeping)." Al-Mubarrad allowed that from it what is a type of the verb, such as *ja'a Zayd mashyan* or *sur'atan* (Zayd came walking or quickly). Sibawayh prohibited the occurrence of *an* with the verb in the position of a circumstantial phrase, so it is not permissible to say *ja'a Zayd an yadhaka* with the meaning of *dahikan* occupying the position of *dahik* (Zayd came laughing).

And as for the first objection, it is answered that the Qur'an may be analogized upon, but it does not follow that it must be analogized upon other than it. Furthermore, it may be said that the analogy of al-Mubarrad (al-Mubarrad, the grammarian) suffices. As for the second objection, [the grammarian] gave as the reason for the prohibition that what results from the composition (al-sabk) is a definite noun (ma'rifa), and a definite noun does not occur as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). But this is open to scrutiny, because the rule is not consistently applicable. In the commentary on al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil) it is stated that it may also be an indefinite noun (nakira). Do you not see that they explained (an yuftara) as (muftara), an indefinite? Ibn Jinni presented this to Abu 'Ali (Abu 'Ali al-Farisi), and he approved of it. And even granting that the rule is consistent, a definite noun may indeed be a circumstantial qualifier when it has the sense of an indefinite, as in wahdahu ("alone"). Restricting oneself to the prohibition is preferable, since this involves excessive forcing (ta'assuf). Many [scholars] have chosen that wahyan ("by revelation"), which is coordinated with it, is in the accusative governed by the verbal noun (al-masdar), because it is a kind of speech (kalam). Or [it is governed] by the implied exception: "except speech of revelation." And min wara'i hijab ("from behind a veil") is a qualifier of an implied speech or hearing, and the qualifier of the verbal noun stands in its place. Sending a messenger is also a kind of speech in terms of its outcome. The exception concerning it is a detached (mufarragh) exception from the most general of the verbal nouns. Al-Zajjaj said: Sibawayh said, "I asked al-Khalil about His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or sends a messenger﴾ in the accusative," and he said: "It is understood as meaning that other than this [mode] which is in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿that Allah speaks to him﴾, because it would follow from that that one would say: 'It is not for a human that Allah should send a messenger,' and that is not permissible. The meaning is: it is not for a human ﴿that Allah should speak to him﴾ except by revelation, or by sending [a messenger]." And on this it must be supposed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or from behind a veil﴾ something like "or that he hears from behind a veil." And what need is there for that, given what you have heard?

It has been disputed whether the exception is connected (muttasil) or disconnected (munqati'). Abu al-Baqa' held it to be disconnected, and some have criticized him, saying that a detached (mufarragh) exception does not carry this characterization. The discussion is well known.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read (aw min wara'i hujub) in the plural. Nafi' and the people of Madina read (aw yursila rasulan fa-yuhi) with both verbs in the nominative, and they justified this as being on the supposition of an implied subject, i.e., "He sends," or as being coordinated with (wahyan), or with what is connected to (min wara'), on the basis that its implied form is "or he hears from behind a veil." The scholar al-Thani (al-Taftazani) said: the second justification and what follows it are evident, namely the coordination of a verbal clause of circumstance upon a singular circumstantial qualifier. As for supposing an implied subject, if it is understood in this sense, then the supposition of the subject is superfluous; and if it is meant that the clause is resumptive (mustanafa), then no apparent thing is coordinated upon except "it is not for a human" etc., and this is not a well-fitting arrangement. It was objected that it is possible for the implied subject to be supposed while taking the circumstantial sense into account, on the basis that a nominal clause whose predicate is a verbal clause conveys what a pure verbal clause does not convey, of what is suitable to the situation of the sending of a messenger. Or it may be said: we do not concede that coordination upon "it is not for a human" is not well-fitting; and in this there is a subtlety that is not hidden.

According to what Ibn 'Atiyya said, the verse is evidence that whoever swears not to speak to a certain person and then sends him a message breaks his oath, since God excepted sending from speech. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti related this in Ahkam al-Qur'an from Malik, and there is discussion in it. And God, Exalted, is the Guide.

﴿Indeed He is Most High﴾, exalted above the attributes of created beings, ﴿Wise﴾, He conducts His acts, may He be glorified, according to the laws of wisdom, so He speaks

Page 58

sometimes through an intermediary and other times without one, either by inspiration (ilham) and address, or by direct vision and address from behind a veil, in accordance with what the earlier disagreement in the interpretation of the verse requires.

﴿And thus﴾, that is, and in the same wondrous manner of revelation, [this indicates that] the reference of "this" is to what came before: ﴿We revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾. This is what was revealed to him, peace be upon him, or it is the Qur'an, which for hearts is like the spirit for bodies, since it gives them an everlasting life. It has also been said: that is, and like the well-known revelation to others, We revealed to you. It has also been said: that is, and like that detailed revelation, We revealed to you, since he, peace be upon him, had all three modes of revelation (al-turuq al-thalath) combined for him, whether revelation (wahy) is explained as inspiration (al-ilqa') or as spoken speech (al-kalam al-shafahi). It has been mentioned that he, peace be upon him, had revelation cast into him in dreams, just as it was cast into Abraham, peace be upon him, and it was cast into him, peace be upon him, while awake, in the manner of the casting of the Psalms (al-Zabur) to David, peace be upon him.

In *al-Kibrit al-Ahmar* by al-Sha'rani, quoting from the second chapter of *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*, it is stated that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was given the Qur'an in summary form before Gabriel, peace be upon him, without the detailed division of its verses and chapters. And from Ibn 'Abbas, the spirit is explained as prophethood.

Al-Rabi' said: it is Gabriel, peace be upon him. Accordingly, "We revealed" is taken to include the meaning of "We sent," and the sense is: We sent him with revelation to you, because one does not say "he revealed the angel," but rather "he sent him."

Al-Tabarsi transmitted from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the intended "spirit" is an angel greater than Gabriel and Michael, who was with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but did not ascend to the heavens. This view is extremely strange, and it is probably not authentically attributed to these two imams. The tanwin on (ruhan) is for magnification, meaning: a great spirit.

﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was﴾. The apparent reading is that the first "ma" is negative, and the second is interrogative, in a nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), with "al-Kitab" as its predicate (khabar). The clause is in a place of accusative by [the verb] "tadri" (you knew). The clause "you did not" and so on is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "We revealed," or it is a new independent clause, and the past tense is relative to the time of revelation.

The verse has been found problematic, because its apparent meaning requires that [the Prophet] not have been characterized by faith before revelation, and this is not correct, since all the prophets, peace be upon them, were believers before their mission, being protected from disbelief by the consensus of those whose opinion counts. It has been answered in several ways:

The first: faith here does not mean bare assent (al-tasdiq al-mujarrad), but the whole of assent, affirmation, and deeds. For it is applied to this in the legal sense as well as the other. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah would not waste your faith﴾. Deeds cannot be known without hearing, so [faith] is composite, and a composite is negated when some of its parts are negated. Therefore, the negation of composite faith due to the negation of deeds does not necessarily entail the negation of faith in the other sense, namely assent, which scholars have agreed the prophets, peace be upon them, were characterized by before their mission. That is why the verse uses "you did not know" rather than "you were not a believer." This is a good answer, and it does not necessitate denying faith to one who does not perform acts of obedience, lest the saying become Mu'tazilism (i'tizal), as is not hidden.

The second: faith is only understood as belief in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, peace be upon him, and not belief in Allah alone, nor what includes deeds. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is addressed to believe in the message of himself, just as his community, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are addressed with that. There is no doubt that before revelation he, peace be upon him, did not know that he was the Messenger of Allah, and he knew that only through revelation. So if faith is assent to Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and this combination was not established before revelation, but what was established was assent to Allah the Exalted alone, which is agreed upon as characteristic of the prophets, peace be upon them, before their mission, then the negation of faith before revelation is valid. This is the view of Ibn al-Munir.

The third: the intended meaning is the rules of faith (shara'i' al-iman) and its signposts, which have no path to them except hearing. This is the view of Muhyi al-Sunna al-Baghawi, who said: the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was before revelation upon the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, and the rules of his religion had not been made clear to him, peace be upon him.

[Page 59]

It is not hidden that if the statement is not considered to involve an omitted genitive (hadhf mudaf), it would necessitate applying the term faith to deeds alone, which is contrary to what is well known.

The fourth: the statement involves an omitted genitive. It is said that the implied phrase is "the call of faith," meaning: you did not know how to call creation to faith. This is what the saying of Abu al-'Aliya indicates.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: that is, the people of faith; meaning: you did not know who would believe, while you knew that he would not accept this except one who is not known.

The fifth: the intended meaning is the negation of knowing the whole, that is: before revelation, you did not know the whole of the Book and faith. This does not contradict his, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knowing faith alone, and the repetition of "la" (not) rejects this.

The sixth: the intended meaning is that you did not know that when you were in the cradle. This is the view of 'Ali ibn 'Isa, and it is contrary to the apparent meaning.

The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the continuation of the negation until the time of revelation. The speech of the *Kashshaf* tends to consider this kind of restriction. It said: perhaps the more fitting view is that faith is in its apparent sense, and the verse comes in the context of favor (imtinan), and revelation includes casting into the heart and sending a messenger. So faith he knew by the first, and the Book by the second. This indicates that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knew both of them after he had not been knowing them, and this is so. As for his knowing them after revelation, this is not [indicated], so it is permissible that he knew them by it, and permissible that he knew one of them specifically by it. The evidence has indicated that what was made known by it is the Book and faith, after reason and before revelation. Using this to argue that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was not bound by the law of those before him is weak, because not knowing does not necessitate not being bound by it, rather it necessitates the removal of sin if there was no negligence. End of quotation.

You know that the more obvious reading is that he, peace be upon him, knew them after revelation. As for his statement, may his secret be sanctified, in weakening the argument from this that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was not bound by the law of those before him, namely that not knowing does not necessitate not being bound, it has been objected to: this is invalid, because if he, peace be upon him, did not know the law, how could he worship by it? It may be answered that the intent of the careful scholar is that the knowledge negated is knowledge in the sense of certain, firm knowledge that corresponds to reality, and its absence does not necessitate the absence of being bound, since for being bound by the law of those before him, peace be upon him, the prevailing presumption (al-zann al-rajih) of its being established suffices. So perhaps this was obtained by him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Such presumption suffices for those who today are bound by the law of our Prophet, peace be upon him, for most of the subsidiary rulings (al-furu') are presumptive. Whoever investigates the reports knows that the Arabs were still upon remnants of the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him: the pilgrimage, circumcision, the pronouncement of divorce, the ritual bath from major impurity, and the prohibition of those within the prohibited degrees by kinship and marriage, and other things. And that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the most eager of people to follow the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him. In the Sahih it is stated that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to practice tahannuth (withdrawal and devotion) in the cave of Hira, before his mission. Tahannuth has been explained as tahannuf, meaning following the hanifiyya (the upright monotheistic religion), which is the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, and the fa' is replaced by tha' in much of their speech. In the version of Ibn Hisham in the *Sira* it is "yatahannaf" with fa' in place of tha'. Indeed, it has also been explained as worship, as in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, and as guarding against sin (al-hinth), meaning sin, like avoidance of wrong and self-accusation. All of this is what al-Hafiz al-Qastallani mentioned in his commentary on the Sahih.

Then, the apparent meaning is that whoever says he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was bound by the law of those before him does not mean that he, peace be upon him, was bound by the entire law of those before him, but by what was prevailingly established to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. What should be preferred is that this is from the law of Abraham, peace be upon him, because he is among his descendants, peace be upon them both, and the Arabs were charged with his religion.

Some have said: his worship, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was contemplation and reflection. Perhaps this too is among what was prevailingly established to him, peace be upon him, that it was from his law, peace be upon him. It may also be said that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knew by [revelation], not in that specific way, from the law of those before him, that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had always been receiving revelation, and that he, peace be upon him, was bound by what was revealed to him. Yet the revelation prior to the mission was casting and breathing into the heart, and he did not act by what was among the laws of his father Abraham, peace be upon them both, except through that casting. And if some of his brother prophets, peace be upon them, were given judgment as children, aged two or three, then he, peace be upon him, is more worthy that this type of revelation be made to him as a child too.

Whoever knows his station, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and believes that he is the beloved who was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay, will not find this far-fetched, so reflect.

﴿But We made it﴾, that is, the spirit which We revealed to you, a light. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the pronoun refers to the Book. It has also been said: it refers to faith, and this was preferred due to proximity. It has also been said: it refers to both the Book and faith, and it is in the singular because their purpose is one, like the Exalted's saying: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾.

﴿a light﴾, great, ﴿by which We guide whom We will﴾ to guidance, ﴿of Our servants﴾, and this is the one whose choice is turned toward being guided by it. The clause is either a new independent statement or an attribute of "light." The Exalted's saying ﴿And indeed you guide﴾ is an affirmation of his guidance and an explanation of its manner. The object of "you guide" is omitted, relying on its being extremely clear, meaning: and indeed you guide, by that light, whom you will to be guided, ﴿to a straight path﴾, which is Islam and all the other laws and rulings.

Ibn al-Sumayqa' read "tuhdi" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the dal, from "ahda." Hawshab read "tuhda," in the passive, meaning: Allah guides you. And it has been read "latad'u" (you call).

[Page 60]

﴿The path of Allah﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the previous noun, and its attribution to the Glorious Name, then His description of it with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, is to magnify His affair, to establish the uprightness of that path, and to affirm the obligation of following it. For the fact that everything in them among the existent beings belongs to Him, Exalted is He, in creation, dominion and disposal, is among the things that make this obligation absolutely binding.

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah do all affairs return﴾: that is, the affairs of all who are in them, entirely, return to none other than Him, Exalted is He. This will be on the Day of Resurrection, when intermediaries are removed. In this there is a promise for those who are guided to the straight path and a warning for those who stray from it, of what is not hidden. The imperfect form (the verb in the present tense), according to what we have established, is upon its apparent meaning of the future. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: its meaning is habitual continuity, as in "Zayd gives" (i.e., it is his nature to do so). The first is more apparent, and Allah, Exalted is He, knows best.

Among what the people of allusions (ahl al-isharat, those who interpret the Qur'an through esoteric indications) have said concerning some verses: He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿So that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾. It was said that this points to warning one's own noble self, because it is the mother of the cities of the souls of Adam and his descendants, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was the first of the worlds in creation, and from him (may the blessings and peace be upon him) the spirits and souls came into being. For this reason Adam and whoever is below him are under his banner (ﷺ). The Sultan of the Lovers, ʿUmar ibn al-Farid, alluded to this with his words, speaking on behalf of the Muhammadan reality:

"Though I am the son of Adam in form,
within me is a meaning that bears witness to my fatherhood."

His words, Glorified is He: ﴿and those around it﴾ point to the souls of the people of the world. He (ﷺ) warned each one according to its receptivity (istiʿdad). It was also said: concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, that it points to transcendence (tanzih) and anthropomorphism (tashbih). The Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, established this at length.

﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, the keys of the heavens of the hearts, in which are the treasures of His gentleness, Exalted is He, and His mercy, Mighty and Majestic is He; and the earth of the souls, in which are the treasures of His subjugation, Glorified is He, and His might, Majestic is His majesty. Every heart is a treasury for a kind of His gentleness, such as knowledge (maʿrifa), love (mahabba), longing (shawq), unification (tawhid), awe (hayba), intimacy (uns) and contentment (rida), and so on. Treasures may be gathered in one heart. Every soul is a storehouse for a kind of the effects of His subjugation, such as denial (nukra), obstinate rejection (juhud), refusal (inkar), polytheism (shirk), hypocrisy (nifaq), greed (hirs), arrogance (kibr), miserliness (bukhl), avarice (sharah), and other things. Treasures may be gathered in one soul.

[Page 61]

The benefit of informing that He, Glorified is He, possesses the keys to these things is to cut the thoughts of the servants away from anyone other than Him, Glorified is He, in bringing what they desire and repelling what they dislike.

﴿Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills, and guides to Himself whoever turns (to Him) in repentance﴾: this points to the two stations, of the one who is drawn (majdhub) and of the wayfarer (salik). The one who is drawn is of the elect (khawass), whom his Lord chose for Himself, Glorified is He, in eternity, and placed on the path of those whom He loves, and fashioned for Himself, Majestic is His affair, and drew him, Exalted is He, away from both abodes with an attraction equal to the deeds of both humans and jinn. So he is in a seat of truth before an All-Powerful King. The wayfarer from among the common people is one whom He placed in the company of those whom He loves, by granting success in guidance and standing upon the feet of striving and turning back to the path of right direction, away from the way of obstinacy.

﴿And those who dispute concerning Allah after it has been responded to﴾: this points to those who argue about the knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, with the doubts of the intellect, which responded to Him, Exalted is He, when He called it, and so it reached the presence (hadra). Such a one is in unveiling (kashf) and direct witnessing (ʿiyan). As for those others, they are behind what they claim to be a proof.

﴿Or do they have associates who have instituted for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾: this points to the unbelievers of the souls, for when they gain control over the spirits and hearts, they institute what Allah, Exalted is He, has not approved of: violations of the Shariʿa and agreements with the natural appetites (tabiʿa).

﴿Allah is Gentle with His servants﴾: this points to the generality of His gentleness, Exalted is He, which consists of kinds that cannot be counted and degrees that cannot be exhausted.

Al-Sulami narrated from the master of the tariqa (the Sufi path), may his secret be sanctified: "The Gentle is the One who illuminates your heart with guidance, nourishes your body with food, brings you out of the world with faith, guards you from the fire of blazing flame, and empowers you until you look and see. This is the gentleness of the Gentle toward the weak servant."

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: they employ the obligations of the Law to subdue the natural nature, break the desire, purify the soul, clarify the heart and polish the spirit.

﴿In the meadows of the gardens﴾: in this world, the gardens of union, of knowledge (maʿarif), and of the goodness of intimacy in seclusion; and in the Hereafter, in the meadows of Paradise.

﴿They shall have whatever they will with their Lord﴾: according to their stations in closeness, union, unveilings, attaining ranks, and in accordance with their aspirations (himam).

﴿Say: I do not ask of you any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾: they are his close relatives (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him), who were created from his noble origin and adorned with his lofty qualities, such as the Imams of the People of the House. Their love returns its benefit to the one who loves them, because it is a cause of overflowing bounty (fayd). They, may Allah be pleased with them, are his gates. His words (ﷺ): "I am the city of knowledge and ʿAli is its gate" point to this. So understand the allusion.

﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾: for the abundance of His generosity, Majestic is His affair. Whenever He grants a servant success in repentance, He accepts it out of munificence and generosity. It is related from one of them that he said to a shaykh: "If I repent, will Allah accept me?" The shaykh said: "If Allah accepts you, you will repent to Him, Glorified is He." So Allah's acceptance precedes repentance.

﴿And He increases them from His bounty﴾: an allusion to the vision (ru'ya), for the gardens and their bliss are created things, which occur in exchange for a created thing, which is the work of the workers. The vision is related to the Eternal, and so it occurs only as a divine bounty. In some reports it is said that this increase is that He will intercede for them on behalf of their brothers' brothers.

﴿Respond to your Lord﴾: response for the common people is through fulfilling His covenant, Exalted is He, establishing His right, Glorified is He, and turning back from disobeying Him, Majestic is His affair, to agreeing with Him, Mighty and Majestic is He. For the elect, it is through surrendering to the eternal decrees, turning away from the world, its adornments and its appetites. For the most elect among the people of love, it is through sincerity of seeking, turning away from both abodes and turning toward the presence of Majesty, by expending existence itself in attaining union and joining.

﴿He bestows females upon whom He wills, and bestows males upon whom He wills, or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren﴾: it was said that this contains an allusion to the states of the shaykhs in regard to their disciples (murids). Some of them Allah bestows upon, and some of them have no power over others in training (takhrij) and guiding on the path (taslik). This is most like the female in lacking the power of disposal. Some of them Allah, Glorified is He, bestows upon one who has the capacity of disposal in training and guiding, and this is most like the male. Some of them He bestows both upon, and some of them He, Majestic and Exalted is He, makes barren for a matter that He knows in origin.

﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills; indeed He is Most High, All-Wise﴾: Our master, the Shaykh ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Shaʿrani, said in his commentary on the aforementioned verse:

[Page 62]

Know that what prevents hearing the speech of the Truth is nothing but humanness (bashariyya). So when the servant rises above it, Allah, Exalted is He, speaks to him in the same way He speaks to the disembodied spirits free from matter. The human (bashar) is so named only because of his engagement (mubasharatihi) with the affairs that hinder him from attaining a rank. So when he does not attain it, Allah, Exalted is He, speaks to him through things, and manifests Himself, Glorified is He, to him through them. This is unlike one who has attained, such as the prophets, peace be upon them, for the Truth, Glorified is He, manifests Himself to others only behind the veil of forms. Were it not for Allah's guidance to the servant, he would not know that He, Glorified is He, is his Lord.

Know that the Reality (haqiqa) refuses that Allah, Exalted is He, should speak to other than Himself or make other than Himself hear. Therefore, when He addresses a servant with the intention of making him hear, it is necessary that all his faculties be present, for it is impossible for the originated being to bear hearing the speech of the Eternal. The Truth, Glorified is He, had not strengthened him at the time of the secret conversation. For this reason Moses, peace be upon him, fell down unconscious (sa'qan), since he had no receptivity that would accept the manifestation befitting his station. Our Prophet (ﷺ) remained firm, and since the mountain did not have the degree of love by which the Truth becomes the hearing, sight and all the faculties of His servant, it could not bear the address, and so it crumbled (duka).

Know that the speech of the Truth, Glorified is He, to creation never ceases, yet among people is one who understands that it is speech, like ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and those who inherited it from the saints. Among them is one who does not recognize this and says: "Such and such appeared to me," and does not know that this is speech from the Truth, Glorified is He, to him. Our shaykh used to say: ʿUmar was of those who had absolute hearing, by which Allah speaks to them in everything. But it has titles: if they respond to Him with it, Exalted is He, it is a hadith (ḥadīth); if they respond to Him with themselves, it is a conversation (muhadatha); and if they hear His speech, Glorified is He, it is not a hadith in regard to them, but rather an address (khitab) or a word (kalam).

It has come in regard to those who pray at night that they are the people of nocturnal conversation (musamara). You know that revelation (wahy) is what Allah, Exalted is He, casts into the hearts of the elect among His servants in the manner of speech (hadith), so that knowledge of some matter comes to them from it. If it is not like this, it is neither revelation nor address. For some people find in their hearts knowledge of some matter like the necessary knowledge (ʿulum darurriyya) among people. This is sound knowledge, but it does not proceed from an address. Our discussion concerns the divine address, which is called revelation. For Allah, Exalted is He, made this kind of revelation a speech through which the one who receives it gains knowledge.

Know that there descends upon the hearts of the saints, from the revelation of inspiration (ilham), only subtle emanations extended from the angelic spirits, not the essence of the angels, for the angel does not descend with revelation to anyone other than a prophet at all, nor does he command any divine command with certainty, because the Shariʿa has been firmly established. Only the revelation of glad tidings (mubashshirat) remains, and this is the more general revelation. It comes from the Truth to the servant without an intermediary, and it also comes through an intermediary. Prophethood requires intermediation, so the angel must be an intermediary in it. But the angel does not appear at the time of casting, unlike the prophets, peace be upon them, who see the angel at the time of speech. The saint does not witness the angel except outside the time of casting. If he hears the angel's speech, he does not see him, and if he sees him, he does not speak to him. The gnostics (ʿarifun) do not attain what they have missed of prophethood, though the glad tidings remain upon them, except that people differ in rank. Among them is one who never leaves the glad tidings through the intermediary, and among them is one who rises above it, like the solitaries (afrad), for they have the glad tidings through the removal of intermediaries, but not prophethood. For this reason rulings are denied them, because they resemble the prophets in that they know by what they see of the Truth's definitions for them, as if it were an independent law outwardly, though it is not a law but an explanation of it. What has ended is only the revelation of legislation (tashrīʿ), and nothing else. As for definition of general matters in the Sunna, it remains for this community, so that they may be upon insight in what they call people to, for it is a divine report, and reports from Allah, Exalted is He, to the servant through the hand of an unseen angel, upon this inspired one. Inspiration is never except toward good. And ﴿He inspired it its wickedness﴾ means inspiring it to avoid that, just as its inspiration of piety is so that it may act by it. The most perfect inspiration is that one is inspired to follow the Law, to reflect on the divine books, and to stop at their limits and commands, until the echo of one's nature disappears and the forms of the world are effaced from them. As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿or from behind a veil﴾,

[Page 63]

(...) ...veil. This is a divine address that He casts upon the hearing, not upon the heart, so that whoever it is cast upon perceives it and understands from it what the one who hears it is meant to understand. It may also happen to him in the form of a manifestation (tajalli), where that form addresses him, and that form is the very veil; he understands from that address the knowledge of what it indicates, and he knows that this is a veil and that the Speaker is behind that veil. Whoever perceives the form of the divine manifestation knows that it is Allah, the Exalted, and the state of this person does not exceed others except through his knowing that the One addressing him is behind the veil.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿or He sends a messenger﴾, it refers to what the angel brings down, or what the human messenger brings to us, when they relay the Speech of Allah, the Exalted, specifically, like the reciters. But if they relay a knowledge that they found within themselves and expressed, then that is not divine speech. Among the friends of Allah (awliya') there are those who are given the rendering (tarjamah) from Allah, glorified is He, at the time of the casting and the revelation specific to each person; so the translator brings into existence the forms of the verbal or written letters, and the spirit of those forms is the Speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and nothing else. The walī may say: "My heart related to me from my Lord," meaning by it from a special aspect. So know this, and reflect upon what I have established for you, for it is precious, and Allah, the Exalted, takes charge of your guidance.

He, may his secret be sanctified, has much speech on this station which we have left out for fear of prolixity, and perhaps what we have mentioned is sufficient for people of understanding. ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾, which is that by which there is the good, eternal life, ﴿you did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ before the revelation.

It was said: by this revelation is indicated the revelation in this created existence (nash'ah), and for him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, in every one of his states within it there was a kind of revelation and a knowledge (dirayah) that is negated, since he, peace be upon him, was in his essential being (kaynunah) and before his being brought out of it, through the manifestation of the Mighty and Majestic's essential being. Otherwise, he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, was a prophet when there was neither Adam, nor water, nor clay, and a prophet cannot reason without revelation. ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾, which is the sound monotheism (tawhid) free from the corners of others (aghyar). His, the Exalted's, saying alludes to this: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned﴾. The surah is completed by the success of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and blessings and peace upon the first light that shone forth from the sun of pre-eternity (azal), and to Him belongs all praise, the Exalted.
